The table shown is the “Input Description” from the ELLA Extended Live Load Analysis manual (Service Pack 2025-4, Build 146). It enumerates all of the keyword‐based input records (or commands) that the program will accept, grouped in logical sequence. Below is a structured, detailed narrative description suitable for indexing in a RAG vector store:

1.   Overview  
     •  Purpose: Defines the syntax and semantics of every input record needed to drive an ELLA analysis.  
     •  Scope: Covers general controls, lane geometry, influence‐line creation, graphical output, action and load‐case definition, plus a comprehensive suite of train‐load libraries.

2.   General Control Records  
     3.1 Input Language  
         – Selects the language of prompts and error messages.  
     3.2 Input Records  
         – Describes record format conventions (fixed/free field, continuation rules).  
     3.3 ECHO  
         – Controls the extent of input data echoed into the output listing.  
     3.4 CTRL  
         – Global control parameters (precision, step‐size, verbosity).

3.   Lane Geometry  
     3.5 Definition of the Lane Geometry  
         – High‐level record to initiate lane definitions.  
     3.6 GAX – Geometry of an Axis  
         – Specifies straight lines, circular arcs or clothoids for a lane centerline.  
     3.7 LANE – Width of Traffic Lanes  
         – Assigns lane widths relative to the axis.  
     3.8 LSEL – Selection of a Defined Lane  
         – Chooses one lane for subsequent operations.

4.   Influence Area and Line Generation  
     3.9 Calculation of Influence Areas (CALC)  
         – Computes influence surfaces (requires static stiffness data).  
     3.10 CALC – Evaluation of Influence Areas  
         – Post‐processing and interpolation of the computed influence areas.  
     3.11 LINF – Influence Lines  
         – Generates 1D influence lines along lanes.  
     3.12 APPL – Control of the Loading Location  
         – Defines start/stop points for moving loads on the lane axis.  

5.   Graphical and Listing Output  
     3.13 SIZE – Graphic Representation of Influence Lines  
         – Sets scaling factors and plotting windows.  
     3.14 SHOW – Representation of Influence Lines  
         – Toggles line types, colors, labels for plots.

6.   Action and Load‐Case Definition  
     3.15 ACT – Definition of an Action  
         – Names and parameterizes a load action (e.g. vertical, moment).  
     3.16 LC – Train Load Loading Case  
         – Groups one or more actions to form a loading scenario.

7.   Train‐Load Definitions (TRAI)  
     3.17 TRAI – Load Train Definition  
         – Master record for defining a moving‐load train.  
         •  3.17.1 Impact Factor – Specifies dynamic allowance or amplification.  
         •  3.17.2 Centrifugal Forces – Applies lateral loads from curving.  
         •  3.17.3 Eurocode Trains – Predefined axle patterns per EN 1991-2.  
         •  3.17.4 SLW & LKW – Standard load trains (Swiss, German norms).  
         •  3.17.5 BS 5400, TMH7 – British code load trains.  
         •  3.17.6 Heavy Trains (BS 5400, TMH7, IS 1227) – Elevated axle loads.  
         •  3.17.7 AASHTO Live Loads – U.S. bridge loading configurations.  
         •  3.17.8 CAN/CSA Trains – Canadian railway service.  
         •  3.17.9 IRC 6-2000 – Indian Road Congress standard.  
         •  3.17.10 JRA Trains – Japanese Road Association patterns.  
         •  3.17.11 AS 5100 – Australian railway loads.  
         •  3.17.12 Swedish BRO 2004 – Nordic prescriptions.  
         •  3.17.13 French Load Trains – NF standards.  
         •  3.17.14 Railway Train Loads – Generic rail traffic models.  
         •  3.17.15 NATO (Stanag 2021) – Military strategic loads.

8.   Subsequent Evaluation Records  
     3.18 TRPL – Point Load of Load Train  
         – Defines a single‐axle (point) load element.  
     3.19 TRBL – Block Load of Load Train  
         – Defines contiguous block loads (tandem or bogie).  
     3.20 SAVE – Saving Case for an Evaluation  
         – Writes out selected results for later combination.  
     3.21 CASE – Evaluation Case  
         – Assembles saved influence cases into an envelope.  
     3.22 POSL – Position of the Load Trains for an Evaluation  
         – Optimizes load positions for maximum effects.  
     3.23 COMB – Intermediate Combination of Evaluations  
         – Allows superposition of multiple envelopes.

This narrative captures the hierarchical structure, purpose and interdependencies of each input record. It can be used to index ELLA’s input capabilities, guide query‐based retrieval, and support automated help systems or “smart” input assistants.

 1 Task Description
 ELLA is a program for the analysis and evaluation of imposed loads that acts on spatial beam or shell structures in the form of load trains which move along certain traffic lanes. The envelopes of the scalar variables for the entire structure are usually the result. In the case of simple statical systems and simple load cases a traditional analysis of the system can be faster for a large number of imposed load cases under circumstances. The evaluation of influence lines or influence surfaces becomes necessary for an accurate analysis of larger systems, as they are usual particularly in the bridge construction. It is not so simple to determine either the most unfavourable load position or the used parts of a load in order to maximize the certain internal forces for important parts of the structure outside its midspan. In addition, different load positions are critical for the different internal forces and moments. The evaluation of the influence lines reduces the extent of the input very significantly.
 The entire surface of a structure at which imposed loads act gets divided into straight or curved lanes of variable width. Any load trains can be assigned to each lane. They can move indepen- dently or in relation to each other. The traffic lanes are defined with axes which may contain circular segments or clothoids. The loading refers always to the lane axis. An influence line is generated for a vertical loading along the lane’s axis for each lane as well as for a moment loading about the same axis due to the eccentrical parts. Additional influence lines for brake or centrifugal loading can be considered upon request.
 The program evaluates influence lines only for corresponding traffic lanes even in the case of plane structures. However, a satisfactory representation of the two-dimensional effects can be achieved for the available element distribution by partitioning the structure into multiple lanes. The influence surfaces can be either transferred from the database or determined as a rule with a calculation with an own static module of the influence line program.
 In the second case, however, all the single element stiffnesses as well as the stiffness matrix of the entire structure must be available. This requires that at least one load case has been anal- ysed with the programs ASE or STAR2 with option CTRL SOLV 1 or 3, and the corresponding data is still available. Load cases with settlement of support or non-linear load cases are not suitable for this.

Influence lines can be calculated with two completely different methods. The first method deter- mines the deformations (e.g. bending line) due to an unit deformation for the searched internal force (e.g. a break for a moment). The bending area is the result of a static analysis with an appropriate program. A load case defines always one influence area. Corresponding areas are own load cases in each case. This method should be preferred when only a few influence areas or particular variables are to be calculated (e.g. support reactions, deformations or sums of scalar variables).
 When a large number of influence lines of the structure has to be calculated with this method, an own load case will have to be analysed for each cross section and for each internal force. This procedure exceeds usually the available CPU time and memory capacities of the static programs.

The second method works in opposite manner. A unit load is defined at each position (node or member cross section). The analysis determines all the other corresponding internal forces. The main advantage of this method is that the single loads do not have to be applied at every loading location. The missing intermediate values can be calculated easily with an interpola- tion, if the known discontinuities at loading location (break, jump) are considered additionally. Therefore, the number of load cases to be analysed can be reduced significantly.
 In the case of plane structures the discontinuity is defined by means of a singularity. This singularity does not result from a finite element analysis in principal. However we have a smooth approximate influence function which may be used to derive the principal problem of precision in a Finite-Element-Analysis very clearly (see Hartmann/Katz - Structural Analysis with Finite Elements, Springer). This should be considered particularly in the case of shear forces!

The image is a black-and-white line drawing composed of two side-by-side schematics, each illustrating the same vertical truck load acting on a two-girder bridge, but with the eccentricity represented in two alternative ways. A single vertical centreline (a heavy vertical line topped by a double-arrowhead symbol) runs through both subfigures to emphasize the reference axis about which eccentricity is measured. Underneath the pair of diagrams is the caption “Figure 2.1: Eccentric lane and eccentric load.”

Left Subfigure (Lane 1, “Eccentric Lane”):  
• At the top, a simplified plan view of a truck load appears as a filled rectangle resting on two narrow rectangular projections (representing the wheel positions). The long axis of the truck is aligned exactly with the vertical centreline.  
• Directly beneath, a two-girder cross‐section is shown in elevation: a T-shaped beam (horizontal flange on top, vertical web below) is drawn to the left of the same vertical centreline.  
• A horizontal dimension line, labelled “a,” spans from the right-hand edge of the T-beam flange to the vertical centreline, with small arrowheads at each end and datum tick marks at the beam flange and the centreline. This indicates that the lane (i.e. the pair of girders) is offset by a distance a to one side of the load’s centreline.  
• The label “Lane 1” is placed just below the truck and girder assembly, centrally between the two elements.

Right Subfigure (Lane 2, “Eccentric Load”):  
• Again, the same truck-load rectangle with its paired wheel-like projections is drawn, but here it is displaced horizontally so that the two‐girder T-beam section lies directly beneath the vertical centreline. In other words, the girders are now “under” the centreline, and the load has shifted by the same distance a to one side of that axis.  
• The T-beam cross section is now shown immediately below the vertical centreline, with no dimension line on this sketch (implicit is that the load is a to one side of the centreline).  
• The label “Lane 2” appears below this arrangement, signalling that in this case the lane itself is centered, while the load is eccentric by distance a.

Overall Purpose of the Figure:  
• These two diagrams together demonstrate the equivalence of modelling a single, vertical load as either an eccentric lane (subfigure “Lane 1”) or an eccentric load (subfigure “Lane 2”).  
• In both cases the vertical load and the torsional moment imparted to the girders about their shear centre are identical, because the moment arm in each scenario is the same distance a.  
• The figure supports the textual discussion that for single loads on a two-girder bridge (or an articulated load distribution), one may simplify the analysis by choosing whichever representation—eccentric lane or eccentric load—is more convenient, knowing they yield the same internal effects (vertical shear and torsional moment).

Stylistically, both schematics use simple orthographic projection, clear centrelines, and minimal labelling to focus attention on the horizontal offset a. The rectangular load block and the T-beam cross section are rendered in solid lines of uniform thickness, ensuring easy identification of the load, the bridge elements, and the critical dimension.

The illustration is a schematic cross-section of a T-shaped girder (a flange at the top and a vertical stem below) together with two “lanes” of uniformly distributed wheel loads partitioned about the section’s shear centre.  From top to bottom and left to right the drawing contains the following key elements:

1. Overall Girder Geometry  
   • A horizontal top flange, drawn as a thick rectangular block, representing the wide part of the T-section.  
   • A vertical stem (the web) extending downward from the middle of the flange, forming the T shape.  
   • All lines are hand-sketched with consistent stroke thickness to emphasize structural members.

2. Shear-Centre Marker  
   • On the vertical stem, below the flange, sits a small filled circle with a cross (or “target”) inside it.  
   • This symbol locates the shear centre of the cross-section, the point through which applied transverse loads produce no twisting.

3. Central Lane Axis  
   • A straight vertical line passes upward through the shear-centre marker and continues well above the flange.  
   • At its top end is a double-arrowed symbol (two opposing single-arrow heads), indicating an idealized traffic “lane” axis of constant width.  
   • Next to this line, the word “Lane” is printed to emphasize that this axis represents the centreline of wheel paths.

4. Partitioned Distributed Loads  
   • Two rectangular, hatched blocks—each with vertical shading lines—depict uniformly distributed wheel loads applied to the slab or deck slab above the girder.  
   • Arrows at the lower edge of each block point downward, indicating the direction of load transfer to the girder.  
   • Left-Hand Load Block:  
     – Smaller in length, attached by a short perpendicular bar to the lane axis, but entirely on the left side of the vertical axis.  
     – Represents the portion of the standard road load carried at the left side of the shear centre.  
   • Right-Hand Load Block:  
     – Longer in length (approximately spanning the entire flange width), attached directly at flange level, with part of it again lying to the right of the central axis.  
     – Represents the larger share of the distributed load acting to the right of the shear-centre.

5. Caption  
   • Beneath the sketch is the label: “Partition of the distributed loads at the shear centre.”  
   • This emphasizes that the total uniformly distributed traffic load has been split into two eccentric components—one on each side of the shear-centre—for subsequent vertical‐and‐torsional moment analysis.

Together, the graphic visualizes how a continuous traffic loading band (the “lane”) is resolved into two concentrated distributed‐load strips on either side of the shear centre.  Such a partition allows the engineer to calculate the resulting vertical shear and the torsional moment (due to load eccentricity) on the girder more efficiently, by treating each strip as acting at its own eccentric position relative to the section’s shear‐centre.

The figure (labelled “Figure 2.3: Distribution two longitudinal girders”) is laid out in three horizontal bands:

1. Upper band – geometry and lane location  
 • A simple bridge‐deck cross-section is shown in elevation. On the left, a T-section represents one of the longitudinal girders; farther to the right, two narrow vertical lines represent the two main girders supporting the deck slab.  
 • Above the slab a rectangular footprint (the vehicle or wheel load) straddles the centre of the deck and is annotated “Lane 1.”  
 • Along the slab underside three span segments are indicated by short break symbols and dimensioned “a,” “3a” and “a,” showing the loaded lane is centred in the midspan region (span length = 5a in total).

2. Middle band – load splitting for a centrally placed lane (Lane 1)  
 • Directly beneath the loaded area there is a single downward‐pointing arrow attached to the slab, labelled “0.8 P.”  
 • A text call-out at left reads “Lane 1: ↓ 0.8 P,” indicating that when the load P is applied in the central lane, 80 percent of P is taken by the nearer girder (the one on the right in this sketch), and the remaining 20 percent by the opposite girder (not explicitly drawn here).

3. Lower band – load and moment splitting for an eccentric lane (Lane 2)  
 • Here the same total load P is assumed to lie off-centre (labelled “Lane 2”). Three items are shown beneath the slab:  
   – A small downward arrow under the left girder labelled “0.2 P.”  
   – A second bigger arrow under the left girder (closer to midspan) labelled “0.6 P.”  
   – A third arrow, directly beneath the vehicle footprint but to the right of centre, labelled “P.” This represents the entire vertical load on the near girder when placed eccentrically.  
 • To the right of that arrow is a curved, half-circle arrow sweeping about the slab’s centroidal axis, annotated “3a P.” This symbolizes the torsional moment generated by the eccentricity (moment arm = 3a times the vertical load P).  
 • Finally, another downward arrow under the right girder is labelled “0.8 P.” Together, the combination of the direct load P plus the moment P·3a resolves into new force components on the two girders (e.g. 0.6 P and 0.8 P), demonstrating up to a 20 percent difference in distribution compared with the centred case.

Key points conveyed by the sketch:  
 • A centrally applied wheel load on a two-girder bridge will split roughly 80 / 20 between the two girders.  
 • If the same load is placed in an adjacent (eccentric) lane, the torsional lever arm (3a) produces a twisting moment, altering the vertical force share on each girder.  
 • Under an articulated (deformable) distribution, both scenarios yield an identical split once the moment correction is applied. Under a rigid distribution, however, up to 20 percent difference can arise.  
 • This simple diagram underpins the text’s advice that for planar shell or slab bridges—where single‐moment loading and eccentricities can produce larger errors—it is safer to use a full transverse influence‐line evaluation rather than approximate eccentric loads.

The image is a schematic, labelled “Figure 2.4: Correct load distribution for three longitudinal girders,” which illustrates how a single concentrated load P (acting in a traffic lane) is shared among three parallel girders. The drawing is arranged in two primary parts, one above the other:

1. Upper diagram (plan/elevation of girders and loading):  
   • A straight horizontal datum line represents the reference axis along which three T-beam cross-sections (the longitudinal girders) are positioned.  
   • From left to right, the spacing between the first and second girder is marked “a,” again “a” between the second and third, and finally “2a” beyond the third. These dimensions denote the centre-to-centre distances of the support girders and illustrate a non-uniform layout (the last span being twice as large).  
   • The three girders themselves are drawn as T-shaped sections sitting on the datum line.  
   • Directly above the middle girder (i.e. at the second girder’s location) a symbolic vehicle or load platform—shown as a small rectangular box supported on two vertical stanchions—applies a vertical load to that girder. A solid‐filled circle at the underside of the box indicates the point of application of the load P (the shear centre of the carriage or wheel load).  
   • A short downward line from that circle meets the top flange of the middle T-section, signifying that the entire load P is initially applied at that single girder.

2. Lower diagram (resulting forces on individual girders):  
   • Two isolated T-sections (without the third) are drawn side by side and each carries a downward arrow labelled “0.5 P.”  
   • This reduction to two girders emphasizes that, after distribution under the assumptions of rigid torsional and vertical blending, only the two outer girders share the applied load equally (each takes one-half).  
   • The absence of a load arrow on the central T-section here implies that, in the final distribution model, it carries negligible direct vertical load—the torsional moment caused by eccentricity shifts the vertical reactions onto the two flanking girders.

Caption: Beneath these sketches sits the legend “Figure 2.4: Correct load distribution for three longitudinal girders.”

Contextual relevance:  
• The diagram concretely demonstrates the concept that, for three-girder systems under rigid load distribution, a lane-centered vertical load need not be borne solely by the girder immediately beneath but instead divides between adjacent members via an equivalent eccentricity moment.  
• The notated spacings (a, a, 2a) underscore that the relative lateral positions of lanes and girders affect how moments and vertical forces are partitioned.  
• In line with the accompanying text, the figure shows that when a load and its designated lane coincide in the same span region, a simple “two-girders share half-and-half” rule can apply—provided the structural behaviour approximates rigid torsional response.  
• It also subtly warns that in finite-element or shell/slab analyses (where neighbours lie farther apart or eccentricity complicates local moments), this simplistic half-load assignment may no longer be sufficiently accurate, and a transverse influence-line approach becomes necessary.

Overall, the image visually encapsulates the principle that a single eccentric vertical load in a three-girder bridge or deck can be represented by two equal “0.5 P” reactions on the flanking girders, with the central girder effectively unloaded, given the rigid distribution assumption.

The image is a two‐part schematic (labelled “Figure 2.5: Wrong load distribution for three longitudinal girders”) illustrating how an eccentric vertical wheel load and its associated torsional moment get (incorrectly) apportioned among three parallel girders.  

Top view (common to both parts)  
• A straight, continuous deck or loading strip is shown as a horizontal line supported at five equally spaced points. Each span between supports is marked “a.”  
• Over the rightmost span a concentrated wheel load P acts downward at an offset from the strip’s shear center. Because of that offset the load also generates a clockwise torsional moment M = 2 α P about the shear center.  

Lower half – two side‐by‐side cross‐sectional load diagrams  
Left diagram (central girder)  
1. Below the deck line, a label “moment M” is aligned with a downward arrow of magnitude 1.0 P, representing the portion of the torsional moment translated into an equivalent vertical force on this girder.  
2. A second label “load P” sits next to a smaller downward arrow of magnitude 0.5 P, representing the fraction of the direct vertical load assigned to the central girder.  
3. At the level of the girder’s T‐section (shown as a vertical stem with a horizontal flange), these two contributions combine into a single “resulting force” arrow of 1.5 P pointing downward.  

Right diagram (outer girder)  
1. The “moment M” arrow here is reversed or of opposite sign, canceling part of the vertical load on this girder. The label “0.0 P” shows that no direct wheel load is carried here.  
2. A small upward arrow (magnitude 0.5 P) indicates the moment‐equivalent vertical force acting upward on this girder.  
3. Below the T‐section, the “resulting force” arrow points upward, illustrating that this girder is incorrectly taken into tension rather than in downward compression.  

Taken together, the two diagrams expose the flaw in simply converting an eccentric load and its torsion into vertical forces on individual girders: the sum of the forces no longer equals the original P and net moment, and one of the three girders ends up with an unphysical uplift. This highlights why, in multi‐girder arrangements, eccentric lane loads must be handled with proper influence‐line or finite‐element methods rather than by crude moment‐to‐vertical‐force conversions.

The loaded traffic area is defined by lanes with a traffic band of constant width and residual areas. Loads will be defined within a lane, but can move arbitrarily along the lane and in some cases also across the traffic band.
 In order to accelerate the evaluation, the loads are simplified within a lane by a vertical loading and a torsional moment due to the eccentric position of the vertical load. Thus the description by means of an eccentric lane or an eccentric load is equivalent for single loads.
 Most of the standard road loadings are internally partitioned into loads at the left-hand side and at the right-hand side of the shear centre. The location of which is automatically determined from the influence values for torsional and vertical loading.
 In the case of two girders and articulated load distribution the result is the same, if the loading is placed centrically at lane 1 or eccentric with respect to lane 2. The eccentricity moment
 offers the necessary correction for the distribution of the loading at the longitudinal girders:
 However, great differences are already available in this case for rigid load distribution. An eccentricity should be then only relatively small. Here up to 20 percent deviations would result in the distribution between the two variants.
 In the case of three or more girders the results can be very different as the next two figures show. It can be stated as a rule that both the load and the lane must be located in the same span region in terms of the lateral behaviour of the structure.
 Different results are always obtained in FE structures, when load and lane are not at the same or neighboring elements. The deviations of the results are negligible in the neighbouring ele- ment, but they increase of course as the distance between lane and load increases. As the loading of single moments for planar shell or slab structures may lead to further errors, eccen- tricities of loads must not be used for these types of the structure, instead an evaluation with a
 transverse influence line should be used.

The image is a schematic, labelled “Figure 2.6: Interpolation of the influence areas,” that shows how a set of influence-line curves for two parallel girders is interpolated transversely to a reference lane axis. Its main components are:

1. Two irregular, roughly parallel wavy lines (one above and one below) representing the axes or edge-traces of the two girders. Each of these curves is drawn in bold black.  
2. Superimposed on each bold curve is a thinner, nearly parallel curve on both sides, so that in total three slightly offset layers of curve appear above and below. These correspond to three different interpolation grades or methods (INT 0, INT 1, INT 2) of the transverse influence line.  
3. At regular—but not uniform—intervals along each curve, small open circles mark “nodes.” From each node a short straight tick-mark projects perpendicular to the dashed centerline; these illustrate the direction along which interpolation is performed.  
4. A lightly drawn, roughly center-running, dashed line with arrowheads defines the lane axis. At two sample stations along this axis, the perpendicular distance between the axis and the nearest node on one girder is labelled “h,” emphasizing that the offset distance from the center must be measured exactly.  
5. A series of vertical dashed lines (appearing as sampling “slices” or search planes) cut across both girder curves and the centerline. These planes represent the perpendicular cross-sections in which the program locates two node series—one on each girder—in order to carry out the interpolation.  
6. The pattern of circles, ticks, and dashed planes makes it visually clear that the program must identify corresponding node pairs in adjacent girders and then interpolate between them at each cross-section. The irregular placement of nodes along the curving girders underlines the difficulty of automating this process: without a simple, straight geometry, an AI may select incorrect node series unless guided by user-defined sequences.  

Altogether, the figure graphically captures the challenge of generating a smooth, continuous influence line across a multi-girder structure when its actual support axes do not lie exactly beneath the user-defined lane. By overlaying three interpolated curves and marking the perpendicular search directions and offsets, it illustrates how eccentric loads produce torsion (INT 0), how secondary torsion arises from rotational constraints (INT 1), and how fixed deck constraints add yet another torsional effect (INT 2).

3. Right sub-figure (INT = 1, Articulated load distribution)  
   - Deck slab: identical in thickness to the left, drawn as a flat horizontal plate.  
   - Wheel loads: the same pair of small solid squares sit atop the slab, now straddling the centerline.  
   - Nodes: a row of small filled circles marks the slab’s top surface; a matching row sits just below the slab, indicating the nodes through which load is transferred.  
   - Supports: instead of one deep girder, two narrow rectangular columns (representing two girders) sit directly beneath the slab at roughly the wheel‐load positions. These are drawn as simple vertical rectangles.

4. Key distinctions between INT 0 and INT 1  
   - In INT 0, the entire eccentric wheel load acts on a single girder, inducing a primary torsional effect without any jump in the shear‐force influence line at the load location.  
   - In INT 1, the wheel load is effectively split and applied at two girders; torsion arises only secondarily through rotational constraints, and the influence line may exhibit jumps.

Visually, the two sub-figures contrast a monolithic load application (single-girder case) with a discretized, articulated load distribution (two-girder case), illustrating how node selection and interpolation differ when the lane axis does not coincide exactly with defined nodes.

The image is labeled “Figure 2.8: Interpolation Grades” and consists of two side-by-side schematic cross-section sketches of a bridge deck (or girder system), each showing:

1. A rectangular “deck” or “beam” section drawn in thin black lines.  
2. A smooth, upward-curving black line above the beam representing the true transverse influence line of some response quantity (shear, moment or torsion) as a function of lateral position over the deck.  
3. One or more bold red line segments that illustrate how the program approximates (interpolates) the continuous influence line in the vicinity of an eccentrically placed wheel or load lane.  
4. Red circular nodes marking the specific points at which the red interpolation lines meet the true curve.

Detailed breakdown of each panel:

— Left Panel (labeled “INT 0”):  
  • The true influence line (black curve) rises smoothly above the deck toward the right.  
  • A single straight red segment, inclined at roughly the same slope as the black curve, is drawn over the entire width of the deck.  
  • A single red dot marks the point where this red line intersects the black curve.  
  • No discontinuities or kinks appear in the red line; it is a one-shot, linear‐fit interpolation of the curve.  
  • This corresponds to interpolation type 0, in which an eccentric load directly produces a torsional moment and the shear‐force influence line remains continuous (no jump) under the load.

— Right Panel (labeled “INT 1”):  
  • The same black curve is shown over the identical deck section.  
  • Here the red approximation consists of two straight segments joined at an interior point (another red dot) on the curve and ending at a red dot at the far right top corner of the deck.  
  • On the far left, a short horizontal red segment sits just above the deck’s top flange, then rises in a second segment to meet the right-hand node.  
  • The red line now has a visible “kink,” representing a jump in the transverse influence line at the load location.  
  • This is interpolation type 1, where the eccentric wheel load is replaced by two concentrated forces at the girders. The resulting torsional effects appear only secondarily, so the influence line may exhibit discontinuities; this is often the most accurate approach for plane‐structure meshes (e.g. using Mindlin elements).

Although not shown here, a third variant (INT 2) would add further segments (and jumps) to account for torsional restraint from a fixed deck slab. Together, these sketches illustrate how the inverse‐principle of influence lines can be viewed as increasing “interpolation grades” in the transverse direction: from a simple single‐segment linear fit (INT 0), to a two‐segment piecewise fit (INT 1), up to still higher order fits when rotational constraints are fully enforced (INT 2).

When the lane axis does not coincide with the defined nodes, the values of the influence line
 must be interpolated. The program searches then for two series of nodes in the direct vicinity of the lane and interpolates perpendicularly to its axis.
 The selection of a neighboring node series is trivial for plane structures. For girders, however, it is in general a problem for the artificial intelligence. It is extremely difficult for a program to develop the human ability of the general overview. Therefore, this part of the program can not execute in a uniquely determined way. A specific constellation not being recognized correctly can occur again and again. The user must take a proper action in such cases by defining a sequence of nodes or beam elements.
 For the interpolation perpendicularly to the lane axis a distinction must be done very exactly between three variations that result from different types of the load distribution:
 In the first case (INT 0) an eccentrically placed loading generates directly a torsional moment. The influence line of the shear force for the effect of the eccentric influence has no jump in the loading location.
 In the second case (INT 1) the load is replaced by two forces that act at the two girders. The torsional moments result only as a secondary phenomenon due to the constraint of the rotations. The influence line for the effect of the eccentricity may include jumps. This is usually the most accurate method for plane structures analysed with Mindlin elements.
 In the third case (INT 2) torsional moments result additionally from the fixed constraint of the deck slab.

Plotted against this baseline are two distinct influence‐line curves, one drawn in red above the baseline and the other in blue below it, each repeated once per span to show two consecutive spans or two load‐application regions:

It reaches zero exactly at the right end of that first span.  This triangular red shape marks the region where a horizontal load applied in the “positive gravity” direction (i.e. braking or wind pushing in the marked travelling direction) produces a positive bending‐moment effect.  
    - Below the baseline in the same span, the blue influence line picks up exactly where the red leaves off.  It starts at zero at the left mid-point, drops to its most negative ordinate just beyond mid-span, and then returns to zero at the right support.  This indicates regions where the same load direction would act unfavourably by producing the opposite sign of bending moment.

    - Immediately to the right of the central support, a second red influence‐line segment shoots up vertically from the baseline to its positive peak and then slopes back down to zero at the far right support.  Graphically it is the mirror of the first red segment but shifted one span over.  
    - Underneath that red peak, the blue line again describes the negative‐sign region: from zero at the left support of span two it jumps downward to its most negative ordinate just past that support, then returns up to zero at the far right end.  

Beneath the entire drawing is the caption “Figure 2.10: Evaluation of Horizontal Loading.”  

Taken together, the two‐span depiction shows how a unidirectional braking or wind load “travels” along consecutive spans, with alternating regions where its contributions to bending moment are either favourable (red, positive) or unfavourable (blue, negative).  In the accompanying text these sign regions are used to determine which load positions must actually be considered in a quick influence‐line evaluation.  Loads acting in positive gravity direction at locations with a positive influence‐line ordinate are classified as unfavourable, vice versa for negative ordinates.  Depending on whether the train is restricted to one travelling direction or may run either way, only the unfavourable portions of these red and blue diagrams are summed to produce the governing bending‐moment effect.

Since each load may use more than one influence line at the same time, a quick evaluation of influence lines is possible only if some assumptions are made about the load positions. ELLA uses also deductional loads, i.e. negative loads, which describe gaps within an uniform traffic band.
 Loads of the load trains are thus considered unfavourable, when a load in the positive gravity direction (downwards) with the same eccentricity at the corresponding point of the influence line would also act unfavourably. Loads that act at regions of the influence line with an opposite sign are considered favourable. This classification decides about the appropriate dynamic factors, the possible use of the reduction factors, and whether the load should be taken into account at all. Horizontal loading will not be included in this decision. However all load directions are considered for the determination of the most unfavourable load position and the final evaluation of the results of cause.
 In order to consider eccentricity effects (eg. torsional loading), the loads may be automatically subdivided if the shear centre is within the width of the lane. However, despite all these fea- tures the user should take care, that the real load situation may be mapped by the load train. Sometimes either the lane axis must be displaced or a secondary lane must be added or the loads must be given explicitly.
 For the evaluation of horizontal loading by braking or wind one has to take care of some more subtle effects. If for example the influence line for a bending moment is taken with respect to the eccentric longitudinal force at the upper deck, we have areas with positive and negative
 values:
 Following remarks should be observed:
 • If the brake load is taken over the total length in the same direction, the contributions will cancel mostly. This kind of loading should be defined as standard load case, but not within ELLA.
 • If the load train has a dedicated travelling direction, only those contributions will be taken into account acting unfavourably, although the design code (e.g. Eurocode) may define the load value by the total, but limited loading in the lane and an overall loaded length. A modification of the load value depending on the loaded length will not occur.

• If the load train has a dedicated travelling direction, only those contributions will be taken into account acting unfavourably, although the design code (e.g. Eurocode) may define the load value by the total, but limited loading in the lane and an overall loaded length. A modification of the load value depending on the loaded length will not occur..
 • If the load train is allowed to travel in any direction, all contributions will be summed up with their unfavourable sign. Thus the areas with the wrong sign will either have traffic in the opposite direction or acceleration forces are effective. Although the Eurocode specifies this possibility only for the total load value, this approach will also compensate for the missing effect of the adoption of the load value to the loaded length from the remark above.

For the load trains there are cases where the load train should be applied in total only or where parts of the load train may be deactivated. This will be controlled by a factor for favorable loading for every load element. Then the distinction has to be made between the cases of a loading which is always present (e.g. cranes) and those where the load may leave the system. But as the resulting forces and moments have to be superimposed with permanent loads, this decision may be postponed until then.
 The most unfavourable load position is sought with a three-stage method. In a first step some typical load patterns are positioned at different locations perpendicular to the traffic axis. This may be done with a transverse influence line (LSEL INT>2) or based on simple mechanics of a lever.
 In a second step the load train is placed at selected positions which either the program selects itself or the user prescribes with POSL. Variable lengths or convoys of loading are estimated separately with a simple method. The lengths of the positive loads are set always equal to their maximum value, whereas negative loads are placed in such a way that their influence value at the end of the load is the largest possible.
 In a third step the most unfavourable value of all analyzed positions keeps on being examined for local extreme values. That means the load train positions and all lengths are varied until
 the most unfavourable position is found.
 A special hint should be given to the Culmann load position. For two adjacent loads the most unfavourable moment is obtained when the larger force and the resultant of the two loads are symmetric to the mid of the span.  The program uses a dynamic working memory which is used mainly for the storage of the values needed for the influence lines. An equation for the necessary memory can not be given, yet the in fact used size can be printed with ECHO STAT. Thus the amount of reserved memory may be specified after PROG ELLA with a parameter Mnnn, where nnn is the size of the memory in millions of 4-byte words. As a very high request will slow down the virtual memory performance, the optimum value has to be found individually.
 The program is executed mostly in a uniquely determined way. There are, however, two types of problems for which a unique solution does not exist or can not be found by the program under circumstances. These are:

 • Load trains with variable length In the case of load trains with loads of variable length the whole problem may become very complex. One should use so few changeable lengths as possible. In addition the user should define first the lengths which have the most significant effects. In the case of doubt it is better to define more evaluation cases with fixed load lengths.

        – “LOC” = local beam axes,  
        – “COR=n” = use coordinate system #n.  
    •  SMIN – “Load Start Abscissa.”  Real fraction (0 ≤ SMIN ≤ 1) of element length where the load begins (default = 0).  
    •  SMAX – “Load End Abscissa.”  Real fraction (0 ≤ SMAX ≤ 1) of element length where the load ends (default = 1).  
    •  DEL  – “Discretization or Increment.”  Real or integer: segment length for load subdivision or explicit number of segments.  Used for integration refinement.  
    •  YEX  – “Local‐Y Eccentricity.”  Real offset in the local y‐direction giving an eccentric line of action (default = 0).  
    •  V    – “Variation Law.”  Character code defining intensity variation along the span:  
        – “CON” = constant,  
        – “LIN” = linear,  
        – “PAR” = parabolic,  
        – “TRI” = triangular.  
    •  P    – “Load Intensity.”  Real magnitude (force per length or force per area).  Can be a single value (CON) or two values (LIN: start/end, PAR: mid‐value).

3.  Format and Field Positioning  
    •  Fixed‐column input.  Each record name occupies columns 1–4, followed by data fields in prescribed column ranges.  
    •  Numeric fields are in free or E‐format; character options are in quoted strings or alphanumeric columns.

4.  Typical Workflow  
    a) Issue a HEAD record to open the load section (see manual).  
    b) List one line per distinct position list (POSL) tying nodes/elements to loads.  
    c) Follow with lines giving NO, TRAI, FACT, …, P to fully describe magnitude and distribution.  
    d) Close with END and optionally PAGE to continue on the next print/output page.

5.  Semantic Relationships  
    •  SMIN/SMAX delimit the span over which FACT × P is applied.  
    •  DEL and V together control numerical integration of the variable load law.  
    •  OPT may override the local/global axis in which YEX and P are resolved.

By extracting each field’s name, data type, default value, allowed range or code list and positional format, you can embed these definitions in a RAG‐based vector store so that downstream agents (e.g. query bots or code generators) can precisely reconstruct a valid SOFiSTiK input deck for distributed loads.

Below is a structured breakdown of the TABLE snippet you provided, suitable for ingestion into a RAG‐style vector store. We focus on the single record type shown (COMB) and its seven “item” fields; in the broader context of SOFiSTiK FEA‐STRUCTURAL input, the other record types (POSL, NO, TRAI, FACT, OPT, SMIN, SMAX, DEL, YEX, V, P) would be handled analogously, while HEAD/END/PAGE are covered elsewhere in the manual.

1.  Record name  
    •  COMB  
    – This is the only record shown in your snippet.  COMB defines a linear combination of load or results cases.  

2.  Item fields (columns)  
    The record COMB comprises seven slots, in this exact order:  
    •  SYNC  
    •  PLON  
    •  PTRA  
    •  FUGA  
    •  IMPA  
    •  EXCE  
    •  EXTR  

3.  First “parameter‐alias” row  
    Directly under the item headers you see a row of short codes, which in SOFiSTiK syntax are simply positional aliases or flags—this row does ​not​ consume one of the ten combination lines.  
    •  Under SYNC ▶ V  
    •  Under PLON ▶ P  
    •  Under PTRA ▶ SYNC  
    •  Under FUGA, IMPA, EXCE, EXTR ▶ (all blank)  

    Interpretation:  
    – V toggles “synchronous” processing of the COMB record.  
    – P is a PLOt-related pointer.  
    – The repeated SYNC under PTRA is a legacy synonym.  

4.  Combination‐line template row  
    The next row is headed by TYPE in the SYNC column.  It establishes the alternating pattern of “load‐case identifier” (Li) and “factor” (Fi) pairs:  

    SYNC: TYPE  
    PLON: L1  
    PTRA: F1  
    FUGA: L2  
    IMPA: F2  
    EXCE: L3  
    EXTR: F3  

    – Here “L1,F1” constitutes the first combination line, “L2,F2” the second, and “L3,F3” the third.  

5.  Additional combination lines  
    COMB supports up to ten Li‐Fi pairs.  Following the template row, three more rows continue the pattern:  

    Row 3:  
      SYNC ▶ L4  
      PLON ▶ F4  
      PTRA ▶ (blank)  
      FUGA ▶ L5  
      IMPA ▶ F5  
      EXCE ▶ L6  
      EXTR ▶ F6  

    Row 4:  
      SYNC ▶ L7  
      PLON ▶ F7  
      PTRA ▶ L8  
      FUGA ▶ F8  
      IMPA ▶ (blank)  
      EXCE ▶ L9  
      EXTR ▶ F9  

    Row 5:  
      SYNC ▶ L10  
      PLON ▶ F10  
      PTRA…EXTR ▶ (all blank)  

    – Any unused trailing slots remain empty.  
    – If you only need, say, five combinations, you would populate L1–L5 and F1–F5, leaving the rest blank.  

6.  Semantic summary  
    •  COMB (SYNC,PLON,PTRA,FUGA,IMPA,EXCE,EXTR)  
      – The first “alias row” (V,P,SYNC) sets record‐level flags.  
      – The TYPE row defines the alternating Li–Fi pattern.  
      – Up to ten (Li,Fi) lines may follow in groups of two fields each.  

7.  How this ties into a RAG vector store  
    •  Entities: COMB record (ID=“COMB”)  
    •  Attributes:  
       – Flags: V (synchronous), P (plot)  
       – Pattern: TYPE → [L1,F1],…,[L10,F10]  
    •  Relationships: each Li references a load or result case; each Fi is the scalar factor.  

In your RAG index you would break this out into triplets such as:  
•  (COMB, has_item_order, [SYNC→PLON→PTRA→FUGA→IMPA→EXCE→EXTR])  
•  (COMB, flag_SYNC, V)  
•  (COMB, alias_PLON, P)  
•  (COMB, combination_line_1, (L1,F1)) … (COMB, combination_line_10, (L10,F10))  

All other record types you mentioned (POSL, NO, TRAI, …, P) follow the same pattern of “record name + ordered fields + per‐field semantics,” and HEAD/END/PAGE are documented in the main SOFiSTiK “Installation and Basics” manual.

This table defines the two keyword-argument fields that control the volume and type of output generated by the ECHO record in your analysis input. Every ECHO record must begin with the literal “ECHO” so that its options cannot be confused with other records of the same name. The subsequent items, OPT and VAL, are both literal strings (unit “LIT”) and each has a default value indicated by “*” (see the hint below).  

1. Item: OPT  
 • Description: Selects which categories of results are printed or displayed.  You must supply one of these literal values:  
  – LANE  Lane geometry data  
  – IL   Influence lines (usually as diagrams; see EXTR below for textual output)  
  – LOAD  Load‐train definitions and positions  
  – EVAL  Evaluation cases (generated load cases)  
  – LPOS  Load positions (actual positions used in each evaluation)  
  – RES   Results (intermediate or final results)  
  – FULL  All of the above categories (equivalent to specifying LANE, IL, LOAD, EVAL, LPOS and RES together)  
  – STAT  CPU time and memory‐allocation statistics  
 • Unit: LIT (literal keyword)  
 • Default: “*” (see hint below)  

2. Item: VAL  
 • Description: Controls how much detail is printed for each of the OPT categories.  Choose exactly one of:  
  – OFF  No calculation, no output at all  
  – NO  Calculation proceeds but no printed output  
  – YES  Regular (default) output  
  – FULL  Extensive output (every detail)  
  – EXTR  Extreme output (very verbose)  
 • Unit: LIT  
 • Default: “*”  

Hint on defaults and interactions:  
• If you omit the entire ECHO record, or list “ECHO” with no OPT/VAL, the system sets OPT = LANE, IL, LOAD, LPOS, RES (all to YES) and sets EVAL = NO, STAT = NO.  
• If you supply “ECHO” followed by OPT or VAL but leave out the corresponding VAL or OPT, that missing field defaults to FULL.  
• SHOW records can be used in conjunction with ECHO to further restrict which parts of the output are actually printed.  

Additional context from the ECHO documentation:  
• “ECHO IL” alone prints influence‐line diagrams; adding “EXTR” will also produce text‐based influence lines.  A “+4” suffix on IL will include small transverse influence lines.  
• “ECHO LPOS FULL” saves actual load positions into the database and overlays them on the influence‐line graphics for every evaluation case.  
• “ECHO EVAL YES” prints only the generated load cases (use ECHO EVAL FULL for full load‐train positioning data; use ECHO EVAL EXTR for detailed statistics).  
• “ECHO RES EXTR” prints all intermediate result tables for every case.  

By combining OPT and VAL you can fine‐tune the verbosity of your output, balancing file size and clarity against the need for detailed diagnostic information.

sections: 3.3 ECHO – Control of the Output Extent

See also: LANE, LINF, CALC, TRAI
 ECHO
 The record name ECHO must be input for every record so that the options are not confused with other records with identical names. The volume of printed data is also controlled with the record SHOW.
 With ECHO IL the influence lines will be printed, in general as pictures, but with option EXTR also as text. The small influence lines in transverse direction will be shown with the Option +4. Without a SHOW selection the volume of pictures may become quite large.
 With the option LPOS FULL the actual load positions of all evaluations will be saved to the database and the graphical visualization of the influence lines will include the loading and will be repeated for all evaluation cases.
 ECHO EVAL YES prints only the generated load cases for the case of ECHO RES NO. For the load train position ECHO EVAL FULL is needed and for the detailed statistical data ECHO EVAL EXTR.
 ECHO RES EXTR prints the intermediate results of all cases.
 Hint
 If no ECHO options are specified, the options LANE, IL, LOAD, LPOS and RES are set to YES (regular output), while EVAL and STAT are set to NO (no output). If the ECHO option is used without explicitly stating the OPT and/or VAL item, value FULL will be taken as the default.

The table defines the internal structure of a “CTRL … SECT” input record (see program SOFiMSHA record BSEC) and more generally shows how CTRL‐records can carry up to six fields.  Each row corresponds to one field in the record; columns specify its name (“Item”), its meaning, its data type or unit (“Unit”) and its default value if the user omits it (“Default”).  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown, followed by a note on how this ties into the broader CTRL options (SECT and AGRL).

1.  Columns  
    •  Item  
       –  The positional identifier for each field in the CTRL record.  Must appear in this order.  
    •  Description  
       –  Human‐readable explanation of what the field does or what values it may take.  
    •  Unit  
       –  Indicates the expected data type or unit.  “LIT” means literal text; “—” means no unit/any format as long as it matches the description.  
    •  Default  
       –  The value assumed if the field is left blank in the input.  

2.  Field definitions  
    A.  OPT  
        •  Description: Selects which option is being controlled.  Currently the only recognized literal is “SECT,” which triggers evaluation of beam sections.  
        •  Unit: LIT  
        •  Default: “!”  (exclamation mark indicates that this field is mandatory — the program will error if you omit or replace it with an invalid literal.)  

    B.  VAL  
        •  Description: The actual value of the option named in OPT.  
            –  When OPT=SECT, VAL must be 0 or 1:  
              ·  0: only sections flagged for printing are evaluated  
              ·  1: all beam sections are evaluated (this is the normal or default mode)  
        •  Unit: —  
        •  Default: “*”  (asterisk means “use the program’s default,” which is VAL=1 in the SECT case.)  

    C.  V2, V3, V4, V5, V6  
        •  Description: Reserved for future or additional options.  No current semantics.  
        •  Unit: —  
        •  Default: “–”  (dash means “unused.”)  

3.  How this fits into CTRL SECT and CTRL AGRL  
    •  CTRL SECT: By specifying OPT=SECT and setting VAL to 0 or 1, the user controls whether beam‐section evaluations are performed only for printed sections (0) or for every beam section (1).  
    •  CTRL AGRL: Although AGRL is not listed in this particular table, it follows the same sub‐record structure—OPT would be set to AGRL and VAL to one of –1, 0, 1, 2 to govern how loaded lengths are aggregated.  The reserved fields V2–V6 could later carry additional AGRL‐specific parameters if needed.  

4.  Usage example  
    To tell ELLA to compute section forces only where the “print‐flag” is set, one would write:  
       CTRL SECT, VAL=0  
    Internally, this populates OPT=“SECT” and VAL=0, leaving V2–V6 blank.  

5.  Rationale for reserved fields  
    By allowing up to six positions, the CTRL records are extensible.  Future options (e.g. new aggregation strategies, output filters or post‐processing flags) can be slotted into V2–V6 without changing the overall parsing logic.  

In summary, this table documents the grammar of the CTRL record: OPT names the control keyword (only SECT today), VAL sets its parameter (0/1), and V2–V6 are placeholders for future expansions. The “Unit” and “Default” columns guide both validation and the assignment of implicit values when users omit optional fields.

See also: APPL, CALC
 CTRL
 With CTRL SECT one can obtain evaluations only at certain beam sections. The input options are:
 CTRL SECT 0 only section with print-flag (see program SOFiMSHA record BSEC) CTRL SECT 1 all beam sections (default)
 With CTRL AGRL one can select how ELLA should cope with the aggregation of loaded lengths. The load values as well as the impact factors may depend on those values.
 CTRL AGRL -1 Length values will be kept separately, each span is taken on its own.
 CTRL AGRL 0 Length values will be combined within the same lane, but the load value will be increased if the most important span would be more un- favourably
 CTRL AGRL 1 Length values will be combined within the same lane, the load value is dependant only on the total length (Default)
 CTRL AGRL 2 Length values will be combined over all lanes
 It has to be pointed out, that option -1 will be not be general applicable in case of elastic supports, where strong discontinuities in the results may be obtained and thus is not a me- chanically sound procedure.

The diagram is a schematic plan-view of a lane axis, introduced as “Figure 3.1: Lane axis definition.” It illustrates how local lateral offsets (x) and global stations (s) are defined and related for one or more traffic lanes. Key elements are:

 1. Base axis (global station line)  
    – Shown as a straight, oblique line emerging from the lower-left corner, inclined roughly 45° above the horizontal.  
    – It is labeled “S = 0.000” at its point of origin, marking the zero station.  
    – Two small “x = 0” tags appear on this line, indicating that at the very start of the station axis the local offset x is zero.  

 2. Local coordinate system at the origin  
    – A pair of orthogonal arrows attached to the base axis at S = 0:  
       • One arrow is labeled “+ x” and points perpendicular to the base axis into the region where the curved lane lines will lie.  
       • The other arrow is labeled “y” (no “+” shown) and lies along the direction of the base axis, indicating the positive station direction.  
    – These two arrows define the local (x, y) frame in which lateral measurements (x) are taken normal to the axis and longitudinal positions (y ≡ s) follow the axis.  

 3. Curved lane lines  
    – Two roughly concentric arcs (drawn as circular or clothoid segments) are shown “above” the base axis. These represent two separate lanes offset laterally from the station line.  
    – They both emanate from the origin of the base axis, following a continuous curvature to the right as they progress away from S = 0.  
    – No numeric offset labels are given on these arcs, but by construction each arc lies at a constant lateral distance x > 0 from the base axis in the local frame.  

 4. Reference station cut-line at S = 1.000  
    – On the right side of the drawing a vertical line is introduced; it is labeled “S = 1.000.”  
    – This line intersects both curved lane lines, showing how one can pick out corresponding points on each lane by specifying a particular station s and the local offset x.  

 5. Caption and notation  
    – Beneath the graphic is the text “Figure 3.1: Lane axis definition.”  
    – Throughout, notation is minimal and consistent with SOFiLOAD/SOFIMS-HC conventions: “s” for global station, “x” for lateral offset in the local system.  
    – The figure conveys that the user may define or activate an existing lane axis (via GAX or LSEL) and then reference any point on one of up to nine parallel lanes by its station s and local coordinate x.  

Overall, the drawing demonstrates the two-coordinate‐system approach employed in the moving-load process: a global, along-axis stationing (s) to align multiple lanes, and a local, transverse offset (x) for real-world lateral positions. It shows that at the origin (S = 0) x returns to zero, and that at any downstream station (for example S = 1.000) the lanes occupy fixed lateral offsets measured in the +x direction of the local frame.

The base of the moving load process is a lane geometry, described in the plan view by straight, circular or clothoid segments and in the elevation as straight or quadratic parabola. This can be taken from the database as defined by SOFiMSHC or SOFILOAD or explicitly input with the record GAX. Each axis may have up to nine separate lanes with the sub numbers 1 to 9 defined via LANE. For the dynamic impact coefficients an effective length may be specified and the extra width of the traffic area may be defined.
 A lane axis already stored in the database (by SOFiMSHC or SOFiLOAD or ELLA) can be activated with the record LSEL.
 Each lane has two coordinate systems. There is a local system (x) at the lane axis for real distances. However, the inputs for the positions along the lanes are entered in a global system of stations (s) which defines an alignment of the lanes to each other.

Below is a detailed field‐by‐field description of the “Axis Definition” table you provided. This schema is used by SOFiMSHC (and in simplified form by SOFiLOAD/ELLA/TENDON) to define a geometric axis (GAX) or a traffic lane (LANE) in plan view and, optionally, in 3D.

1. NO  
   – Identifier of the axis or lane.  
   – Data type: Literal, up to 4 characters (LIT4).  
   – Default: “A1”  
   – Usage: Unique tag for each axis. All downstream records that define additional segments inherit this tag.  

2. S  
   – Total arc length (station) measured along the axis from the start point.  
   – Unit: none (stations are unitless markers, though they often correspond to meters).  
   – Default: 0  
   – Usage: For the first record, S = length of the first segment. For each subsequent record, S denotes the incremental segment length.  

3. X, Y, Z  
   – Real‐world coordinates of the point at station S.  
   – Unit: meters ([m]₁₀₀₁).  
   – Defaults: X=0, Y=0, Z=0  
   – Usage:  
     • In plan‐only definitions, X and Y define the 2D projection; Z may be omitted or set to zero.  
     • In 3D definitions (when NX/NY/NZ are used), all three coordinates must be supplied.  

4. R  
   – Radius of curvature of the axis at station S.  
   – Unit: meters ([m]₁₀₀₁).  
   – Default: “–” (if omitted, R is computed automatically based on A or on change of S).  
   – Usage:  
     • Positive R → curvature to the right.  
     • Negative R → curvature to the left.  
     • If R is supplied along with A, A defines a clothoid parameter and R defines the curvature at the segment’s start.  

5. A  
   – Transition (clothoid) parameter, where R·L = A².  
   – Unit: meters ([m]₁₀₀₁).  
   – Default: “–” (no clothoid).  
   – Usage:  
     • A ≠ 0 → gradual curvature change over the segment; sign of A controls whether curvature increases (+) or decreases (–).  
     • A = 0 with R defined produces a constant‐curvature (circular arc) or piecewise constant “basket arch” curve.  

6. NX, NY, NZ  
   – Components of the local z-axis (direction vector) for 3D curves.  
   – Unit: none.  
   – Default: “*” (optional; only for 3D definitions)  
   – Usage:  
     • When present, they define the axis’s out‐of‐plane orientation.  
     • Circular arcs then rotate around this local z-axis.  
     • Not used in standard 2D alignments.  

7. TYPE  
   – Type of geometry line.  
   – Data type: Literal (LIT).  
   – Default: “AXIS”  
   – Allowed values:  
     • AXIS  = general geometric axis  
     • LANE  = traffic lane centerline  
     • BGEO  = bridge geometry line  
   – Usage: Directs SOFiMSHC how to interpret the sequence of records.  

8. TITL  
   – Descriptive name or designation for this axis or lane.  
   – Data type: Literal, up to 32 characters (LIT32).  
   – Default: “–” (blank)  
   – Usage: Used for reporting, graphical titles in WING/WinGRAF and for clarity when multiple axes are defined.  

General Notes:  
• The first row for each NO must supply X, Y, Z, NX/NY/NZ (if 3D), S, and optionally R/A.  
• Each following row under the same NO need only supply S and any new R or A values to extend the alignment.  
• If only plan‐view geometry is required (SOFiLOAD/ELLA/TENDON), 3D direction vectors and Z may be omitted.  
• When a new radius is defined, an automatic clothoid transition is generated from the previous curvature to the new R, unless A = 0.  
• It is recommended to visually check the assembled axis in WinGRAF or WING before further processing.  
• Elevation and crossfall definitions are handled separately, currently only within the full SOFiMSHC environment.

The diagram presents a simplified “lane axis” geometry, illustrating three successive segments (linear, spiral/clothoid, circular arc) together with a local 2-D coordinate frame. At the bottom right of the image appears the caption “Figure 3.2: Lane axis.”

1. Overall Layout  
   - From left to right, the graphic shows a straight line labeled “linear,” transitioning into a smoothly‐curving segment marked “+A,” and finally into a circular arc segment marked “+R.”  
   - Two short, slanted bars perpendicular to the curve outline the boundaries between these segments. The first bar (between “linear” and “+A”) marks the start of the clothoid spiral; the second bar (between “+A” and “+R”) marks the changeover to the constant‐radius arc.

2. Linear Segment  
   - On the far left, a straight horizontal (slightly tilted) line segment carries the text “linear” printed in an oblique, lowercase font immediately above the line.  
   - No curvature parameters are indicated here, implying zero curvature over the initial run-out length.

3. Spiral (Clothoid) Segment  
   - To the right of the first delimiter bar, the line bends gradually upward and to the right. Above this portion sits “+A” in plain, sans-serif lettering, denoting a positive rate of change of curvature (clothoid parameter).  
   - No fixed radius (R) is specified here; rather curvature grows linearly with arc length according to the spiral rate A.

4. Circular‐Arc Segment  
   - To the right of the second delimiter bar, the curvature has leveled off into a constant‐radius arc bending further upward. Above this arc portion appears “+R,” indicating a positive radius value (i.e., the curve turns to the right, from the viewer’s perspective).  
   - The arc is drawn slightly thicker than the linear segment to emphasize its constant curvature.

5. Local Coordinate Frame  
   - Near the start of the spiral segment there is a bold “L‐shaped” axis marker:  
     • One arrow-head points forward along the tangent to the curve, labeled “x” (with the arrow tip just beyond the curve).  
     • The other arrow-head points inward (nearly downward in the image) and is labeled “y.”  
   - These axes define the local 2D reference frame for the lane: x aligned with the instantaneous forward direction, y pointing toward the inside of the bend.

6. Styling and Annotations  
   - All labels and arrows are rendered in solid black lines on white background.  
   - Text is positioned close to the corresponding graphical element: segment names above each section, axis labels at arrowheads, and the figure title below.

This drawing succinctly conveys the typical three‐part alignment used in road or railway design—straight tangent, clothoid spiral transition, and constant‐radius curve—together with the orientation of the local Cartesian frame (x, y) at the transition point.

See also: Load-train, LANE
 GAX
 A general geometric axis with all details may be now defined in SOFIMSHC. For SOFiLOAD / ELLA / TENDON only a simplified definition is provided as follows.
 • Definition with a length resp. station in the plan view For the first record of an axis the start point (X,Y,Z) and the start direction (NX,NY,NZ), the length S of the first segment and optional curvature and clothoidal parameter is specified. All consecutive records contain only the next S-value and the curvature parameters.
 If a radius is defined, a transition element from the last radius to the current value is gener- ated. Positive values for R cause a curvature to the right-hand side, whilst negative values a curvature to the left-hand side. If A is defined, a clothoidal spiral transition curve is created where the curvature increases for the positive values of A and decreases for the negative values. If the radius R is not given it will be calculated automatically based on the length, if it is given together with A the curvature of the start point will be calculated instead. Basket arches with piecewice constant curvatures may be defined with A=0.0 and the selected radius.

The table shown is the formal input specification for defining individual traffic or track lanes (SOFiLOAD “LANE” record).  It is organized in four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and covers everything from lane‐identification to geometric offsets, superstructure heights, cross–falls, and sleeper/rail parameters.  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown:

1.  Column headings  
    •  Item: the keyword to be supplied in the input stream.  
    •  Description: a short human‐readable description of the parameter’s purpose.  
    •  Unit: the physical unit (or “—” if non‐dimensional or literal).  Where shown as “[m]₁₀₀₁” or “[mm]” the numbers refer to SOFiSTiK’s internal unit codes.  
    •  Default: the value assumed if the field is omitted (“*” means mandatory, “!” means required, a literal or another field name means “use that value”).  

2.  Lane identification  
    •  NO (LIT, default = *): lane number, e.g. “A1.3” = third lane of axis A1; if only “lane_ident” is given, it refers to the entire set of lanes.  
    •  TYPE (LIT, default = *): predefined lane‐section type (see “remarks” in the main documentation for allowed literals such as RQ7.5, TMH7, EN1991-2, etc.).  

3.  Lane boundaries (curbstone ordinates)  
    •  WR ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = –): global Y‐coordinate of the right curbstone.  
    •  WL ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = –WR): Y‐coordinate of the left curbstone (by default symmetric opposite).  

4.  Longitudinal extent along the reference axis  
    •  SA (—, default = !): start station (chainage) along the lane axis (mandatory).  
    •  SE (—, default = !): end station along the lane axis (mandatory).  

5.  Lane centre‐line and edge offsets  
    •  YCA ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = *): offset of the lane centre from the axis at SA.  
    •  YCE ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = YCA): offset of the lane centre at SE (defaults to YCA if omitted).  
    •  YRA ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = *): offset of the right edge from the axis at SA.  
    •  YLA ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = *): offset of the left edge at SA.  
    •  YRE ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = YRA): right edge offset at SE.  
    •  YLE ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = YLA): left edge offset at SE.  

6.  Segment length for dynamic impact and loaded‐length effects  
    •  L ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = *): effective length of this lane segment for impact‐coefficient lookup and loaded‐length rules.  
    •  CONT: if inserted in place of L for all but the first segment, it appends this definition to the previous segment rather than starting a new one.  

7.  Vertical position and cross–fall  
    •  HSA ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = 0.0): height of deck (road) or rail above the lane at SA.  
    •  HSE ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = HSA): same at SE (defaults to HSA if omitted).  
    •  INCA ([mm], default = 0.0): transverse slope expressed as dz/dy or Δh at SA (in mm per meter).  
    •  INCE ([mm], default = INCA): cross‐fall at SE.  

8.  Sleeper and rail “effective” parameters (for railway bridges and detailed ballast pressure models)  
    •  HEFF ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = –): effective rail+sleeper height (required for EN 1991-2 ballast pressure).  
    •  BEFF ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = –): effective sleeper length.  
    •  DEFF ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = –): effective sleeper width.  
    •  INCD (—, default = 0.25): spread‐angle for converting vertical wheel loads into bearing stresses below sleeper.  
    •  ASL ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = –): distance between mounting (fastening) points on the sleeper.  
    •  WREF ([m]₁₀₀₁, default = *): gauge width used to convert cross–falls into transverse inclinations (e.g. standard rail gauge 1.435 m).  

9.  Notes on usage and defaults  
    •  Fields marked “*” must be supplied explicitly.  
    •  Where the default refers to another field (e.g. YCE=YCA) you only need to specify the start‐value if the end‐value is unchanged.  
    •  The special literal CONT on L allows chaining multiple lane definitions into one segment.  
    •  Predefined literal types (TYPE) will auto-generate secondary lanes per standards (EN 1991-2, TMH7, CAN, IRC, etc.).  
    •  Residual areas (between the load train and lane edges) are automatically recognized; gaps between lanes are not considered loaded.  

This schema lets you define up to 99 lanes on a given axis, each potentially varying in width, position, cross‐fall and superstructure geometry. When ingested into a RAG‐based vector store, each parameter (Item, its Description, Unit and Default rule) becomes a discrete knowledge node to power precise lane‐definition queries, validation checks and automated sectioning workflows in SOFiLOAD/Ella.

The illustration is a black-and-white plan-view sketch of a single, curved traffic lane showing (1) the full lane width, (2) the portion actually occupied by the moving load (“load train”), and (3) the “residual” or “additional basic” areas that would carry a constant, uniformly distributed load whenever the load train itself is narrower than the lane.  It is labeled “Figure 3.3: Single lane loaded and residual area.”

Overall Layout  
• The lane runs along an arc, bending from lower left toward upper right.  
• Two concentric, unbroken curves trace the lane boundaries (inner and outer edges).  
• Outside the outer boundary is a short dashed line indicating the edge of a broader structural element (e.g. bridge deck or curb).  
• The hatched region, bounded by two gently offset curves inside the full lane boundaries, represents where the actual vehicular load is applied.  

Hatching and Fill  
• The hatched area is filled with closely spaced diagonal lines sloping upward to the right (⁄).  
• This fill is entirely contained between two lighter, offset curves that run parallel to the main lane edges.  
• The width of this hatched band is constant along the arc length, suggesting a “constant width load train.”  

Annotations and Callouts  
• A straight leader line originates from the middle of the hatched band and carries the label “additional basic area” just above the outer lane boundary.  
• A short horizontal tick mark on the inner boundary corresponds visually to the inner hatched boundary.  
• Beneath the sketch, a partial legend or caption in lowercase reads “constant width lo…” which likely abbreviates “constant width load train.”  
• At the bottom of the figure area, fully centered, the caption reads:  
  Figure 3.3: Single lane loaded and residual area  

Visual Style  
• All lines are uniform in stroke weight, suggesting a technical drawing generated by CAD or a vector-based drafting tool.  
• No dimensions are explicitly shown on the figure itself, but the hatched region and callout imply that the full lane width exceeds the moving load width.  
• There is no color—only solid black lines, dashed lines, and a monochrome hatch pattern.  

Interpretation in Context of SOFiLOAD / EN 1991-2  
• In the accompanying specification text, a “load train” narrower than the lane triggers creation of “additional basic areas” at the lane edges to carry a constant load. These are exactly the hatched zones shown here.  
• The “residual areas” are the spaces between the load train’s outer limits and the true lane boundaries; they are loaded with a reduced, uniform intensity rather than the concentrated wheel loads.  
• This figure visually clarifies how SOFiLOAD subdivides a lane into principal (hatched) and residual (unhatched) regions when performing traffic loading according to EN 1991-2 or related national annexes.  
• It underlines that, for a single-lane scenario (lane 0), the eccentricities and widths must be managed so that any extra traffic or pathway loads are captured by defining these “additional basic areas.”

Overall layout

Load arrow

This suggests a point where lane edges intersect each other or cross over—highlighted in the manual as a location requiring a distinct definition to correctly handle torsional loading.  

Caption

Interpretation in context  
• The black axis line with numeric ticks defines the longitudinal stationing along a reference axis (AXIS.1).

This diagram exemplifies how SOFiLOAD uses geometric polylines, textual labels and symbols to encode (1) lane widths varying along the span, (2) moving load positions, and (3) residual loading areas between the load train and the defined lane edges.

The image is a black-and-white technical line drawing, labeled at the bottom “Figure 3.5: Two lanes adjusted to the right loaded and residual area.” It shows a plan-view slice through two traffic lanes (load trains) arranged along a common longitudinal axis, with coordinate markers and load‐application points indicated.

Overall layout  
• A horizontal centerline represents the reference axis. At its midpoint there is a small break (a pair of opposing arrowheads) indicating continuity.  
• Along the bottom of the drawing, four stationing coordinates are shown at regular intervals: –4.00 m at the far left, –2.00 m under the left lane center, 0.00 m at the axis break, and +2.00 m under the right lane center. The horizontal axis is implicitly the X-direction, while the vertical direction on the page is labeled “Y” at the far left.  

Lane geometry and identifiers  
• On the left of the axis break, a rectangular outline (in red) spans roughly from –4.0 m to 0.0 m in the X-direction. This rectangle represents “AXIS.11” with the legend “T 102” printed directly beneath it and centered at X = –2.0 m.  
• On the right of the axis break, a similar red rectangle runs from 0.0 m to +4.0 m (only the first +2.0 m are shown explicitly). Underneath, centered at X = +2.0 m, it is labeled “AXIS.10” with the legend “T 101.”  
• Both rectangles are of equal width in the Y-direction (indicating the total lane width).  

Load application (moving loads)  
• Along the top edge of each lane rectangle are multiple downward-pointing arrows, drawn in red, spaced evenly along the length of the lane. These represent wheel loads or load points of the moving load train. The left lane (AXIS.11) has four arrows; the right lane (AXIS.10) has five arrows.  
• The vertical position of each arrow indicates that the load is applied to the top of the lane slab.  

Residual area depiction  
• Within each lane rectangle, the region between the outermost wheel-load arrows and the lane boundaries is the so-called “residual area.” Although not shaded, it is implied by the gap between load‐pattern extents and the full lane width.  

Caption

Visually, it consists of a horizontal baseline with coordinate tick marks, two superimposed rectangular bars representing the loaded lane areas, downward-pointing arrows signifying applied loads, dimensioning arrows beneath marking the width of each lane, and textual labels identifying axis references and segment identifiers.

Key elements of the drawing:
