Overall, the figure conveys how multiple traffic lanes—each defined by its own axis label, station coordinate, width, and loading pattern—are laid out in plan view. It highlights the geometrical relationship between lanes (residual versus loaded) and how these are referenced back to an established centerline or axis for structural analysis.

The image is a schematic cross‐section entitled “Figure 3.7: Ballast and sleepers.”  It illustrates how the load from a railway sleeper is transmitted into the underlying ballast, and defines the key geometric parameters used in SOFiLOAD (and related modules such as ELLA) to compute stresses and torsional effects.

1. Overall Layout  
 • A heavy horizontal baseline represents the ground or support level.  
 • At mid-span there is a vertical central axis, marked by a bold dot on the baseline and a line rising through the sleeper. At the foot of this axis a downward arrow is labeled “z,” denoting the global vertical coordinate (positive upward).  

2. Sleeper and Rail Representation  
 • Resting atop the ballast is a single sleeper shown in plan-view cross‐section: a long, slightly inclined rectangular block. On its top face are two small black rectangles (rail pads or rails), indicating the points of application of wheel loads.  
 • The sleeper itself is drawn with a slight tilt, emphasizing that it may carry an imposed cross‐fall or be subject to torsion if the rails are not exactly level.  

3. Ballast Geometry and Inclination  
 • Beneath each end of the sleeper is a wedge‐shaped ballast prism on both the left and right. The sides of each prism are straight lines that flare out from the sleeper base down to the ground line.  
 • Each side of the ballast prism carries the label “INCD,” denoting the inclination (slope) of the ballast shoulders relative to horizontal.  In SOFiLOAD, INCD defines how the effective load width expands with depth.  

4. Effective Load Width (BEFF)  
 • Superimposed centrally over the sleeper block is a lightly drawn rectangle, inside which sits the text “BEFF.”  This denotes the effective width of the bearing pressure distribution at the sleeper–ballast interface.  BEFF is computed based on sleeper geometry, track height, and load-train parameters.  

5. Key Dimensions  
 • “s”: A horizontal dimension line with two short vertical ticks spans between the two rail pads on the sleeper. It is labeled “s” above the line, indicating the spacing of contacts (or sleeper spacing) in the longitudinal direction.  
 • “H”: On the right side of the diagram, a vertical dimension line marked at the top of the sleeper and at the bottom baseline is labeled “H.”  This is the total height of track superstructure above the reference level, used to calculate bending moments and lever arms in the analysis.  
 • “YL” and “YR”: At the ground level directly beneath the outer toe of each ballast prism are the notations YL (left) and YR (right).  These define the lateral distance from the track centerline (z-axis) to the edges of the loading lanes or to the extremes of ballast support.  

6. Contextual Notes (from the adjoining text)  
 • The diagram ties into the concept of subdividing the total loading area into traffic lanes relative to a reference axis.  Lane 0 (the entire traffic envelope) and secondary lanes are defined by their widths and eccentricities.  
 • If the load train is narrower than the lane, “residual areas” outside the sleeper footprint but within the lane receive a constant basic load.  If wider, load reductions apply.  
 • Inclination parameters (INCA/INCE for cross fall, INCD for ballast slope) feed into additional moment calculations in SOFiLOAD and ELLA (INT<3).  
 • For railway bridges, this ballast model works in concert with EN 1991-2 or DIN FB 101 tables to select the governing length and effective pressure below ballast, requiring inputs HEFF and ASL in SOFiLOAD.  

Taken together, this figure defines the geometry by which vertical wheel loads acting through the sleeper and rail pads spread out into the ballast prism.  The inclinations INCD, the effective width BEFF, the total track height H, and the lane offsets YL/YR all enter into the finite‐element or direct‐pressure algorithms of SOFiLOAD to ensure accurate stress and moment calculations under moving trains.

These may be created automatically by a predefined standard section or with explicit coordinates. One may subdivide each segment with different widths and dynamic impact factors. All lanes have to be defined together to an existing axis, any new definition will delete all previously defined lane definitions.
 The width of the lane is defined through the left and the right boundaries. The lane can be widened or narrowed by different input data at different stations. If the lane edges happen to intersect the lane, this should be defined only at distinct points to allow for correct treating of torsional loading.
 The width of the load train may be less than those of the lane. In that case additional basic areas are established loaded by a constant load specified with the load train. If the load train is larger than the lane width, reductions of the applied loading are possible.
 The lane 0 has to be defined always, for the following procedures two cases have to be distin- guished:
 • There is only lane 0, the width of the moving loading is defined only by the load train. Only then, the eccentricities of the load train are applied absolutely for all lanes.
 • There are other lanes within the curb stone limits. Then lane 0 defines the total extend of the traffic load including pathways. The width of the moving load is the maximum extend of the other lanes.

Below is a field‐by‐field description of the LSEL input table used by ELLA (see also LaneGeometry, GAX, LANE, LSEL).  It summarizes the parameters you must supply when you activate (“select”) a lane for influence‐line evaluation.  Where applicable, the default values and units are noted.

1.  NO  
   – Lane identifier  
   – Type: literal (up to 8 characters, “lit8”)  
   – You must supply a unique axis/lane label, for example “A1.3” or use wildcards “A1.?”  
   – Default: “!” (i.e. mandatory field)  

2.  INT  
   – Load‐distribution or evaluation type (integer)  
     • 0 = single lane  
     • 1 = articulated distribution  
     • 2 = rigid distribution  
     • 3, 5, 7, 9 = transverse influence‐line using QUAD elements  
   – No units  
   – Default: 1  

3.  DX  
   – Maximum longitudinal spacing of load points or, for INT = 0–2, maximum allowable angle deviation between lane axis and nodal‐sequence edge (degrees, signed)  
   – Unit: metres [m]  
   – Default: 99  

4.  DY  
   – Influence width of the lane in the transverse (Y) direction  
   – For nodal‐sequence search (INT ≤ 2) defines how far out from each side of the axis ELLA will look for adjacent nodes  
   – Unit: metres [m]  
   – Default: 99  

5.  DZ  
   – Influence height beneath the lane axis  
   – Only nodes with vertical coordinate no more than DZ below the axis are considered  
   – Unit: metres [m]  
   – Default: 99  

6.  RSEL  
   – Explicit selection method for centric or right‐hand‐side nodes  
   – Type: literal (“LIT”)  
   – Options:  
     • EDGE = by nodal sequence (use RSEQ to point to a previously defined sequence)  
     • SZUG = by continuous beam (RSEQ)  
     • GRP = by beams of a group (RSEQ)  
     • QGRP = by QUAD elements of a group (RSEQ)  
   – Default: EDGE  

7.  RSEQ  
   – Index number of the sequence, beam group or QUAD group referenced by RSEL  
   – No units  
   – Default: none (“–”)  

8.  LSEL  
   – Explicit selection method for left‐hand‐side nodes (same options as RSEL)  
   – Type: literal (“LIT”)  
   – Default: inherits RSEL value if you don’t specify  

9.  LSEQ  
   – Index number corresponding to LSEL  
   – No units  
   – Default: none (“–”)  

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
   The following parameters apply only when INT > 2 (i.e. transverse‐direction QUAD‐element evaluation):  

10. TRAI  
    – Load case of a train for transverse evaluation  
    – No units  
    – Default: none (“–”)  

11. B  
    – Width of the traffic band in transverse direction  
    – Unit: metres [m]  
    – Default: must match the width specified in the selected train (no standalone default)  

12. BWH  
    – Transverse distance between wheel groups  
    – Unit: metres [m]  
    – Default: inherited from the train definition  

13. YMAX  
    – Override maximum eccentricity from TRAI (positive side)  
    – Unit: metres [m]  
    – Default: +YEX (value from train load case)  

14. YMIN  
    – Override minimum eccentricity from TRAI (negative side)  
    – Unit: metres [m]  
    – Default: –YEX  

Notes and special features:  
•  If you supply INT < 0, all geometry and influence lines for that lane are cleared.  
•  If you omit explicit RSEL/LSEL definitions, ELLA attempts an automatic nodal‐sequence search (INT 0–2) within the DY/DZ window.  
•  For plate‐and‐shell models, a prior transverse‐influence‐area check is recommended (types 3,5,7,9), based on selected QUADs.  
•  Always use secondary‐group or primary‐group ranges to confine QUAD search in elevation when no explicit DZ limit is given.  
•  Once a load train (TRAI) is chosen, its transverse geometry (B, BWH, YMAX, YMIN) is locked for all longitudinal evaluations.  
•  To visualize transverse influence lines interactively, issue the command “ECHO EL +4” after selection.

content:
The image is a schematic, labelled “Figure 3.8: Node selection for a lane,” illustrating how nodal sequences are identified within a prescribed transverse region around a traffic lane axis. Across the top and bottom of the sketch two smooth, roughly parallel curves define the outer limits of the lane’s influence zone. Between these curves, a dashed-dot line runs longitudinally, representing the theoretical central axis of the lane.  

On either side of that central axis two distinct polyline chains are drawn. Each chain is made up of a series of small, hollow circles—graphical symbols for finite-element nodes—connected by straight line segments. The upper chain starts level, then rises to a peak at its middle node before descending slightly toward the right. The lower chain mirrors this pattern with a gentle incline and decline, though its rise is more subdued and its overall slope remains positive from left to right. These two node sequences lie within the bounds set by the curved outer lines, implying they fall inside the transverse selection region.  

To the left of the drawing a double-arrow dimension line spans from the top boundary curve down to the lower boundary curve. This arrow is explicitly labelled “2 * DY,” indicating that the vertical thickness of the selection zone is twice the user-specified parameter DY. No other dimensions are shown, but the annotation clearly ties back to the procedure whereby nodes within ±DY on each side of the lane axis are considered for influence-line evaluation.  

Overall, the figure conveys that once a lane has been activated via LSEL, the software locates adjacent nodes by searching within a rectangular strip of width 2 * DY across the lane’s direction. The open circles connected by lines illustrate two example sequences of nodes that ELLA might automatically assemble, one above and one below the axis, in preparation for further structural analysis.

sections: 3.8 LSEL – Selection of a Defined Lane

See also: LaneGeometry, GAX, LANE, LSEL
 LSEL
 An already defined lane gets activated for evaluation with the record LSEL. At NO one has to specify the axis identifier (4 chars) optionally appended by a dot and a digit for the lane number (e.g. A1.3 but also with wild cards like A1.? or A1.1?). Without a lane number all lanes of that axis are selected, which is not always a good choice to minimize analysis time. At the same time parameters can be specified for the selection of the neighbouring nodes.
 Lanes which are defined with the record GAX in the same block are selected automatically with the standard values for DX, DY and DZ. A special feature can be achieved with an input of a
 negative value for INT. In this case all geometric parameters and influence lines are deleted for this lane.
 If the user does not define an explicit sequence of neighboring nodes, Ella will try in a first step to look for all nodes which are adjacent to the lane and tries to link them to one (INT 0) or two (INT 1,2) nodal sequences.
 For this search DY and DZ describe a region in which the corresponding nodes must be situ- ated. DY is measured in this case at the right-hand side and at the left-hand side of the lane. A value of about 90 percent of the distance between the main girders is a sound definition.
 The parameter DZ defines the limits of the region under the lane which is to be examined. This is for example necessary for three-dimensional structures at which parts of this structure lie sometimes beneath the lane. Nodes above the lane axis are never considered.
 For INT>2 DX specifies a maximum distance of the load points along the axis. While the default is to use a load point at every edge crossing the lane, a smaller value will insert additional points between.
 For INT 0 to 2 the parameter DX specifies, how large the angle between the lane axis and an edge of the nodal sequence is accepted. An input is necessary, if transverse girders and longitudinal girders have similar angles of intersection to the lane. If the node sequences may intersect the lane, DX has to be input with a negative value.

For INT 0 to 2 the parameter DX specifies, how large the angle between the lane axis and an edge of the nodal sequence is accepted. An input is necessary, if transverse girders and longitudinal girders have similar angles of intersection to the lane. If the node sequences may intersect the lane, DX has to be input with a negative value..
 If ELLA is not able to find suitable sequences of nodes, then it is possible to specify two sequences explicitly by boundary or beam elements containing the desired nodes with RSEL/RSEQ and LSEL/LSEQ.
 For plates and shells structures it is recommended to make an evaluation of the influence area in transverse direction before establishing the longitudinal influence values. With types 3,5,7 and 9 these numbers of load points in transverse direction will be examined based on the existing and selected QUAD elements.
 QUAD elements are searched only based on the plan view. If a secondary group or a range of primary groups is specified, no further checks about the elevation will be made. However if no such definitions are given, only those QUAD elements will be considered situated with a maximum of DZ below the loading or where the loading is within the element. Thus it is strongly
 recommended to use a group definition to specify the traffic area properly. One secondary group or a range of primary groups may be specified.
 For the evaluation the transverse width of the traffic lane, the distance of the wheels and the minimum and maximum eccentricities are required. For this purpose a loadtrain has to be specified with TRAI providing the necessary information. For the evaluation in the longitudinal direction these values may not be changed any more. Therefore the width of the traffic lane of the given load train must match the values of the load trains positioned in the lanes. The distance between the wheels should also match, but differences often result only in small devi- ations, which are flagged by a warning message only. If several load trains with different wheel spacings are used, a load train must be selected containing all possible wheel spacings. In the case of an LM3 with accompanying LM1, the LM3 must be selected for the evaluation. It also contains the information about the LM1 wheel distance, but not vice versa. For special cases a USER defined train containing all necessary wheel spacings may be applied. In ex- ceptional cases an explicit definition of the values with B, BWH, YMAX and YMIN in LSEL is also possible.

 A graphical control of the transverse influence lines may be obtained with ECHO EL +4.

Influence areas are calculated from unit load cases, when the record CALC is input. In every case all the influence areas are produced for the corresponding internal forces. The record CALC specifies for which elements and for which scalar variables the evaluation of the influ- ence area will be performed.
 For each extreme value of any scalar variable a load case can be generated and stored in the database. The corresponding values of the rest of the internal forces are calculated automati- cally too.
 As an alternate way one may read influence lines or areas which were stored as load cases in the data base with the input option LINF. The values are then interpolated to the defined lanes. The results, however, do not get stored in the database.

The table under discussion defines the keywords and their attributes for the CALC entry, which selects structural elements and influence‐line parameters for subsequent ELLA or influence‐line analyses.  Each row corresponds to one keyword (Item), accompanied by a brief Description, the expected Unit, and the Default value used when the keyword is omitted.

1.  TYPE  
    – Description  
      • Specifies which scalar variable or result‐set quantity is to be evaluated by influence lines.  
      • This can be any internal force or moment in beam elements (N, VY, VZ, MT, MY, MZ, MB, MT2), axial forces in truss/cable/spring elements (TRUS, CABL, P, M, PTX, PTY, PTZ), shell/disk/plate bending moments and membrane/shear forces (MXX, MYY, MXY, VXX, VYY, NXX, NYY, NXY), or nodal displacements/rotations (UX, UY, UZ, PHIX, PHIY, PHIZ).  
      • It may also reference SOFIMSHA result sets via “RSET:xxxxx” (either by ID or ordinal number), provided the set does not employ formula expressions.  
    – Unit  
      • LIT (literal string)  
    – Default  
      • “–” (Mandatory: no default; TYPE must be specified.)

2.  LMAX  
    – Description  
      • Load‐case number for which the positive (maximum) influence‐line ordinate will be reported.  
      • A value of zero inhibits maximum evaluation.  
    – Unit  
      • — (integer load‐case index)  
    – Default  
      • “*” (reuse last defined LMAX)

3.  LMIN  
    – Description  
      • Load‐case number for which the negative (minimum) influence‐line ordinate will be reported.  
      • A value of zero inhibits minimum evaluation.  
    – Unit  
      • — (integer load‐case index)  
    – Default  
      • “*” (reuse last defined LMIN)

4.  FROM  
    – Description  
      • Identifies the smallest element number (or group name via FROM ’GRP’ group) to include in the influence‐line calculation.  
      • If omitted (and TO/DELT also omitted), all elements in the model are selected.  
      • Supports wildcard patterns when specifying result‐set identifiers.  
    – Unit  
      • — or LIT4 (integer or 4‐character literal)  
    – Default  
      • 1 (first element)

5.  TO  
    – Description  
      • Identifies the largest element number (or group) to include.  
      • Combined with FROM and INC, it defines a sequence of elements.  
    – Unit  
      • — or LIT4  
    – Default  
      • Same as FROM (i.e. single‐element selection if TO is omitted)

6.  INC  
    – Description  
      • Increment step between element numbers in the range FROM…TO.  
      • Enables skipping elements or sampling every n-th element.  
    – Unit  
      • — (integer)  
    – Default  
      • 1

7.  SYST  
    – Description  
      • Restricts the analysis to a subsystem, reducing CPU/memory by omitting certain influence‐line evaluations.  
      • SPAC: full spatial element set;  
      • GIRD: only those internal forces/moments relevant to a 2D girder (axial and transverse bending); axial force influence lines for other directions are not computed.  
    – Unit  
      • LIT (literal string)  
    – Default  
      • “*” (inherits from previous CALC or project defaults)

8.  PHI  
    – Description  
      • Impact factor (if given without units) or characteristic length when specified with a length unit.  
      • Used to scale static influence lines to quasi‐dynamic (impact‐adjusted) values.  
    – Unit  
      • — (dimensionless) or length unit  
    – Default  
      • “*” (no impact modification unless explicitly set)

Notes on Usage and Context  
– Multiple CALC definitions may overlap; only the last positive (non-zero) definition for any set of FROM–TO–INC wins.  
– In the absence of any CALC block, the system reuses the influence lines saved in projectname.CDI from the previous run.  
– CALC interacts closely with LSEL parameters (e.g. matching result‐set filters) and with the broader ELLA framework, which does not support certain configurations (e.g. plane frames or shear‐wall influence lines) due to potential ambiguities.

See also: CalculationofInfluenceAreas, APPL, CTRL, CASE
 CALC
 With CALC the elements will be selected for which the influence lines will be established. The parameters specified with LSEL will be applied for this calculation. Without any CALC definition the last influence lines in file projectname.CDI will be reused.
 If no input occurred for FROM, TO and DELT, all elements of the structure will be selected. Multiple overlapping definitions are possible, the latest positive definition is valid. Instead of the element numbers a group may be selected via or FROM ’GRP’ group.
 The parameter SYST can define a reduced influence line evaluation. This may result in a significant reduction of the CPU time and the memory requirement e.g. in the case of girders, if a three-dimensional model was defined due to the prestress and the temperature, while the imposed loads are acting only at a two-dimensional girder. The influence lines for the axial force as well as for the transverse bending are not calculated or evaluated with the input SYST GIRD.
 List of the Scalar Variables
 1. Beam Elements
 N, VY, VZ, MT, MY, MZ, MB, MT2 Forces and moments
 2. Truss, Cable and Spring Elements
 TRUS Axial forces in truss elements
 CABL Cable forces
 P, M Spring force, spring moment PTX, PTY, PTZ Transverse spring force component (PT is not directly available, as it is nonlinear)
 3. Shell, disk and plate elements
 MXX, MYY, MXY VXX, VYY Shear forces NXX, NYY, NXY
 Bending moments
 Membrane forces
 4. Nodes
 UX, UY, UZ PHIX, PHIY, PHIZ global rotations
 global displacements
 5. Result sets
 Result sets defined in SOFIMSHA will be selected with TYPE RSET:xxxxx, where xxxxx is either the ID of the item within a set to be evaluated or a number if the x-th item of all result sets should be evaluated. Supported are all forces and moments of beam, truss and cable elements, forces and stresses in the center of QUAD and BRIC elements and nodal displacements, support forces and spring forces (but not resultant PT) Also any formula expressions within a result set definition will inihbit to select this item as an influence line for ELLA.

Supported are all forces and moments of beam, truss and cable elements, forces and stresses in the center of QUAD and BRIC elements and nodal displacements, support forces and spring forces (but not resultant PT) Also any formula expressions within a result set definition will inihbit to select this item as an influence line for ELLA..
 At FROM and TO the idents of the result sets may be specified in lexical order (FROM may also contain wildcards, e.g. "SU*") .
 The evaluation of the influence lines for nodal support forces is possible by an import of a deflection area caused from a nodal displacement, as force of a supporting spring or via the result sets.
 The evaluation of the influence lines for pile elements does not include the effect of the bedding, thus only the results at the nodes are correct.
 The application of ELLA for plane frames or shear walls provides so many possibilities for miss-understandings, that we do not support this feature.

The table defines all of the input fields required to specify up to six influence‐line or influence‐area load cases in the “LINF” routine.  Each influence line is identified by a two–letter item code and is described by a “type” (T1–T6) and a “load‐case number” (L1–L6).  In addition, two global parameters (PHI and TITL) control the impact factor or characteristic length and the title string.  The table is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default—and can be mapped directly into a RAG‐style vector store as follows.

1. Column Definitions  
   • Item  –  Unique code for each parameter.  
   • Description  –  Short textual explanation of what the parameter controls.  
   • Unit  –  Unit type or data‐format code (e.g. LIT for literal text, LIT24 for a 24‐character literal).  
   • Default  –  Value used when the user does not provide one.  A dash (–) means no default; an asterisk (*) typically indicates a free‐text or length‐based input with no preset.

2. Influence‐Line Definition Fields (T1/L1 through T6/L6)  
   • T1, T2, T3, T4, T5, T6 (Unit = LIT; Default = MAMI)  
     –  “Type of the nth influence line.”  This literal text field accepts one of four keywords:  
       ­ MAMI  –  Evaluate both minimum and maximum influence envelope  
       ­ MAX   –  Only evaluate the maximum envelope  
       ­ MIN   –  Only evaluate the minimum envelope  
       ­ ACC   –  Use the case only as a corresponding (accumulated) influence line  
     –  If the keyword is omitted, MAMI is assumed.  
   • L1, L2, L3, L4, L5, L6 (Unit = —; Default = –)  
     –  “Load case number for the nth influence line.”  This integer refers to a previously stored influence‐line or influence‐area load case.  
     –  Positive numbers trigger bending‐type impact factors; negative numbers trigger shear‐type factors (see “CalculationofInfluenceAreas,” “LANE,” “ECHO,” and “SHOW” for details).  
     –  No default is provided, so a valid load case index must be specified.

3. Impact Factor / Characteristic Length (PHI)  
   • Item = PHI (Unit = —; Default = *)  
   –  Defines either an impact factor directly or a characteristic length if given with a length unit (e.g. “2.0m”).  
   –  If omitted, a default rule internal to the LINF routine applies (typically based on span length or national annex).  
   –  The asterisk indicates that the field is optional but free‐format.

4. Influence‐Line Title (TITL)  
   • Item = TITL (Unit = LIT24; Default = *)  
   –  A 24-character literal title assigned to the entire influence‐line set.  
   –  Useful for distinguishing multiple LINF runs in reports and prints.  
   –  The default “*” means no title is printed.

Usage notes:  
– You may define from one up to six influence‐line definitions in a single LINF record.  
– Only the results are printed; they are not written back into the database.  
– For each Tn/Ln pair, the keyword controls envelope type while the load‐case number tells the system which pre‐computed influence line to import.  
– The separation of positive/negative indices for bending versus shear impact factors ensures that influence lines originally generated for different internal actions can be handled in one pass.

See also: CalculationofInfluenceAreas, LANE, ECHO, SHOW
 LINF
 Influence lines or areas which were stored as load cases can be taken over for the evaluation along the defined lane axis. However, results are only printed and do not get stored in the database.
 Up to six corresponding influence lines can be defined together.
 For type T1 to T6 one can enter:
 MAMI = Evaluation for minimum and maximum
 MAX = Evaluation for maximum
 MIN = Evaluation for minimum
 ACC = Evaluation only as corresponding line
 Positive load case numbers are processed with the first set of impact factors (bending), while negative load case numbers use the second set (shear).

The table summarizes two key input parameters—TYPE and TGEN—used when computing influence lines (or influence areas) in structural‐analysis software. Both items control how and where unit loads are applied along beam elements, and they interact with other settings (for example, APPL, CALC, CTRL) to balance accuracy against CPU time.

1. General Structure  
   - Columns  
     • Item: Parameter name;  
     • Description: What the parameter governs;  
     • Unit: Measurement unit or notation;  
     • Default: Pre‐set value if the user does not override.  
   - Rows  
     • TYPE: Defines the direction(s) of unit forces;  
     • TGEN: Governs the generation of additional loading locations within an element.

2. ITEM = TYPE  
   • Description  
     “Direction of the unit forces.” This setting determines along which axes or planes the software will place its unit (“1.0”) loadings when constructing influence lines or surfaces. It effectively controls the family of influence functions generated.  
   • Supported Options (labeled by keywords):  
     – MONO: Only centric vertical loading. A single, centrally located, purely vertical unit force; suitable for the simplest bending influence.  
     – STAN: Only vertical loading, but not restricted to the centroid; the standard vertical‐load influence. (This is the default.)  
     – TRAV: Adds transverse (horizontal) loading cases in addition to vertical. Useful for two‐and three‐dimensional beam‐and‐frame models where lateral effects are important.  
     – FULL: Further augments the set by including longitudinal (axial) unit loads. Recommended only in full 3D analysis, where combined axial–flexural interaction must be captured.  
   • Unit: LIT (an internal code used by the program to recognize load‐type lists)  
   • Default: STAN  
   • Context / Notes  
     Use the default STAN for typical 2D beam models. Switch to TRAV or FULL once your model has out‐of‐plane stiffness or axial effects that cannot be neglected. According to the APPL discussion, using fewer directions (e.g., retaining STAN) reduces CPU time; only in fully 3D problems do the extra load directions (TRAV, FULL) become essential.

3. ITEM = TGEN  
   • Description  
     “Accuracy of the cross‐section jumps.” Internally, the software examines adjacent cross sections along each beam element and computes their stiffness difference via the reciprocal‐stiffness measure. Where this difference exceeds (TGEN × reference), an extra loading location (node) is inserted.  
   • Purpose  
     To adaptively refine the influence‐line discretization in regions where stiffness changes sharply (for example, at changes in section modulus or taper). This avoids missing localized peaks in the influence function.  
   • Unit: — (dimensionless tolerance)  
   • Default: 0.0  
   • Context / Notes  
     – A TGEN of zero triggers placement of extra points whenever any non‐zero stiffness jump is found, maximizing resolution at the cost of more load cases.  
     – Increasing TGEN reduces the number of inserted points, improving speed but potentially under‐resolving abrupt stiffness changes. Balance TGEN against the desired accuracy for bending‐moment or shear‐force influence shapes.  
     – See also the “CalculationofInfluenceAreas” and “CTRL APPL” topics for recommendations on setting TGEN in large or three‐dimensional systems.

4. How These Items Interact with APPL  
   • APPL controls the breadth of load cases (monodirectional, standard, traverse, full) and thus the CPU time required.  
   • Keeping TYPE at its default and TGEN at zero delivers maximum fidelity in typical 2D analyses.  
   • For three‐dimensional structures, selectively enabling transverse or longitudinal load cases (TRAV, FULL) and fine‐tuning TGEN allows you to capture critical interaction effects while preventing a combinatorial explosion of influence‐line computations.

In summary, TYPE and TGEN form a complementary pair: TYPE chooses the directions of unit loadings, and TGEN governs where along each element extra loading points are inserted. Properly adjusting these parameters lets engineers tailor computational effort to the complexity and dimensionality of their models.

sections: 3.12 APPL – Control of the Loading Location

content:
See also: CalculationofInfluenceAreas, CALC, CTRL
 APPL
 The CPU time for obtaining the influence lines can be reduced by using the default value of APPL. The options TRAV and FULL are only useful for three-dimensional systems with the corresponding loads.
 The item TGEN specifies at which cross sections within a beam element the additional loading locations are defined. A loading location is inserted, when the difference of the reciprocal stiffness of two neighbouring cross sections is larger than a multiple of TGEN.

The table defines a set of “SIZE”-type records used to control sheet layout, scaling, framing and pen assignment whenever influence-line graphics are produced.  In effect, these inputs govern the paper format, borders, subdivisions, and the pen (line-style) numbering for various influence-line plots.  Below is a detailed walk-through of each table entry, its purpose, units, and default setting:

1. TYPE  (paper orientation)  
   • Description: selects the basic sheet format.  
   • Behavior:  
     – Positive value → Landscape orientation.  
     – Negative value → Portrait orientation.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: –lp (i.e. landscape by default)

2. SC  (scale factor)  
   • Description: overall graphic scaling.  
   • Special setting: when set to 0, the drawing is filled to the sheet (“format filling”).  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: * (i.e. automatic or user-defined)

3. W  (paper width)  
   • Description: physical width of the drawing sheet.  
   • Unit: cm  
   • Default: none (must be specified if overriding default format)

4. H  (paper height)  
   • Description: physical height of the drawing sheet.  
   • Unit: cm  
   • Default: none

5. MARG  (frame border)  
   • Description: toggles drawing of inner and/or outer borders.  
   • Possible values (literal text, LIT):  
     – OFF → no border drawn.  
     – NO → only the inner (primary) border is drawn.  
     – YES → adds a secondary border in addition to the primary.  
     – FULL → draws both primary and an extra outer border around the sheet.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: FULL

6. FORM  (border style)  
   • Description: selects the form or style of the border frame.  
   • Options (LIT):  
     – STAN → standard frame.  
     – ZTVK → ZTVK-88 frame definition.  
     – URS → URSULA standard.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: ZTVK

7. HDIV  (sheet subdivision)  
   • Description: number of horizontal subdivisions (strips) per sheet, enabling multiple influence-line plots on one page.  
   • Positive values: subdivide the paper height, drawing lane axes parallel to the width.  
   • Negative values: subdivide the paper width instead.  
   • If unspecified, the system defaults to three lanes along the larger dimension.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: * (i.e. automatic, three strips)

Pen-number assignments (C1 through C9)  
Each C-item assigns a “pen number.”  A negative pen number suppresses plotting of that line type altogether.  If you do not input a SIZE record, no graphics are produced.  You also control which lines get plotted via the SHOW record, and whether load positions appear (ECHO LPOS).  

• C1  – Pen number for vertical influence lines  
       Unit: none; Default: 1000  
• C2  – Pen number for torsional influence lines  
       Default: 1001  
• C3  – Pen number for transverse influence lines  
       Default: 1002  
• C4  – Pen number for longitudinal influence lines  
       Default: 1003  
• C5  – Pen number for positive uniform loadings  
       Default: 0  
• C6  – Pen number for negative uniform loadings  
       Default: 0  
• C7  – Pen number reserved (no current assignment)  
       Default: – (none)  
• C8  – Pen number for general loadings (point loads, moving loads, etc.)  
       Default: 2001  
• C9  – Fill-area number for plotted load areas  
       Default: 2235  

Contextual notes:  
– Graphic output is only generated once a SIZE record is given.  
– If a pen number is set below zero, that type of influence or load line is omitted.  
– SHOW controls exactly which lines appear; ECHO LPOS adds markers at actual load positions (otherwise only the influence envelopes are shown, reducing the number of plots).  
– Lines are coded per the GPLI standard.  
– HDIV subdivides the sheet so multiple influence-line diagrams share the same page. Positive HDIV values split along the height; negative split along the width; unspecified defaults to three parallel strips.

Without ECHO LPOS only the influence lines will be shown, with ECHO LPOS the actual load position will be also visualized, which will need more pictures in general.

The table below defines the input parameters for the SHOW record (often invoked together with ECHO IL and/or SIZE) that controls which influence‐line or influence‐value outputs are printed or plotted. In combination with the auxiliary records (SIZE, ECHO, LINF), it lets you select specific lanes (SNO), element types (TYPE), individual elements (NO), beam positions (X), the kind of lines to display (ETYP), the spacing of output points (DSV), and a minimum scaling threshold (YMAX).

1. SNO  (Lane Number)  
   – Description: Selects which traffic or load lanes to include in the output.  
     • 0 → all lanes  
     • lit4 → all lanes defined on axis “lit4”  
     • lit4.n → only lane n of axis “lit4”  
   – Unit: (none)  
   – Default: 0  

2. TYPE  (Influence Location)  
   – Description: Filters by structural entity or region when computing influence lines/values.  
     • ALL → all element types (default)  
     • LINF → only explicit bending‐area influence zones (equivalent to LINF record)  
     • BEAM → beam elements  
     • TRUS → truss elements  
     • CABL → cable elements  
     • SPRI → spring elements  
     • QUAD → plane (quadrilateral) elements  
   – Unit: LIT (literal tag)  
   – Default: ALL  

3. NO  (Element or First LINF‐Case Number)  
   – Description: Specifies a single element number or, when TYPE=LINF, the first bending‐area case.  
   – If omitted, all elements (or all LINF cases) are included.  
   – Unit: (none)  
   – Default: 0  

4. X  (Position Along Beam Elements)  
   – Description: Defines the local X–coordinate for output on beam‐type elements.  
   – If omitted, results are computed at all standard beam integration points.  
   – Unit: (none)  
   – Default: –  

5. ETYP  (Type of Influence Lines)  
   – Description: Chooses whether to plot only extreme‐value lines or all corresponding influence lines.  
     • EXTR → only the lines showing extreme maxima/minima  
     • ALL → include all individual component lines plus the extremes  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: ALL  

6. DSV  (Distance of Output Values)  
   – Description: Minimum interval (along a beam or influence axis) between printed or plotted sample points.  
   – Extreme (end) points are always included, even if they fall closer together than DSV.  
   – Unit: (none)  
   – Default: “*” (automatic spacing)  

7. YMAX  (Minimum Value to Scale the Line)  
   – Description: Values whose absolute magnitude falls below YMAX are suppressed (effectively zero) in the display.  
   – Unit: (none)  
   – Default: 1.0 × 10⁻⁶  

Additional context:  
– SHOW works in tandem with ECHO IL (which controls the lines printed) and SIZE (which can rescale or rearrange the graphic presentation).  
– DSV ensures that sample points along an influence line are not too densely packed; however, the first and last (extreme) points always appear, guaranteeing that peak values are captured.  
– Up to four superimposed lines may appear per result set, representing the three orthogonal force components plus the torsional moment (where applicable).  
– By combining SNO, TYPE, NO, and X, you can isolate exactly the lane, element family, element ID, and local position for which you want influence results.

See also: SIZE, ECHO, LINF
 SHOW
 With SHOW the lines which should be printed (record ECHO IL) and / or plotted (record SIZE) are selected. The item DSV controls the distance between marked positions in the output. Available values are shown then at least in this distance. However, extreme values are output additionally in all cases. There will be up to four lines for three force components and the torsional moment. The presentation may be changed with record SIZE.

The table shown defines the parameters you must supply whenever you declare or redefine an “action” (loading type) in SOFiLOAD (and downstream in MAXIMA/AQB). It has four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and the rows correspond to all of the fields you can set. Below is a guided tour through each row and how it ties back to the RAG-vector store and to the additional context on combination rules, categories and superposition.  

1.  TYPE  
    •  “Designation of action” (e.g. G, Q, L_T, UDL, A, E)  
    •  Literal up to 4 characters; reserved codes come from the INI-file for your design code (EN, DIN, etc.)  
    •  You may append up to two category letters (A–Z) separated by an underscore (e.g. Q_A, Q_B).  CATEGORY “Q” alone means “all Q_?”  
    •  Unit: LIT4  
    •  Default: “!” (mandatory—you must supply it)  

2.  GAMU  
    •  Unfavourable partial safety factor γ<sub>G</sub> (e.g. 1.35 for dead load)  
    •  Drives ultimate limit‐state combinations; if the sign is unfavourable, it is applied.  
    •  Default: “*” → inherits from the INI-file or previous definition  

3.  GAMF  
    •  Favourable partial safety factor γ<sub>G,fav</sub>  
    •  Used when the action produces a favourable effect (e.g. upward self‐weight).  
    •  Default: “*”  

4.  PSI0, PSI1, PSI2, PS1S  
    •  Combination coefficients ψ<sub>0</sub> (rare), ψ<sub>1</sub> (frequent), ψ<sub>2</sub> (quasi‐permanent), ψ<sub>1S</sub> (infrequent)  
    •  Used to reduce accompanying variable actions in combination rules (EN 1990 Table A2, DIN 1055, OENORM, etc.)  
    •  Default: “*”  

5.  GAMA  
    •  Partial safety factor for accidental actions (γ<sub>A</sub>)  
    •  Default: “*”  

6.  PART  
    •  Partition (load group) into which this action is classified for combination formulas:  
       –  G  permanent (dead loads)  
       –  P  prestress  
       –  Q  variable action (live loads)  
       –  Q_1 … Q_99  sub-groups of variable actions for advanced grouping (e.g. different truck loads on bridges)  
       –  A  accidental action  
       –  E  seismic action  
    •  PART determines which sum or max‐rule the superposition engine uses (see “superposition equations” in EN 1990, MAXIMA manual)  
    •  Default: “*” (must follow TYPE or be set explicitly for user-defined actions)  

7.  SUP  
    •  Default superposition behavior of multiple load cases within this action:  
       –  PERM  permanent with unique factor (sum all load cases, use one γ)  
       –  PERC  permanent with per-case factors  
       –  COND  conditional (add only if unfavourable)  
       –  EXCL  mutually exclusive within category  
       –  EXEX  mutually exclusive across all categories of this action  
       –  UNSI  COND but only if sign is unfavourable  
       –  USEX  EXCL but only for unfavourable sign  
       –  ALEX  permanent‐alternative (always one case per action, even if favourable)  
    •  If you do not specify SUP, it defaults via INI-file rules: leading “G”→PERM, “Q”→COND, else EXCL.  
    •  Default: “*”  

8.  TITL

How this ties into RAG/vector storage for a Retrieval‐Augmented Generation system:  
•  You can index each action definition (TYPE, PART, SUP, safety factors, ψ’s, title) as one document or vector entry.  
•  Queries like “What is the ψ₂ coefficient for bicycle loads in EN 1990?” or “Which SUP rule applies to permanent actions?” will map to these fields.  
•  The context text explains how categories subdivide an action, how default values are inherited from the INI-file, and how MAXIMA performs intermediate and final superpositions based on PART and SUP.  

By documenting each parameter this way, the RAG system can supply precise answers about combination factors, load grouping, superposition rules and code defaults whenever an engineer or analyst poses a question.

The table summarizes two preset “actions” (that is, action types to which load cases may be assigned) and shows for each action how it is designated in three different contexts—normal, additional and special loading—and provides a short remark on its meaning.

Columns  
1. Normal: the basic literal used when defining a load case with ACT … (e.g. ACT G means dead‐load action)  
2. Add.: the variant of the action used when the load case is treated as “additional loading” (ZG… for Z‐prefix actions)  
3. Spec.: the variant for “special loading” (SG… for S-prefix actions)  
4. Remark: a human‐readable note, often indicating which subcategories or coefficients the action comprises  

Rows  
Row 1: “no action”  
– Normal = “—” (displayed as a dash) and italic “NONE”  
– Add. = (empty)  
– Spec. = (empty)  
– Remark = “for LC only: not assigned to an action”  
  • This row covers load cases that are purely local or intermediate calculations and are not tied to any permanent, variable or accidental action.  
  • In SOFiLOAD syntax you would not use any ACT … statement for such load cases.

Row 2: “dead‐load action G”  
– Normal = Gᵍ (the superscript g emphasizes that this is the ordinary dead‐load group)  
– Add. = ZGᵍ (prefix Z for additional dead load)  
– Spec. = SGᵍ (prefix S for special dead load)  
– Remark = “dead load (G + G_1 + G_2)”  
  • The basic action label is ACT G; it implicitly comprises the two subcategories G_1 and G_2 unless those are addressed individually (ACT G_1, ACT G_2).  
  • If the user wants to mark a load case as “additional dead load” it is defined with ACT ZG, and “special dead load” with ACT SG.  
  • When combining these actions in MAXIMA or AQUA superposition rules, all three—G, G_1 and G_2—belong to the same permanent‐action group (PART G) and follow the default superposition (usually SUP PERM).

How to use in context  
– In an INI file or via ACT commands you select one of these literals as the action type for each load case.  
– For permanent actions (G) the PART item defaults to PART G, so they enter the G‐term of the limit‐state superposition.  
– Z‐prefixed and S-prefixed variants inherit the same PART but can be treated separately in combination rules if needed (e.g. add vs. special dead loads).  
– The “none” entry ensures that LC records without an ACT assignment do not erroneously pick up a default action.

The table establishes a one-to-one correspondence between SOFiLOAD’s SUP codes (the way in which multiple load cases belonging to the same action are superposed) and the equivalent MAXIMA “LC TYPE” identifiers, and then defines in plain language how each mode behaves in combination.  In a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) vector store you would want to capture at least these three facets for each entry: the SUP literal, its MAXIMA counterpart, and a concise but precise description of the combination rule.  Below is a descriptive enumeration of all entries:

1.  SUP = PERM  
    • MAXIMA LC TYPE = PERM, G  
    • Explanation: “Always” (permanent) superposition.  All load cases of this action are summed; a single partial safety factor (γ) is applied action-wise rather than load-case-wise.  

2.  SUP = PERC  
    • MAXIMA LC TYPE = PERC  
    • Explanation: Also “permanent,” but each load case may carry its own partial safety factor.  Load cases are combined unconditionally, yet their γ’s can vary individually.  

3.  SUP = COND  
    • MAXIMA LC TYPE = COND, Q  
    • Explanation: “Conditional” superposition—only those load cases that produce an unfavourable (i.e. worst-case) effect are included.  Favourable contributions are omitted.  

4.  SUP = EXCL  
    • MAXIMA LC TYPE = An₀ (alternative-group syntax)  
    • Explanation: Mutually exclusive within each category.  Only one load case per category is chosen, based on alternative-group numbers specified in the MAXIMA LC record.  Different categories get different group numbers.  

5.  SUP = EXEX  
    • MAXIMA LC TYPE = An₀  
    • Explanation: “Exclusive-exclusive”—load cases are mutually exclusive but inclusion is conditional.  Here all categories of an action share the same alternative-group number, so only one category’s load cases can ever be active.  

6.  SUP = UNSI  
    • MAXIMA LC TYPE = W  
    • Explanation: “Unsigned” or sign-changing loads (e.g. seismic).  Positive or negative excursions can both be considered, depending on which extreme is more unfavourable.  

7.  SUP = USEX  
    • MAXIMA LC TYPE = Xn₀  
    • Explanation: Sign-changing and mutually exclusive.  Each load case that changes sign also belongs to an alternative group (specified via the MAXIMA record), so that only one sign-direction or position is active at a time.  

8.  SUP = ALEX  
    • MAXIMA LC TYPE = AGn₀  
    • Explanation: “Always but exclusive” within the same action.  All load cases of an action are treated as permanent alternatives: exactly one is selected, even if it contributes favourably, and each is assigned to an AGn group in the LC record.  

9.  SUP = F  
    • MAXIMA LC TYPE = (none)  
    • Explanation: A special tag indicating an additional load case that should be combined in every superposition, regardless of other rules.  

Key points for RAG indexing:  
- “SUP” defines the default interaction among load cases of the same action.  
- “LC TYPE” is the literal or notation used in MAXIMA input to enforce that rule, often including an alternative-group suffix number.  
- The plain-language “Explanation” notes whether load cases are summed, mutually exclusive, conditional on unfavourability, sign-changing, or treated as permanent alternatives.  

Capturing these three columns in your vector store will allow downstream prompts or agents to retrieve, for any given SUP code, exactly how MAXIMA expects the load cases to be labeled and combined.

The table below defines the structure and semantics of the LC (Load Case) record, which is used to assemble and control all subsequent loading definitions (trains, combinations, factors) in a bridge or structural‐analysis data set.  Each row corresponds to one parameter of the LC record.  Whenever the user invokes an “LC” record, it must be followed by one or more TRAI/TRPL/TRBL records that fully specify each load train in that case.  In the post‐processing phase, the program MAXIMA will collect the maximum values across all defined trains and combination factors to generate the final design load cases.

1.  NO (Number of Load Case)  
 •  Description: Unique identifier (integer) of the load case.  No two LC records in the same file may share the same NO value.  
 •  Unit: none  
 •  Default: 1  
 •  Remarks: Serves as the primary key for referencing this set of loads in later commands, combination definitions, or result extraction.

2.  TYPE (Action Type of Load Case)  
 •  Description: A literal code (LIT) that selects the action category (e.g. permanent, variable traffic, wind, temperature, accidental, etc.).  This choice influences the default combination (“ψ”) values and safety factors if not explicitly overridden in this record.  
 •  Unit: LIT (text string)  
 •  Default: none (must normally be specified unless inherited from a higher‐level template)

3.  PSI0 (Combination Value ‐ Standard)  
 •  Description: Partial‐factor or combination factor ψ0 used to scale secondary actions when assembling ultimate limit‐state load combinations under the “standard” rule.  
 •  Unit: none  
 •  Default: “*” (indicates use of the default value defined in EN 1990/EC1 Part 3, App. C or in national annexes)

4.  PSI1 (Combination Value ‐ Frequent)  
 •  Description: Partial‐factor ψ1 for assembling serviceability limit‐state combinations under the “frequent” rule (loads expected to occur frequently during the structure’s life).  
 •  Unit: none  
 •  Default: “*” (see EC1 default table or country‐specific settings, e.g. ÖNORM augmentations)

5.  PSI2 (Combination Value ‐ Quasi-Permanent)  
 •  Description: Partial‐factor ψ2 for “quasi‐permanent” combinations (loads that are present for very long durations).  
 •  Unit: none  
 •  Default: “*” (applies the EC1 Part 3 Appendix C default or user’s national annex)

6.  PS1S (Combination Value ‐ Non-Permanent)  
 •  Description: A variant of ψ1 used for non-permanent or exceptional actions (e.g. very rare loads, extreme wind or temperature).  
 •  Unit: none  
 •  Default: “*” (defaults as defined by the relevant design code)

7.  GAMU (Unfavourable Safety Factor)  
 •  Description: γ<sub>0</sub> factor applied to actions or materials in the Ultimate Limit State (ULS) in an unfavourable sense (increasing load or reducing resistance).  
 •  Unit: none  
 •  Default: “*” (EC1 default or national annex)

8.  GAMF (Favourable Safety Factor)  
 •  Description: γ<sub>0</sub> factor applied in a favourable sense (decreasing load or increasing resistance) for ULS checks, if permitted.  
 •  Unit: none  
 •  Default: “*” (defaults from EC1 or DIN‐Fachberichte, as applicable)

9.  TITL (Title of Load Case)  
 •  Description: Human‐readable name or title (up to 24 characters) for this LC record, used in reports and plots.  
 •  Unit: Lit24 (character string length ≤ 24)  
 •  Default: none  

Additional Notes:  
•  Whenever any of the combination factors (PSI0, PSI1, PSI2, PS1S, GAMU, GAMF) is marked with “*”, the program will automatically retrieve the appropriate boxed value from the code database (EN 1990/EC1 or national annex such as ÖNORM B 4750).  For example, ÖNORM may add +0.1 to ψ1 and ψ2 for truck loads within the 30–60 kN category.  
•  The LC record must precede all TRAI (load train definition), TRPL/TRBL (explicit line‐by‐line assignment of loads) entries.  The system computes for each resulting load case the maximum effort across all load patterns and trains.  
•  Deviations in partial coefficients for wind and temperature loads are common when modelling bridges or other non‐building structures.  Users should verify that the national annex values and DIN‐Fachberichte combination rules are consistent with project requirements.

Below is a structured, field‐by‐field description of the “TRAI” input table, which defines all the parameters needed to model moving load trains (road, rail, wind, braking, etc.) in a multibody‐dynamics or static‐loading analysis.  Wherever relevant, cross‐references to COPY, TRPL, TRBL, LANE, TREX are noted.

1. Table Layout  
   • Four main columns:  
     – Item: the parameter name or keyword.  
     – Description: a concise statement of the parameter’s meaning.  
     – Unit: the physical unit or data type (LIT = literal/text, “–” = dimensionless, specific units like kN, m, kN/m²).  
     – Default: the value assumed if the user does not specify otherwise (“*” means user must provide or default from the standard train).

2. First Parameter Block: Core Load-Train Definitions  
   • TYPE (LIT; default = CONS)  
     – Keyword that selects a predefined load train (e.g. LM71, SW/0, UIC71, HB) or “USER” for a fully custom arrangement.  
   • P1, P2, P3, P4 (kN or m; default = *)  
     – Up to four numerical input values that define axle loads, spacings or moments depending on TYPE.  For instance, P1 could be the class of train (LM71), or an explicit wheel load if TYPE=USER.  
   • P5 (kN/m²; default = *)  
     – Residual area loading on zones not covered by wheel lines (between train width and lane boundary), without dynamic or centrifugal factors.  Used for GR4 pedestrian loads, pathways, etc.  
   • P6 (–; default = *)  
     – Wind loading magnitude.  Can represent area, line load (AASHTO), or combined wind‐traffic band.  
   • P7 ([m]; default = *)  
     – Height at which P6 acts (wind‐attack area), or height of line load in AASHTO style.  
   • P8 (–; default = *)  
     – Brake or acceleration load parameter.  Sign determined by train direction (positive for braking in forward travel, negative for acceleration).  
   • P9 ([m]; default = *)  
     – Height of mass center for applying centrifugal force or cross‐fall moment.  
   • PFAC (–; default = 1.0)  
     – Global load factor for all elements of the train.  Typical values follow EN 1991‐2 clause 6.3.2(3) (0.75 … 1.46).  
   • PFAV (–; default = * )  
     – Favorable load factor (reduces effect when beneficial).  Defaults vary: rail LM71→0.0, other rail→1.0, most road trains→0.0.  
   • WIDT ([m]; default = *)  
     – Total transverse width of the load train.

3. Second Block: Impact, Speed and Centrifugal Factors  
   • PHI (–; default = *)  
     – Explicit user‐defined impact factor for bending.  Overrides standard impact algorithms.  
   • PHIS (–; default = *)  
     – Explicit impact factor for shear.  
   • V ([km/h]; default = *)  
     – Traveling speed of the train.  Influences dynamic amplification.  
   • FUGA (–; default = 1.0)  
     – Mass‐factor multiplier for calculating centrifugal forces (affects P9 application).

4. Third Block: Convoy Spacing, Eccentricity and Directionality  
   • XCON ([m]; default = 0)  
     – Minimum convoy distance when repeating the same train multiple times.  Ensures repetition with a specified gap between the last axle of one train and the first axle of the next.  
   • YEX ([m]; default = 0.0)  
     – Eccentricity of the entire train within its lane (±).  For railway loads, default ±r/18 in either direction per EN 1991-2 6.3.5; for heavy road loads an explicit offset may be defined.  
   • DIR (LIT; default = B)  
     – Direction of longitudinal loading:  
       R = positive/right (forward braking),  
       L = negative/left (acceleration in reverse),  
       B = both directions allowed,  
       N = do not apply (no dynamic factors, no braking or wind).  
   • DIRT (LIT; default = B)  
     – Direction of transverse (side) loading: same code as DIR, but if N is chosen that lateral load is suppressed.  

5. Usage Notes & Cross-References  
   – If TYPE=USER, the user must manually subtract the default P5 area load where the custom wheel lines act, and verify convoy spacing.  
   – TRPL / TRBL can be appended to define additional point loads or uniformly spaced line loads on top of the TYPE train.  
   – For multi‐body dynamics (TREX), interactive masses, springs, dampers and bogie/wheel properties can be generated; P8 or negative fractions of total mass may define bogie/wheel masses.  
   – Wind and traffic can be combined with record P6/P7 or via section definitions in COPY.  
   – ELLA filters may deactivate loads based on DIR/​DIRT choices or user‐defined logic.  
   – Standard named load trains include:  
     • Rail: LM71 (UIC 71), SW/0–SW/2 (DS 804/EC), HSLM, RL, ASRT, RFAT fatigue.  
     • Road: CSA pedestrian, BS 5400 HA/HB, French Fascicule 61, Australian AS 5100 M1600/S1600, Indian IRC AA/B, JRA T/L, Swedish BRO types.  

This table thus centralizes all numeric and categorical inputs required to represent moving‐vehicle and wind‐loading scenarios on a structure, ensuring consistency with various national codes and dynamic‐loading standards.

1. Table Identity

   • Context:  Record used in structural analysis software to define moving loads (“load trains”) and dynamic parameters for multi-body train models.

2. Column Definitions  
   The TRAI table appears to follow a simple four-column layout—each row defines one input parameter:

   • Column 2: Human-readable description of what the parameter controls (e.g. “Frequency for body spring Cb”)  
   • Column 3: Engineering units (e.g. “1/sec”)  
   • Column 4: Default or recommended value (e.g. “∞” for infinite stiffness).  

3. Example Row  
   • FRB | Frequency for body Spring Cb | 1/sec | ∞  
     – Governs the natural frequency of the “body” spring in a multibody train model.  If set to infinity, that degree of freedom is effectively rigid.

4. Narrative Annotations and Usage Rules  
   Beyond the pure table, the text supplies detailed instructions and constraints:  
   – XCON (convoy distance): allows repeating a train definition at fixed spacing along the bridge.  
   – P5 (residual area load): applied without impact factors or centrifugal forces on areas outside the train’s finite width, on inter-lane regions and for pedestrian-only load group GR4.  
   – PFAC: general multiplier for all wheel/axle loads (values typically drawn from EN 1991-2 clause 6.3.2(3): 0.75 – 1.46).  
   – PFAV: favorable‐loading factor for wheel loads only; default railway LM71 = 0.0, other trains = 1.0; road trains default 0.0 unless overridden per train.  
   – YEX: eccentricity of the load set within the lane; for railways default ±r/18 in any direction per EN 1991-2 6.3.5; for road trains a single lateral offset.  
   – DIR: specifies traffic direction (N = no dynamic impacts & zero braking/wind loads; B = bidirectional braking sign changes).  Also defines sequence of axle applications.  
   – P6/P7: wind‐loading magnitude and band height for combined wind+traffic cases; AASHTO uses them as line loads.  DIRT + POSL options allow automatic worst‐case wind direction.  
   – P8: meaning varies by train type, generally the braking load magnitude, sign taken from DIR; can be deactivated or reversed in ELLA/SOFILOAD modules.  

5. Multi-Body-Dynamics Extension (TREX)  
   – TREX record allows automatic generation of masses, beams, springs and dampers for a moving train.  
   – Bogie and wheel masses may be absolute positive values or negative fractions of the total train mass.

6. Predefined Load-Train Library  
   Following the parameter rules, the document enumerates a comprehensive library of standard trains drawn from global codes.  Each entry is effectively a value for P1 in TRAI.  Examples include:  
   • CSA pedestrian load  
   • HA/HB (BS 5400/BD 37-01)  
   • UIC 71 (LM71)  
   • SW/0, SW/2 heavy loads (DS 804/EC)  
   • AASHTO “Fatigue” and HSLM (Eurocode)  
   • AS 5100 series (Australia)  
   • Indian IRC classes  
   • Swedish BRO types 1–5 (axle patterns)  
   • French Fascicule 61 and Cerema/Leclerc heavy loads  
   • “USER” literal for custom-user trains (inherits PFAC, PFAV, etc.)

7. Extension Mechanisms  
   • TRPL/TRBL records can further append individual axle loads or bridges to any predefined train.  
   • USER trains require manual subtraction of default P5 residual area load and careful check of inter-axle distances.

The table excerpt defines seven numeric parameters used to configure a multi-body dynamic model—most likely via the TREX record in a “TRAI” loading definition. Each row names one parameter (Item), gives a concise Description, specifies its physical Unit, and lists a Default value applied if the user does not override it. These settings allow the user to introduce mass, spring and damping properties for the vehicle body, bogie and wheels when simulating dynamic load effects on a structure.

Columns  
• Item  
  – A short alphanumeric code (up to four characters) that the solver recognizes when parsing TREX or related records.  
• Description  
  – A human-readable label explaining what mechanical property the parameter controls.  
• Unit  
  – The unit of measure. A dash “–” denotes a dimensionless quantity (e.g. a ratio). “1/sec” is a natural frequency, and “–/kN” indicates a mass value specified either as a positive absolute force (kN) or as a negative fraction of total mass.  
• Default  
  – The value assumed if the user omits the parameter. Zeros turn off that effect; “∞” (infinite frequency) effectively makes a spring rigid (no compliance) by default.

Rows and Their Roles  
1. DAB  
   • Modal Damping of body support  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless damping ratio)  
   • Default: 0.0 (no damping applied to the vehicle body)  
2. BOGI  
   • Load value of bogie  
   • Unit: –/kN (mass of the bogie)  
   • Default: 0.0 (bogie mass ignored unless specified)  
3. FRBO  
   • Frequency for bogie spring Cb0  
   • Unit: 1/sec (natural frequency of the spring that supports the bogie)  
   • Default: ∞ (spring is infinitely stiff by default)  
4. DABO  
   • Modal Damping of bogie support  
   • Unit: – (damping ratio at bogie spring)  
   • Default: 0.0  
5. WHEE  
   • Load value of wheel  
   • Unit: –/kN (mass of an individual wheel or wheel set)  
   • Default: 0.0  
6. FRWH  
   • Frequency for wheel spring Cwh  
   • Unit: 1/sec (natural frequency at the wheel–bogie interface)  
   • Default: ∞ (rigid wheel support unless changed)  
7. DAWH  
   • Modal Damping of wheel support  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless)  
   • Default: 0.0  

How It Fits in RAG/VSM Context  
In a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflow for structural-dynamic queries, these parameters help index the specifics of multi-body vehicle models. When a user asks for “wheel damping effects” or “bogie mass distribution” in a bridge load analysis, the vector store can retrieve this table description, then guide downstream prompts to set DABO or BOGI accordingly. Mentioning related records—TREX, TRPL, TRBL or broader TRAI definitions—ensures that users link these spring and mass parameters with braking, wind, residual area loads or convoy spacing settings elsewhere in the input deck.

The provided table, titled “Table of most important Standard Load Trains,” is organized as a two-column reference list. Its primary purpose is to map concise code identifiers (P1 values in the TRAI record) to their corresponding load train definitions and normative sources, so that structural-analysis software (e.g. ELLA, SOFILOAD) can generate characteristic moving loads for bridges, roadways, railways and other traffic-bearing structures.

Structure of the table  
• Column 1 (“Code”): A short alphanumeric label (typically 2–5 characters) used within the TRAI input record.  
• Column 2 (“Description”): A brief name and the applicable standard or guideline reference that fully defines axle spacings, wheel loads, spacings, dynamic factors, etc.

Key entries and their groupings

1. USER  
  – “constant Area Loading P5 / user defined Load Train”  
  – A generic placeholder. When P1=USER, the software omits standard axle arrangements but retains default factors (impact, PFAC/PFAV, YEX eccentricity, etc.). It’s the engineer’s responsibility to define all individual wheel or area loads and to subtract the residual area load (P5) where required.

2. Eurocode-based axle load models (LM-Series)  
  – LM1: double-axle load model 1 (Eurocode 1 Part 2)  
  – LM2: single-axle load model 2 (Eurocode 1 Part 2)  
  – LM3: special case load model 3 (Eurocode 1 Part 2), typically heavy-vehicle variant  
  – LM4: pedestrian load model 4 (Eurocode 1 Part 3), for footbridges and decks

3. Special traffic and fatigue models  
  – SV, SOV: special vehicles according to BS EN 1991-2  
  – FLM1–FLM4: fatigue load models 1–4 (Eurocode 1 Part 3), addressing high-cycle rail or road fatigue effects

4. Truck load categories  
  – SLW: heavy load truck (DIN / ÖNORM / IAB standards)  
  – LKW: standard truck per country code (general road design)  
  – LKWD: German truck definition (in Austria)  
  – LKWA: specifically Austrian truck

5. Regional and specialized loading codes  
  – NBR: Brazilian load trains (NBR 7188 / NB6 similar to SLW)  
  – HS: Highway Load according to AASHTO (e.g. HL-93 or earlier H20)  
  – HT: Highway Truck according to AASHTO  
  – CAN: Highway Load according to Canadian Standard CSA

Each code automatically packages axle spacings, magnitudes, sequence and convoy-distance (XCON) if defined. Default parameters such as PFAC (general load multiplier for classified traffic), PFAV (favourable loading factor for wheel loads), YEX (lateral eccentricity), DIR (directional flag controlling impact application and braking loads) and optional wind loads (P6/P7) remain consistent across all entries unless overridden by an individual load-train specification (via TRPL, TRBL).  

Beyond Eurocode and national standards, additional load trains (e.g. IRC Class AA/B, Swedish BRO types, French Fascicule 61 and Cerema heavy-load definitions, AS 5100 loads) can be appended or customized. When multiple identical trains are required, XCON ensures a minimum separation between convoy modules. Pedestrian or path‐bound load groups (GR4) use area load P5 only, without dynamic or centrifugal factors, limited to lane widths or polygonal lane boundaries.

In summary, this table serves as the core lookup for defining standardized moving loads—covering rail, road, fatigue, truck, pedestrian and wind-coupled scenarios—ensuring compliance with regional and international bridge‐design codes within a RAG vector‐store retrieval workflow.

The final table defines a special fatigue‐design truck load (often called FLM3) as implemented in ELLA under EN 1991-2. It lays out the six input parameters (P1–P5 and P8) for three discrete “classes” of this model—300, 200 and 100—each corresponding to a different severity of fatigue loading. Below is a breakdown of each parameter and how the three columns are used in practice:

1. P1 – Class  
   • 300, 200 or 100  
   • An index identifying the fatigue load severity. Higher classes (e.g. 300) carry a larger axle load and more demanding design requirements.

2. P2 – Axle load [kN]  
   • 300 kN, 200 kN or 100 kN  
   • The characteristic load applied to each of the two double axles. In FLM3 this is fixed per class and remains constant over the fatigue assessment.

3. P3 – Reserved [kN]  
   • Always 0 in this table  
   • A placeholder parameter. Currently not used in FLM3 but must be provided in the input record. It can accommodate future extensions or national‐annex tweaks without altering the record format.

4. P4 – Traffic lane UDL [kN/m²]  
   • 9.0 kN/m² for class 300, 2.5 kN/m² for classes 200 and 100  
   • This is the uniformly distributed load (UDL) representing the weight spread over the entire lane width. It covers residual loading in the same lane, beyond direct wheel footprints.

5. P5 – Residual area [kN/m²]  
   • 2.5 kN/m² for all three classes  
   • An additional UDL covering the lane outside the direct axle/wheel line, simulating “background” traffic effects or unloaded patches that still contribute to fatigue.

6. P8 – Brake loading [kN]  
   • “*” for class 300, 0 for classes 200 and 100  
   • Indicates an optional brake force applied to the foremost double axle. The “*” means that for the highest fatigue class a user must supply a brake load value (or let the software compute it via national provisions), while the lower classes have no brake load contribution.

Contextual notes for RAG vector‐store indexing and retrieval:  
• This load model is mandated when fatigue checks are required on highway bridges under EN 1991-2, clause 4.3.4.  
• It represents two double axles spaced at 6.0 m (this spacing is fixed and not an input parameter in the table).  
• P4 and P5 ensure that both point loads and distributed lane loads are captured—critical for combining local stresses (from wheel loads) with global effects (from UDL).  
• P8 allows modelling of brake forces, which can significantly affect bending moments and fatigue damage in girders.  
• The reserved slot P3 permits national annexes or future code updates to introduce an additional concentrated force without changing the I/O record structure.  

How this table is used in practice:  
– In the ELLA INI‐file you would define a load case, e.g.  
    TYPE = FLM3  
    P1 = 300  
    P2 = 300  
    P3 = 0  
    P4 = 9.0  
    P5 = 2.5  
    P8 = 50   ; an example brake force  
– ELLA then places two double‐axle units 6 m apart, applies the specified axle loads, adds the uniform lane load, includes residual loading, and superimposes any brake force.  
– The output (in RAG vector form) captures each wheel load as a point load at the appropriate longitudinal positions plus a UDL over the full lane width—ready for response‐surface indexing or influence‐line convolution.

The image reproduced as “Figure 3.12: Load model 3” consists of two side-by-side schematic layouts, each showing three parallel notional traffic lanes and the position of a heavy‐vehicle load train under Load Model 3 (EN 1991-2). Both schematics share the same overall geometry and annotations, but the left-hand drawing illustrates the “narrow version” (all axles in one 2.5 m-wide lane plus clipped elements), while the right-hand drawing shows the “broad version” (axles spread across two synchronized lanes, with any overhanging axles clipped).

Common elements in both panels:
• Three vertical “lanes,” each represented by a band of dot‐fill shading.  
  – Lane 1 (left) is lightly stippled and carries the circled label “1.”  
  – Lane 2 (middle) is more densely stippled, labeled “2.”  
  – Lane 3 (right) uses a third dot pattern and shows an upward-pointing arrow marked “x” (traffic direction).  
• On the left edge of the paired diagrams are two dimension lines, each annotated “25 m.” One sits above the loaded zone, the other below, indicating that no other loading is applied within 25 m upstream or downstream of the heavy‐vehicle model.  

Left diagram (“narrow version”):  
– Within Lane 1, two double‐axle symbols (small pairs of adjacent rectangles) are placed centrally on the lane axis. In front of those axles, a solid square block is drawn. This block represents the portion of the vehicle that falls outside the 2.5 m lane width and is conceptually “clipped” when applying the load model—exactly the case where parts of the load train exceed the lane limits.  
– Lane 2 hosts three evenly-spaced double‐axle symbols aligned along its centerline. Lane 3 has no axle symbols in this view.  

Right diagram (“broad version”):  
– The clipped square block is omitted, showing only the axle symbols that lie fully inside the notional lanes.  
– Lane 1 now carries a single set of double‐axle symbols, Lane 2 carries three sets, and Lane 3 carries no axles—this arrangement represents a two-lane synchronized load train where only the axles within the designated lanes are applied.  
– The 25 m “no‐load” buffers at the upstream and downstream ends remain the same.  

Interpretation in EN 1991-2 terms:
• The model assumes each tandem axle system travels on the center‐line of its notional lane (no lateral synchronization with adjacent lanes).  
• For the “narrow version,” all axles (even those partly outside the lane) must be applied in full, hence the clipped block in the left diagram.  
• For the “broad version,” a load train spanning two lanes uses a transverse offset (±0.75 m for the main lane, ±2.25 m for adjacent lanes), so any axle outside the lane limits is automatically excluded (i.e. “clipped”)—hence the cleaner right-hand schematic.  
• Both layouts illustrate the requirement of a 25 m clear run before and after the vehicle, and the placement of double‐axle symbols corresponds to P2 = 240 kN cases where three-axle configurations are used.  
• The arrow “x” indicates the traffic direction, relevant because an impact factor only applies above certain speeds (v>5 km/h) and influences whether front/rear spacings are enforced.  

Together, these two diagrams visually clarify how Load Model 3 is positioned on one or two lanes, how off‐lane axles are treated, and the mandatory 25 m load‐free margins.

The provided illustration is a black-and-white line drawing, titled “Figure 3.20: Load Train SLW,” showing the characteristic configuration of an SLW (Schwerlastwagen) heavy-load train as defined in DIN 1072 (and related standards such as ÖNORM B 4002 or the Spanish IAP).  It is intended for use in bridge-loading analyses alongside the uniformly distributed area loads P3 and P5.  

Overall Layout  
• A heavy rectangular block labeled “P3” occupies the left portion of the drawing.  It sits directly on a horizontal baseline (representing the bridge deck or roadway surface) and represents the secondary traffic band load P3.  Its right edge is marked by a thin vertical line.  
• To the right of that vertical line, still on the same baseline, are a series of down-pointing arrows—each arrow consisting of a slender vertical stem topped by a filled triangular head—indicating the concentrated wheel sets of the SLW train.  

Dimensional Annotations  
• Beneath the baseline, directly under the down-pointing arrows, the spacing between consecutive wheel loads is annotated as “1.5,” indicating 1.5 m center-to-center spacing.  Four such “1.5” marks appear, showing an almost uniformly spaced group of wheel loads.  
• Above the uppermost arrow grouping is a dimension line spanning from the first wheel load position to a point directly over the last; the left marker of that line is labeled “0,” and the right marker “3.3,” denoting a total span of 3.30 m for the concentrated-load region (in accordance with SLW fatigue checks where PFAC factors and axle spacings are prescribed).  

Graphic Style  
• All elements are drawn in crisp, single-weight black lines on a white background.  The P3 block is an unshaded rectangle with its label centered.  Dimension lines terminate in small arrowheads and are accompanied by clear numeric text.  Arrow stems and heads are uniformly scaled.  There is no shading or color—this is a purely schematic, to-scale representation.  

Interpretation in Context  
• The P3 block on the left corresponds to the secondary traffic band loading, which is applied over the width of the lane preceding the first axle group.  In official bridge-design workflows this area load may be set to 5 kN/m² (basic load P5) or a country-specific secondary load P3.  
• The clustered series of wheel loads to the right represent the constant axle loads of an SLW train—each wheel load being taken at its nominal value (e.g. 390 kN per wheel set for fatigue checks, amplified by the impact factor to 468 kN if PFAC = 0.78).  The 1.5 m spacing matches the DIN spacing requirement for successive wheelsets.  
• The 3.3 m overall dimension ties back to standard rules for positioning load trains on bridges, ensuring that the set of wheel loads can be moved across the span in defined increments when checking for maximum bending or fatigue stress.
