At the bottom, centered beneath the baseline, the title reads “Figure 3.20: Load Train SLW,” reinforcing that this is the standardized load model to be used whenever dynamic lane-by-lane analysis is performed under SLW provisions.

The figure is a side-elevation schematic (labelled “Figure 3.21: Load Train LKW”) showing how the standard heavy-truck live loads (LKW, Lastkraftwagen) are idealized for bridge design according to DIN 1072 and related European standards.   Key elements of the drawing are as follows:  

1. Coordinate Reference  
 ‐ At the top center there is a marker “0” with an arrow pointing right, labelled “x.” This denotes the origin of the longitudinal axis (x‐direction) running along the bridge lane. All distances are measured from this origin.  

2. Principal Load Arrows  
 ‐ Two vertical downward arrows represent concentrated axle load groups:  
   • The left arrow is positioned 1.5 m to the left of the origin and carries a magnitude of 6.66 × P1.  
   • The right arrow is positioned 1.5 m to the right of the origin (i.e. at x = +1.5 m) carrying 3.33 × P1.  
 ‐ The two arrows are spaced 3.0 m apart, reflecting the typical wheelbase or axle grouping distance for the design load train.  

3. Continuous Distributed Loads (P3)  
 ‐ On either side of the concentrated loads, extending beyond the 1.5 m margins, are rectangular blocks labelled “P3.” These blocks sit atop a continuous line that represents the traffic lane. The P3 regions correspond to the “rest of the traffic band” area loading, applied outside the primary wheel paths.  

4. Dimensional Layout  
 ‐ From left to right along the lane centerline:  
   • A P3 distribution region extends from the far left up to the first 1.5 m segment.  
   • A concentrated load of 6.66 × P1 at x = –1.5 m.  
   • A clear span of 3.0 m between the two concentrated loads (from x = –1.5 m to x = +1.5 m).  
   • A second concentrated load of 3.33 × P1 at x = +1.5 m.  
   • A P3 region extending from x = +1.5 m outward to the right.  

5. Notational Conventions and Context  
 ‐ P1 denotes the characteristic axle load parameter for the design train (e.g. according to DIN 1072 or OENORM B 4002), which is multiplied by the factors 6.66 and 3.33 to distribute the total design live load between the front and rear axles or bogie groups.  
 ‐ P3 corresponds to the complementary uniform load applied to the remainder of the traffic lane outside the concentrated wheel paths. In practice, P3 is specified in kN/m² and is used to model the area load contribution from additional wheels or lighter vehicles.  
 ‐ The overall loading pattern ensures that the bridge designer captures both the peak effects under wheel paths (through the concentrated P1‐based loads) and the general lane loading (through P3).  

6. Applicability  
 ‐ This Load Train LKW model is one of several “classical load trains” used across Europe—under DIN 1072, OENORM B 4002 (Austria), Spanish IAP, Brazilian NBR, etc.—to check bending, shear, and fatigue effects in bridge decks. Lane widths, dynamic impact factors, and national variants may alter P1, P3 magnitudes or the 3.0 m/2.5 m/4.0 m spacing in other codes, but the two‐axle‐group plus peripheral area‐load concept remains consistent.  

By combining the two concentrated axle‐group loads (6.66 × P1 and 3.33 × P1) with the distributed P3 load on each side, the schematic fully defines the longitudinal load pattern of a heavy‐truck design vehicle as it would be “rolled” across a bridge lane for structural analysis.

Key observations and contextual notes:

•  National variants are selectable via country codes (e.g. DIN 1072 for Germany, OENORM B 4002 for Austria, IAP for Spain, NBR for Brazil).  
•  The typical moving load width is 3.0 m, except OENORM (2.5 m) and Spanish IAP (≥4.0 m to maintain secondary‐truck clearance).  
•  Traffic lanes not occupied by moving concentrated loads are assigned P3; residual lane area uses P5.  
•  For two‐lane configurations with independent load trains, P5 defined under P3 must be reused and “impact factor” disabled (set to 1.0).  
•  IAP specifies a uniform 4 kN/m² over the entire deck (no SLW deduction); for fatigue, a single SLW of 390 kN with impact factor 1.2 (≈468 kN) is applied via PFAC = 0.78.  
•  Separate horizontal wind loading P6 = 1.25 kN/m² and a lateral width P7 = 3.50 m apply.  
•  Brake loads (P8 = 1.00 factor) are treated as an independent load class:  
   –  DIN 1072 caps total braking at 900 kN (min. 30 % of heavy trains in main+secondary lanes or 25 % of the main lane).  
   –  Spanish IAP: 140 kN ≤ brake load ≤ 720 kN.

The sketch is a schematic “plan‐view” of a single‐lane load train of type HB or NB, showing two concentrated band‐loads (P3) at the ends and a group of four equally intense axle loads (P1) between them.  Visually, the drawing consists of:

 • A single horizontal line representing the centreline of the roadway or bridge deck.  
 • At each end of that line sits a rectangular “block” rising above the deck, each block labelled P3.  These blocks symbolize the traffic‐band (uniform line) loads defined by factor P3 in BS 5400.  
 • Between the two P3 blocks are four identical, solid black, downward‐pointing arrows.  Each arrow denotes one axle load, P1.  The fourth (rightmost) arrow is explicitly annotated “P1.”  
 • Along the horizontal line, five numerical spacing annotations sit beneath it, from left to right:  
   ­  “25.0” — the distance (in metres) from the right edge of the left P3 block to the first axle arrow.  
   ­  “1.8” — spacing between the first and second axle loads.  
   ­  “x” — the variable spacing between the second and third axles (this is the user-selectable distance x, typically 6.0, 11.0, 16.0, 21.0 or 26.0 m for BS 5400-type HB/NB loads).  
   ­  “1.8” — spacing between the third and fourth axles.  
   ­  “25.0” — distance from the fourth axle to the left edge of the right P3 block.  

Below the drawing the caption reads “Figure 3.23: Load Train HB, NB.”

In combination with the accompanying text, this figure defines a standard heavy‐vehicle load train:  
 • P1 is the uniform axle load (default 30.0 kN per axle, with a class range of 24–45 translating to 240–450 kN per axle in modelling).  
 • P3 is the magnitude factor for the simultaneous traffic‐band (line) loading; its position and eccentricity (P2) determine how the band load is superimposed relative to the lane centre.  Here P2 is zero (bands centred), but P3 = 1.0 or 2.0 may be used depending on single or double centring.  
 • The 25.0 m “overhang” zones at each end represent the length of end‐loaded band segments beyond the first and last axles.  
 • The 1.8 m spacings reflect close grouping at the inner end of the train, while x is the variable inter‐bogie spacing that changes with national variants (BS 5400, TMH7 NB, IS 1227, etc.).  

Altogether, this concise diagram anchors the definition of the HB/NB load train for bridge analysis: two end‐bands of uniform pressure P3 flanking four concentrated axle loads P1, with specified inter‐axle and overhang distances.

The image is a schematic, taken from an ELLA-based bridge-load input description, illustrating the “Load Train HS” model (single and tandem axle) used in the HL-93 live-load standard.  It is labelled at top with a narrow blue band containing the title “ELLA | Input Description,” and, immediately below, the heading “Load Train HS, Single and tandem axles.”  Centered under that heading is a simple line-drawing of a beam (representing the bridge deck or lane) onto which both concentrated wheel loads and a uniform strip load are applied.  

Key elements of the drawing are as follows:  
• A straight, horizontal heavy line represents the deck or loaded span.  At its left end is a small vertical tick marked “O,” denoting the reference origin for longitudinal positioning.  
• Two black, downward-pointing arrows are drawn above the beam to represent the concentrated wheel loads.  Each arrow is identical in style, and the arrow to the right is labelled “P” (implicitly the single-axle load magnitude).  In tandem-axle configurations, the two arrows remain spaced by the parameter P4, so that one might interpret both as carrying the same label “P” but offset by P4.  
• Directly beneath the beam, a long, narrow rectangle or stripe spans essentially the full width of the drawing.  This stripe is labelled “P3” in its center.  It represents the uniform lane or band loading that accompanies the HS axle loads—i.e. the longitudinal strip load distributed continuously along the deck.  
• A horizontal dimension indicator (though only partially visible in the snippet) would normally show that the total footprint of the stripe equals the parameter P3, which in HL-93 defines the full longitudinal length over which the lane load is active.  
• The spacing between the two arrow loads—when a tandem-axle truck is modeled—is governed by the parameter P4 (not explicitly re-shown in this cropped view but referenced in the surrounding text).  Single-axle configurations simply use one arrow plus the uniform band.  
• At the bottom right of the image appears the caption text “Figure 3.24: Load Train HS,” tying the diagram back into the broader manual or code commentary.  

Visually, the drawing is very clean and schematic: only straight lines, arrows and simple text-labels are used, with no shading or color except for the thin blue text bar at the top.  The font is a standard sans-serif for figure labels and a slightly larger, bold serif for the figure title.  There are no additional supports drawn (no bearings, no side rails), since the purpose is purely to define the relative positions, load magnitudes, and nomenclature of the HS truck/axle model:  
  – P1 would select the HS-class (10, 15 or 20) under the old AASHTO definitions, or the equivalent HL-93 classification in newer practice.  
  – P2, when set nonzero, recalls the antiquated AASHTO shear load definitions.  
  – P3 is the strip or lane load (uniformly distributed).  
  – P4 is the spacing between wheel loads in a tandem set.  

In sum, this diagram serves as the input template for specifying an HS load train in either SI or U.S. customary units, showing both the point loads (single or tandem axles) and the companion uniform band load that must be applied simultaneously for live-load analysis.

The input table summarizes parameter sets for AASHTO‐based vehicle load models, distinguishing the three historic “HS” classes from the modern HL-93 scenario in both U.S. (US) and SI units. It is organized into four columns—P1, Load train, P2 (HS), P3, and P4—where:

• P1  
  – A code or numeric identifier for each load scenario.  
  – Values: 10, 15, 20 correspond to the old AASHTO HS10-44, HS15-44, and HS20-44 classes; “US” and “SI” identify the HL-93 truck in U.S. customary or SI units.  

• Load train  
  – Designation of the specific axle‐load configuration.  
  – HS10-44, HS15-44, HS20-44 refer to single/tandem axle Classes 10, 15, and 20 from the 1944 AASHTO standard.  
  – HL-93 is the composite truck plus lane load model introduced in AASHTO LRFD (editions 2002/2005), offered here in two unit systems.  

• P2 (HS)  
  – Total concentrated axle loads (in kip or kN) for each train.  
  – For HS classes, two values are given in parentheses: (front axle / tandem axle).  
     • HS10-44: (13.0, 9.0) kip  
     • HS15-44: (19.5, 13.5) kip  
     • HS20-44: (26.0, 18.0) kip  
  – HL-93 in U.S. units: single‐axle total = 24.0 kip  
  – HL-93 in SI units: single‐axle total = 110 kN  

• P3  
  – Uniform “lane” or “band” load applied longitudinally along the bridge deck.  
  – HS classes:  
     • HS10-44: 0.32 kip per foot (klf)  
     • HS15-44: 0.48 klf  
     • HS20-44: 0.64 klf  
  – HL-93:  
     • U.S.: 0.64 klf  
     • SI: 9.3 kN/m  

• P4  
  – Nominal spacing between the two primary axles (or load groups) for tandem configurations.  
  – HS classes: 0 ft (axles are treated as coincident loads in the specification)  
  – HL-93:  
     • U.S.: 4 ft  
     • SI: 1.2 m  

Contextual notes drawn from the accompanying text:  
- The older HS‐44 trains represent one‐ and two-axle configurations with concentrated loads plus an optional uniform loading stripe of fixed width (10 ft or 3.048 m, or 3.000 m for SI). No variable axle spacing is defined (P4 = 0).  
- The HL-93 model comprises a three-axle truck (32 kip on each outer axle, 8 kip on the center axle) plus a companion uniform band load (P3) active over the full span. Standard spacing between outer axles may vary between 14 ft and 30 ft but can be fixed by P4. In this table the simplified HL-93 is given with a 4 ft (1.2 m) tandem spacing.  
- The HL-93 model in SI employs an analogous set of values converted from kip/klf to kN/kN·m: total axle load 110 kN, band load 9.3 kN/m, spacing 1.2 m.  
- Dynamic impact factors, alternate “USF”/“SIF” load train types for fatigue or local design, and negative‐moment load reduction (50 ft minimum spacing at 90% loading) are referenced in the broader specification but not enumerated in this table.

By laying out P1–P4 for each train type, the table provides a concise reference for selecting appropriate vehicle‐load parameters—whether using legacy HS loads for shear design (via P2) or the modern HL-93 model in either unit system. This standardized schema facilitates consistent data indexing and retrieval within a RAG‐based vector store.

The image is a two-part excerpt from an ELLA “Input Description” manual, illustrating AASHTO load-train models HS and HT (also known as HL-93 in later editions). At the very top is a header bar bearing the ELLA logo and the title “Input Description.”

Part 1 – Figure 3.24: Load Train HS (Single and Tandem Axles)  
• Diagram: A horizontal line represents the bridge lane, with the longitudinal axis marked by an arrow labeled “O → x.”  
• Uniform Load (P3): A thick stripe along the full span depicts a constant lane load P3 (klf or kN/m).  
• Concentrated Load(s): One or two downward arrows above the stripe indicate single or tandem axle loads, each of magnitude P (defined by P2), spaced by a distance P4.  
• Legend/Text below the figure summarizes: “The loading HS is described by a uniform load and an additional concentrated single or tandem load with spacing P4. The value P1 specifies the load-train class according to AASHTO. The value P2 of the old load definitions should be selected for shear explicitly.”  

Immediately beneath is a table of permissible parameter sets for P1, P2, and P3. Columns are labeled P1, Load train, P2 (HS), and P3:

  • P1 = 10, Load train = HS10-44, P2 = (13.0, 9.0) kip, P3 = 0.32 klf  
  • P1 = 15, Load train = HS15-44, P2 = (19.5, 13.5) kip, P3 = 0.48 klf  
  • P1 = 20, Load train = HS20-44, P2 = (26.0, 18.0) kip, P3 = 0.64 klf  
  • P1 = US, Load train = HL-93 (US), P2 = 24.0 kip,   P3 = 0.64 klf  
  • P1 = SI, Load train = HL-93 (SI), P2 = 110 kN,   P3 = 9.3 kN/m  

Part 2 – Figure 3.25: Load Train HT (Two- and Three-Axle Truck, ed. 2002/2005)  
• Diagram: A second horizontal line shows the same longitudinal axis (“O → x”). Three concentrated downward arrows sit above the line.  
  – First and second arrows each carry 32 kip (145 kN).  
  – The span between these two is variable: P4 = 14′ 0″ to 30′ 0″ (4.3 to 9.0 m).  
  – A third arrow, located 14′ 0″ (4.3 m) beyond the second, carries 8 kip (35 kN).  
• Uniform Load (P3): Again represented by a stripe beneath the arrows spanning the full length.  
• Caption notes: “Figure 3.25: Load train HL/HST (three axle truck, ed. 2002/2005).”  

Additional Context (from adjacent text, not shown in the diagrams):  
• Width of both HS and HT loads is limited to 10 ft (3.048 m) or 3.000 m in SI mode; uniform loading is applied via two strips of that fixed width.  
• Common parameters include wind loading P6 = 0.10 klf (1.46 kN/m), height for wind/brake loads P7/P9 ≈ 1.829 m (6 ft), and brake-load friction coefficient P8 = 0.05.  
• Older AASHTO 1944 loads (HS10-44, HS15-44, HS20-44) can be selected explicitly for shear by choosing P2.  
• The HL-93 model (US/SI) activates the lane load P3 over the full longitudinal length and may be modified for local/fatigue design (USF/SIF) by fixing axle spacing at 30 ft (9.0 m) and increasing the dynamic impact factor to 1.15.  
• A minimum 50 ft (15 m) spacing at 90 % intensity is used for negative moment regions.  

Overall, the image clearly lays out the geometry, loading magnitudes, and parameter options for HS (single/tandem axles) and HT (three-axle truck) load-train models, bridging both historical AASHTO definitions and the modern HL-93 standard in US and SI units.

The input table defines a set of standardized load‐train models (both historic AASHTO types and the modern HL-93) by assigning each a code (P1) and specifying three key parameters (P2, P3, P4).  It is intended for use in a Retrieval‐Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store so that any query about bridge loading configurations can be matched quickly to one of these predefined cases.

1. Column definitions  
   • P1 – “Load Train Class”  
     – A numeric code (10, 15, 20) for the old AASHTO 1944 models or an alphanumeric code (US, SI, US2, SI2, USF, SIF) for HL-93 variants.  
   • Load Train – human‐readable name of the load model  
     – H10-44, H15-44, H20-44 refer to AASHTO classes 10, 15, 20 (from the 1944 standard).  
     – HL 93 is the modern design vehicle; HL 93 (fat) indicates the fatigue design version.  
   • P2 – Total concentrated axle‐train weight  
     – For AASHTO 1944: 20, 30 or 40 kip.  
     – For HL-93 US: 72 kip; HL-93 SI: 325 kN.  
     – US2/SI2 and USF/SIF repeat the same P2 as US/SI but differ in spacing or dynamic factor.  
   • P3 – Line (lane) load intensity  
     – Historic classes: 0.32, 0.48, or 0.64 klf (kips per linear foot).  
     – HL-93 US: 0.640 klf; HL-93 SI: 9.3 kN/m.  
     – This is applied as a uniform “traffic band” across the full span length when P3 ≠ 0.  
   • P4 – Axle‐spacing or variant spacing of tandem loads  
     – Historic AASHTO rows leave P4 blank (“–”) since these are single concentrated loads without a second axle.  
     – HL-93 US: spacing variable from 14 ft to 30 ft (4.3 m to 9.0 m).  
     – HL-93 SI: 4.30 m to 9.00 m.  
     – US2/SI2 fix this spacing at the minimum (14 ft / 4.30 m) to model compact two‐axle trucks.  
     – USF (fatigue) fixes spacing at 4 ft; SIF fixes spacing at 1.20 m, and also sets the dynamic impact factor to 1.15.

2. Grouping and application context  
   • Historic AASHTO (P1 = 10, 15, 20)  
     – Three discrete load‐train classes dating back to 1944.  
     – Only a single concentrated load plus a uniform band (no second axle).  
     – P2 increases in 10 kip increments; P3 scales accordingly (0.32 → 0.48 → 0.64 klf).  
   • Modern HL-93 (P1 = US, SI, US2, SI2, USF, SIF)  
     – Two unit systems: US (English) and SI (metric).  
     – US/SI: standard HL-93 live‐load model with two axles; spacing variable to simulate different truck lengths.  
     – US2/SI2: “compact vehicle” variant fixing the axle spacing at the shortest interval (14 ft/4.30 m).  
     – USF/SIF: fatigue‐design variant, dynamic impact factor locked to 1.15, spacing reduced to 4 ft/1.20 m.

3. Interactions with other parameters (from context text)  
   • Common width for concentrated loads is limited to 10 ft (3.048 m) in US, or 3.00 m in SI, so the uniform band is simulated via two parallel stripes of fixed width.  
   • Additional loads (wind P6, height P7, brake P8, mass-center P9) are specified elsewhere and apply equally to all train types.  
   • If P4 is set to zero in a model, the software reverts to a simplified (single‐axle) HL model.  
   • The traffic band load P3 for HL-93 is always “active” over the full span unless overridden (alternate loading by setting P3 = 0).  

In summary, this table provides nine predefined load‐train configurations: three legacy AASHTO classes and six HL-93 variants (in two unit systems, each with standard, compact and fatigue‐design forms).  Each row codifies the total concentrated weight (P2), the uniform lane load intensity (P3), and the axle‐spacing or band spacing (P4), keyed by the class identifier P1.

 The width of the train is limited to 10’ = 3.048 m or for the SI version to 3.000 m. Thus, uniform loading is modelled with two stripes with a fixed width.

Figure title and context  
• Figure 3.26 is labelled “Load trains according CAN/CSA” and illustrates the default four-axle vehicle train (P1 = CAN, level CL4) with its axle loads, longitudinal spacing and wheel‐set geometry for Canadian highway bridge loading as defined in CSA S6.  

1. Axle-load tables (top block)  
  – Column headings “Axle no. 1, 2, 3, 4” identify the four wheelsets in sequence.  
  – Under the heading “–W” (fractional-W load train):  
     • Axle 1 carries 0.04·W (static) and, in parentheses or second line, 0.08·W (dynamic-augmented).  
     • Axles 2 and 3 each carry 0.10·W (static) and 0.20·W (dynamic).  
     • Axle 4 carries 0.40·W (static) and 0.28·W (dynamic-limited).  
  – Under the heading “–625” (class-625 load train in kN):  
     • Axle 1: 25 kN static (50 kN with dynamic allowance).  
     • Axles 2 & 3: 62.5 kN static (125 kN dynamic).  
     • Axle 4: 87.5 kN static (175 kN dynamic).  
  – The blank check-boxes before the “–W” and “–625” labels indicate user selection of either the W-based or 625-class loading.  

2. Longitudinal spacing (middle block)  
  – A straight horizontal centreline represents the vehicle path.  
  – Downward arrows mark the vertical projection of each axle onto that centreline (Axles 1–4).  
  – Distances between those arrows are dimensioned as:  
     • 3.6 m between Axles 1 and 2  
     • 1.2 m between Axles 2 and 3  
     • 6.6 m between Axles 3 and 4  
  – A final 6.6 m segment beyond Axle 4 completes a total train length of 18 m (3.6 + 1.2 + 6.6 + 6.6 = 18 m).  

3. Wheel-set geometry (bottom block)  
  • Left half – Plan view over two rails (thick parallel lines):  
     – Each wheel contact point is shown as a small square.  
     – Typical lateral offset of the contact patch from the track centreline is 0.25 m (labelled “0.25 m (Typ.)”).  
     – Dashed centrelines mark the symmetry axes of the wheelsets.  
  • Right half – Detail of one axle group:  
     – Two wheels on either side of the gauge (each square) are shown in alignment with the rails.  
     – Dimension “1.80 m” denotes track gauge (centre-to-centre of rails).  
     – Dimension “2.40 m” denotes the lateral span between the outer wheel-load application points of that axle group.  
     – Vertical arrows indicate the elevation of the wheel-load application (nominally 0.25 m above top of rail).  

How it fits into the CAN/CSA parameters  
– P1 = CAN (default four-axle load train CL4)  
– P2 = 625 (class-625, hence the “–625” kN values)  
– The figure may be adapted for ON/BC variants (ON4, BC4) by changing axle loads or spacing per Annex A14.4 or A14.9.  
– P3, P7, P8, P9, etc. (constant lane loads, wind-attack height, braking loads, centrifugal heights) are handled separately; this diagram establishes the static and dynamic axle loads and physical geometry for summary load modeling.

The Canadian standards define a truck load in several variants. The type CAN is used for the default load train according chapter 14.9.
 The value P1 defines the level of the load train (CL, CL4 = only 4 axles, CL3 = only 3 axles) The definitions ON, ON4 and ON3 select the variants for Ontario according Annex A14.4. The definitions BC, BC4 and BC3 select the variants for Britisch Columbia. The definition MV selects the maintenace vehicle according 3.8.11.
 The value P2 defines the class of the load train (default 625).
 If the value P3 is defined ( 9.0, 8.0 or 7.0 for class A, B or C and D) a constant lane load will be defined with reduced load values of the load train without any dynamic allowance. For this loading a braking load P8 of min(700,180+0.1*L) will be applied. So P8 should become zero for secondary lanes.
 The height of the wind attack area P7 is 3.0[ m] , the zentrifugal force is acting at P9=2.0[ m] aove the lane.
 The value P4 defines the fixed distance to the 4th load of the vehicle, it is 6.6 in general, but up to 18 m in British Columbia.
 Further wit Literals EP1 and EP2 the special load trains EPLL1 and EPLL2 may be selected.
 The value P8 defines a factor on the braking load which is applied as 180+0.1*P3*L but not larger than 700 kN distributed along the total length. P8 0.0 deactivates this type of loading.

The image is a composite of two schematic, perspective‐style renderings of simply supported bridge decks, presented side by side under the general heading “JRAT” (Japanese Road Association Trains) and captioned as Figure 3.27: Japanese Load Trains. Both sketches share the same basic structural vocabulary—a flat deck slab or plate (shown in light gray with a colored top surface) spanning two longitudinal girders (shown in solid pink)—but differ in the way the live load is applied.

Left‐hand diagram (single-axle “JRAT” loading)  
• Deck & supports:  
  – A rectangular deck slab (light gray outline) with a violet‐shaded top surface.  
  – Two parallel I-girder supports in pink beneath the deck, running in the longitudinal (front-to-back) direction.  
• Load representation:  
  – Two single‐axle wheels (rendered as gray cylinders with black tires) sit on the deck, side by side.  
  – From each wheel is a downward arrow labeled “100 kN,” indicating each wheel imposes a vertical force of 100 kN.  
  – A horizontal dimension line with arrowheads between the two wheel centers reads “1.75 m,” denoting the axle spacing.  
• Annotation:  
  – Beneath the deck slab is the text “JRAT.”  
  – A small URL “www.road.or.jp” is printed just below, anchoring the source.

Right‐hand diagram (area & lane loading)  
• Deck & supports:  
  – Similar light-gray deck plate, but with a blue‐tinted surface underneath a pink translucent block.  
  – Identical pink longitudinal girders support the slab.  
• Base area load (blue zone):  
  – A shallow, light‐blue translucent prism spans the entire deck width of 5.5 m (dimension called out by a green arrow and text “5.5 m”).  
  – From a grid of small downward arrows rising from that blue prism is the label “3.5 kN/m2,” signifying a uniform area load across the full width (these arrows represent the basic lane load P2 for JRAL‐type loading).  
• Extra lane or special load (pink zone):  
  – A taller pink translucent block is placed longitudinally along one portion of the deck; its plan length is dimensioned as “10 m” by a green arrow line.  
  – Downward arrows from its top face carry the label “10 kN/m2,” representing an additional lane load (P3) stacked on the basic load zone.

The image is a technical, two-view schematic titled “Figure 3.28: Load trains AS 5100.” It illustrates one of the standardized moving‐load arrangements prescribed in the Australian bridge design code (AS 5100).  

1. Elevation View (top half of drawing)  
   • Three identical concentrated load clusters (“axle groups”) are shown riding across a bridge deck. Each cluster is labelled “360 kN.” Within each group, four wheel symbols are arranged: two pairs separated by 1.25 m edge-to-first-wheel spacing, 3.75 m between the two inner wheels, then 1.25 m and 1.25 m again to the next group.  
   • Between the second and third clusters is a uniform line load of 6 kN/m, depicted as a continuous series of small semicircles under the deck outline.  
   • Above the deck line, dimension arrows annotate the horizontal spacings: 1.25 m, 1.25 m, 3.75 m, 1.25 m, 1.25 m, then a longer span labelled “Varies – 6.25 min.”, followed by 1.25 m and 1.25 m to the right‐hand group. This “varies ≥ 6.25 m” segment represents the adjustable distance between eight-axle blocks when modelling influence-line effects.  

2. Plan View (bottom half of drawing)  
   • The plan shows the top surface of the deck rendered as a rectangular field with diagonal hatching. Small solid squares mark each wheel or axle location directly above the deck.  
   • A dashed vertical line divides the hatch at a point 0.4 m from the left edge, then a 3.2 m “standard design” central span, and finally another 0.4 m to the right edge. These denote the end-zone regions (0.4 m each) and the main span length between bearings or supports.  
   • The same 1.25 m in-plane spacings between wheel positions are implied by the pattern of squares, matching the elevation view. The dashed line also corresponds to the minimum group separation noted above.  

Contextual Notes (as drawn from AS 5100 provisions):  
   – Each 360 kN cluster represents an axle‐group load (P2) used for influence‐line checks.  
   – The 6 kN/m distributed load between clusters corresponds to the uniform track load (P3).  
   – The “Varies 6.25 min.” dimension references the minimum 6.25 m distance required by the code between two eight-axle groups when performing multiple-lane or fatigue analyses.  
   – The hatched deck in plan reinforces that loads can occur anywhere across the deck width but are modelled at these specific lateral positions.  

Together, the elevation and plan views convey the precise geometry and magnitudes of the AS 5100 moving‐load train for ultimate and fatigue design checks, including concentrated axle loads, inter-axle spacings, uniform line loading, and variable group‐to‐group distances.

2. A central vertical rectangle spanning the gap between the two rail lines

3. Distributed loads on either side of the block

   - To the right of the rectangle, symmetrically placed between the rails, is another “80 kN/m.”

Interpretation in context of the surrounding technical text:  
• For load train LM 71 (also called UIC 71 or RU per BS 5400) under “excellent maintained track,” sleeper spacing P1 is set to 6.4 m.

– The SW Schwerlastzug is defined with a constant block load P2 = 133 kN/m (alternative default 150 kN/m also mentioned in the standard).

– When more than two tracks run in parallel, subsequent tracks’ loads may be reduced by prescribed factors (0.85 for track 3, 0.70 for track 4, etc.).  
– This block‐load representation replaces individual axle loads, simplifying influence‐line calculations by using a uniform intensity over a fixed length (here 5.3 m).

Overall, the image provides a concise visual of a uniform, constant‐intensity load of 133 kN/m applied over a 5.3 m segment of track for the SW Schwerlastzug scenario, with the origin and positive direction clearly marked for use in structural or geotechnical influence‐line analyses.

The image is a schematic line‐diagram labelled “Figure 3.37: Load train SW/2 Schwerlastzug.” It represents the simplified block‐load model for the SW/2 heavy‐freight train as used in railway loading codes. The principal elements of the sketch are as follows:

1. Coordinate reference  
   • Along the top of the figure, there is a right‐pointing horizontal arrow marked with “0” at its tail. This arrow denotes the positive x‐direction and shows the orientation of increasing distance along the track.  

2. Track baseline  
   • A single straight horizontal line runs beneath the arrow and forms the reference axis (the rail line). In the middle of this baseline there is a small rectangular cutout (a “notch”) indicating the unloaded gap between two block loads.

3. Block‐load rectangles  
   • To the left of the notch sits a filled‐outline rectangle representing a uniformly distributed load of 150 kN/m. Beneath this left block is the number “25.0,” indicating that this block occupies 25.0 m of track length.  
   • To the right of the notch is an identical rectangle, also labelled “150 kN/m,” with the same “25.0” m length indicated beneath it.  

4. Unloaded gap  
   • Between the two 150 kN/m blocks, the notch in the baseline is annotated with “7.0,” signifying a 7.0 m long span with no load applied.  

5. Interpretation in context of SW/2 loads  
   • According to the SW/2 Schwerlastzug (heavy‐freight train) definition, the model uses two equal block‐loads of 150 kN/m to approximate the combined weight of locomotive units and wagons.  
   • The 25 m length of each block corresponds to the effective loaded length of each major vehicle grouping, while the 7 m gap simulates the approximate spacing or coupler distance between those groupings.  
   • This simplified block‐load representation replaces more detailed axle‐by‐axle models when a uniform block is sufficient for global structural checks.  

6. Relation to parameters from the accompanying text  
   • SW/2 defaults call for P2 = 150 kN/m block load (as drawn), P4 = 100 kN nosing force (not shown explicitly here), plus wind (P6, P7) and brake loads (P8) applied separately per the code.  
   • The figure’s load blocks would be applied as constant distributed loads on the track structure.  

In sum, Figure 3.37 provides a clear visual of the SW/2 heavy freight load train as two 150 kN/m blocks, each 25 m long, separated by a 7 m clear span, progressing in the direction indicated by the arrow (the +x axis). This abstraction aids in rapid assessment of bending moments and shear forces on track‐supported structures without resolving every individual axle.

The figure presents a schematic “influence-line” style representation of the BS 5400 railway loading (load train RL) as a simplified block‐and‐point-load model on a single track span.  Everything is drawn on a horizontal “beam” that stands in for the rail plus its supporting structure.  Key features are:

1. Coordinate system  
   - A small origin symbol “0” is marked at the left edge of the primary loaded zone, with an arrow pointing to the right labeled “x.”  This defines the positive x-direction along the track.

2. Concentrated axle load (P1 = 200 kN)  
   - At x = 0 a single downward arrow represents the characteristic axle load of 200 kN.  This corresponds to the RL default P1.

3. Main block (constant) load (P2 = 50 kN/m)  
   - Immediately to the right of the point-load arrow begins a rectangular “block” that extends for exactly 100.0 m along the beam.  Inside this block is the label “50 kN/m,” denoting a uniform distributed load of 50 kN per metre.  This is the simplified block‐load approximation of the train’s lane loading (P2) over the core span.

4. Flanking lane loads (P3 = 25 kN/m)  
   - On each side of the 100 m block (both left and right) there is a shorter horizontal line segment, each annotated “25 kN/m.”  These represent the lower uniform lane loads that act on track sections adjacent to the fully loaded zone, in accordance with P3 = 25 kN/m.

5. Overall span length  
   - Beneath the central block is the dimension “100.0 m,” clearly indicating the length over which the 50 kN/m block‐load is applied.

6. Caption and context  
   - Below the drawing the caption reads “Figure 3.38: Load train RL = Railway Loading BS 5400,” linking the graphic to the BS 5400 standard.  

Interpretation in context of RL parameters:  
- P1 (axle loading) is shown by the single 200 kN arrow at x = 0.  
- P2 (equivalent block load) is the 50 kN/m over the 100 m span.  
- P3 (adjacent lane loading) appears as the 25 kN/m strips on either side.  

By combining a concentrated axle load with a constant central block load plus lighter side‐lane loads, the diagram captures the essential “RL” loading pattern used for bridge and track analysis under BS 5400.

The image is a schematic diagram titled “Figure 3.39: Load train ASRT = Railway Loading 300LA according AS 5100.” It consists of two horizontal assemblies drawn one above the other, each illustrating the wheel‐axle loads and spacings that define the 300LA train model used for bridge and track loading analysis under the Australian standard.

Top Assembly (Axle‐Load Detail)  
• A single straight line represents the rail.  
• Four wheelloads are shown as circles in line on the rail. Above each circle is a vertical arrow pointing downward with its associated load value: the first two wheels (labeled “VEHICLE”) each carry 300 kN; the center two (straddling a vertical dashed coupler line labeled “Ç COUPLER”) also carry 300 kN each; and the rightmost two (under “SIMULATED LOCOMOTIVE”) carry 300 kN on the first axle and 360 kN on the trailing axle.  
• Horizontal dimension lines beneath the rail indicate the exact spacing between adjacent axles:  
   – 1.7 m between the first and second axle (vehicle wheels)  
   – 1.1 m between the second axle and the coupler centerline  
   – 1.7 m between the coupler and the first locomotive axle  
   – 2.0 m between the two axles of the locomotive  
• A bracketed label below reads “300LA RAILWAY TRAFFIC LOADS–AXES LOADS,” tying the axle loads to the AS 5100 300LA definition.

Bottom Assembly (Vehicle Consist Layout)  
• A longer rail line shows a series of repeating vehicle units, each depicted by two pairs of small circles (wheelsets) connected by a short vertical line (representing the bogie or truck).  
• Between each pair of vehicles is a short gap indicating the coupler.  
• Beneath each vehicle unit a dimension notes “12 to 20 (Varies)” metres, reflecting the variable inter‐bogie vehicle length allowed by the standard.  
• A repeating arrow under the line indicates that as many of these vehicles as necessary may be concatenated to form the full train consist.

Caption  
• Centered below the bottom assembly is the caption: “Figure 3.39: Load train ASRT = Railway Loading 300LA according AS 5100.”

Overall, this diagram conveys both the concentrated axle loads (300 kN–360 kN) and inter‐axle spacings for the front portion of the 300LA loading train (including a simulated locomotive) as well as the modular series of vehicles (12–20 m lengths) used to extend the train to its full consist. It serves as a visual reference for engineers implementing AS 5100’s Railway Loading 300LA in structural models, linking the P-values (axle loads P1/P2, block loads P4, etc.) specified in the standard to an explicit wheel‐arrangement geometry.

The image is a technical diagram (captioned “Figure 3.40: Military NATO Load Trains (Stanag 2021)”) showing two distinct parts:

1. Top row – Armoured vehicle outlines and basic data  
   • At the very top, a label “136,08 t” indicates the total mass of the tracked vehicle (tank).  
   • Left: a side‐view silhouette of the tank, drawn in profile. Below it is a horizontal dimension line marked “–7,32–” m, denoting the length of track in contact with the ground (i.e. the hull’s bearing length).  
   • Right: a front‐view silhouette of the tank’s lower hull and road wheels. Two dimension arrows appear: one spanning between the outermost road wheels labeled “–4,67–” m (the track gauge), and a smaller arrow from the left wheel centre to the vehicle’s centreline marked “1,27 m” (the lateral offset of the centre of mass from one track).

2. Bottom row – Loaded rail‐wagon assembly with axle and support loads  
   • Centered above this assembly is the label “154,22 t” denoting the total weight of the two coupled wagons plus the load platform and tank.  
   • The drawing consists of three rigid blocks in line: two bogie-equipped rail wagons at each end and a central flat cradle for the tank’s support pads.  
   • Beneath each wheelset (and beneath each of the two central support pads) a downward arrow indicates the vertical load at that point, with the numeric value given in tonnes inside a small rectangle. From left to right these are:  
     – Front wagon bogie: 18,96 t on its leading axle; 38,10 t on its trailing axle.  
     – Central cradle supports (no wheels): 38,10 t on each of two support pads.  
     – Rear wagon bogie: 29,03 t on each of its two axles.  
   • A long horizontal baseline is overlaid by dimension lines marking distances between these points:  
     – 3,66 m from the front wagon’s leading axle to the first support pad,  
     – 2,13 m between the two support pads,  
     – 6,71 m from the second pad to the rear wagon’s leading axle,  
     – 1,83 m between the two axles of the rear bogie.

Overall, the figure combines the vehicle’s geometry and mass data with the resulting load distribution on a specialized heavy-load rail train, suitable for use in structural and track‐loading analyses under NATO STANAG conditions.

The table summarizes all of the parameters that a user can specify when defining an arbitrary “load train” in ELLA or SOFiLOAD.  Each row corresponds to one input‐field (Item), gives a short English description, its physical unit (where applicable), and the default value if the user omits it.  Items are grouped in two blocks—static loading parameters first, then multibody‐dynamics parameters.  Below is a detailed walk‐through of every field in the order shown in the table:

1. Static load components  
  • P  
    – “Load value of vertical load.”  
    – Units: kN.  
    – Default: 0.0.  
    – This is the vertical wheel or axle load that acts downwards onto the bridge.  
  • PB  
    – “Load value for braking.”  
    – Units: kN (positive = braking force in direction of travel, negative = acceleration in reverse).  
    – Default: 0.0.  
  • PW  
    – “Load value transverse (bumping, wind).”  
    – Units: kN.  
    – Default: 0.0.  
    – Represents lateral wheel forces (e.g., wind pressure or track irregularities).  
  • PF  
    – “Value of vertical load for centrifugal load.”  
    – Units: kN.  
    – Default: mirrors P.  
    – Used when including centrifugal‐force effects at curves.  
  • PFAC  
    – “Factor for favourable components.”  
    – Dimensionless.  
    – Default: 0.0.  
    – Scales loads that act in a direction beneficial to the structure.  

2. Geometric and positioning controls  
  • DIST  
    – “A is Minimum (MIN) / absolute (ABS) distance.”  
    – Non‐dimensional flag (LIT).  
    – Default: ABS.  
    – Selects whether the A‐distance is treated as absolute from the reference or merely a minimum separation.  
  • A  
    – “Distance to last load of train.”  
    – Units: m.  
    – Default: 0.0.  
    – For a freely defined train, the first wheelset is at x=0; every subsequent load is placed at A meters from the previous.  
  • DPOS  
    – “Minimum distance to load reference point.”  
    – Units: m.  
    – Default: 0.0.  
    – When A is variable, enforces a minimum spacing from the origin.  
  • DMIN / DMAX  
    – “Influence area before / behind.”  
    – Units: m.  
    – Default: 0.0 each.  
    – Define an upstream (DMIN) and downstream (DMAX) influence region for special code checks.  
  • Y  
    – “Eccentricity to lane axis ( > 0 = to the right).”  
    – Units: m.  
    – Default: 0.0.  
    – Horizontal offset of the wheelset; to guarantee symmetry in ELLA you must also supply the mirror image (Y < 0).  
  • HW  
    – “Total height of wind attack area.”  
    – Units: m.  
    – Default: 0.0.  
  • ZW  
    – “Height of horizontal force.”  
    – Units: m.  
    – Default: HW/2.  
    – Most wind or centrifugal loads are applied at mid‐height of the wind‐attack surface.  
  • HF  
    – “Height of mass center.”  
    – Units: m.  
    – Default: 0.0.  
    – Used when generating an equivalent mass in multi‐body analyses.  
  • PHI  
    – “Impact and special options (bit‐coded).”  
    – Dimensionless.  
    – Default: 1.  
    – Flags include:  
      1 = apply impact factor  
      2 = multiply P by uniform‐distribution load from design code  
      4 = multiply PB by code‐specified longitudinal load  
      8 = split transverse load if unfavourable  
      16 = treat as area load distributing total load over lane width  
      32 = load is always centric (ignore YEX)  

3. Wheel and footprint definition  
  • NW  
    – “Number of wheels on axle (0–7).”  
    – Default: “*” (inherit from global default).  
    – If zero, P/PF are converted into a uniformly distributed line‐load based on WIDT (lane width) or PHI rules.  
  • B  
    – “Distance of wheels across the lane.”  
    – Units: m.  
    – Default: 0.0.  
    – If B < WIDT, wheels form a pair; if B = WIDT or BW defined, loading is distributed across the full width.  
  • BW / LW  
    – “Width / Length of wheel contact area.”  
    – Units: m.  
    – Default: 0.0 each.  
    – If nonzero, each wheel becomes an area load of size BW×LW.  Otherwise, all loads are concentrated point‐loads.  

4. Multibody‐dynamics parameters  
   (Only used when the user activates record TREX to generate a mass‐spring‐damper model.  Defaults “*” mean “take from TRAI record.”)  
  • SNO  
    – “Section number for Animation.”  
    – Default: “–” (none).  
  • FRB  
    – “Frequency for body spring Cb.”  
    – Units: 1/sec.  
  • DAB  
    – “Modal damping of body support.”  
    – Dimensionless.  
  • BOGI  
    – “Load value of bogie.”  
    – Units: –/kN (positive = absolute value, negative = fraction of total vehicle mass).  
  • FRBO  
    – “Frequency for bogie spring Cbo.”  
    – Units: 1/sec.  
  • DABO  
    – “Modal damping of bogie support.”  
    – Dimensionless.  
  • WHEE  
    – “Load value of wheel.”  
    – Units: –/kN (same convention as BOGI).  
  • FRWH  
    – “Frequency for wheel spring Cwh.”  
    – Units: 1/sec.  
  • DAWH  
    – “Modal damping of wheel support.”  
    – Dimensionless.  

How it all ties together  
• Users may define an arbitrary number of wheel‐or‐axle loads in series; the first fixes x=0, subsequent are offset by A (subject to DIST, DPOS, DMIN/DMAX).  
• ELLA assumes symmetric loading: every Y>0 entry must have a matching Y<0.  
• If NW>0, loads on the same axle add algebraically; if NW=0, P is converted into a line‐load over WIDT, clipped by lane width or PHI rules.  
• PF and PW can introduce torsional moments if applied at heights ZW and HF.  
• PHI’s bit flags let you control impact factors, code multipliers, area‐vs‐concentrated loads, centricity, and direction‐splitting of transverse loads.  
• Multibody options via TREX let you attach these loads to nodes in a user‐defined structural model (CONT record) or automatically generate mass, springs, and dampers with the parameters above.

sections: 3.18 TRPL – Point Load of load train

content:
The figure presents a schematic “freely defined load train” consisting of two parallel horizontal baselines, a series of three identical point‐load icons and a set of dimensional labels (A1, A2, A3, A4, ≥ DPOS(4)) that govern their relative positions.  At the very top of the drawing sits a slender horizontal reference line.  At its leftmost end, a double‐ended arrow marked “A1” spans from the left margin to a small open circle on the line; that circle denotes the first user‐defined load reference point, which the accompanying text declares to be x = 0.  Immediately to the right of the circle, a right‐pointing arrow labeled “x” indicates the positive longitudinal axis along which further loads will be placed.  

Along that same top line, three vertical down‐arrows—each identical in size and shape and each carrying the label “P”—indicate successive point loads applied perpendicular to the beam or lane surface.  The very first “P” coincides with the x = 0 reference; the next two are offset further along the x‐axis.  Above the horizontal line, just beyond the third inter‐load gap, the dimension “≥ DPOS(4)” appears.  This notation signifies that the distance between the third load and whatever may follow can be either fixed or variable, provided a minimum separation (DPOS) is respected; the subscript “(4)” ties this minimum requirement to the fourth parameter field in the data record.  

Directly beneath the load icons, a second horizontal line mirrors the layout of loads above but replaces the pictorial arrows with a purely dimensional interpretation.  A left‐hand “+” symbol on this lower baseline marks the start of measurement; between each pair of successive “+” signs, the segments are labeled A2, A3 and A4.  These labels correspond one‐to‐one with the distances separating the first and second point loads (A2), the second and third loads (A3) and the third load to the next potential load position (A4)—with A4 constrained by the previously noted DPOS minimum.  

Beneath the lower baseline the caption reads “Figure 3.41: Freely defined load train.”  In the broader context of the ELLA/SOFILOAD system (see also records TRAI, TRBL, LANE, TREX, TRPL and CONT), this diagram illustrates how an arbitrary number of vertical point loads (each of magnitude P) can be user‐defined in terms of relative distances:  
 • The first load sets the reference point (x = 0).  
 • Subsequent loads are placed at distances A2, A3, … from the preceding load.  
 • A variable-distance option (DPOS) allows A4 (and any further spacing) to have only a minimum value, promoting flexible modeling of load trains of differing axle spacings.  

Additional parameters (DMIN, DMAX) can define influence‐region bounds for influence‐line evaluation, and the system enforces symmetric definitions of transverse offsets Y at each position (using paired +Y and –Y entries rather than a separate Y2 field).  Where wheels are grouped into axles or trucks, the NW and B parameters specify number of wheels and transverse spacing, allowing aggregate loads to be split among multiple wheel contacts or distributed across a lane width (WIDT, PHI).  Optional flags under “OPT” govern impact factors, code‐based UDL multipliers, splitting of unfavorable transverse loads, area‐load adoption, and centricity (YEX).  Finally, the CONT record can link each train position to a node in a user‐defined multi‐body structural model (TREX), enabling the generation of masses, beams, springs and dampers for dynamic simulation, with the node either following full structural deformations (positive CONT) or simply offset for visualization (negative CONT).  All of these conventions find their pictorial summary in the arrangement of P‐arrows, distance labels and reference markers shown here.

sections: 3.18 TRPL – Point Load of load train

content:
The figure presents the decomposition of a single wheel‐contact load into its principal components, all referenced to a local lane coordinate system.  At top left there is a slightly curved line representing the bridge deck or lane surface.  From that line two orthogonal arrows establish the in‐plane axes:  
• “x” points tangentially along the direction of travel, following the curve.  
• “y” points vertically downward toward the deck (i.e. normal to the tangent).  

Centered beneath those axes is a solid dot marking the point of application of the wheel load.  Four arrows radiate from this dot, each labeled with the corresponding force component:  
1. Vertical component P (sometimes augmented by an impact factor PF).  This is shown as a straight arrow pointing downward, normal to the deck.  
2. Longitudinal component PB, drawn as a horizontal arrow in the positive x‐direction.  In the user‐defined loading scheme this corresponds to braking forces when PB is positive (acting in the direction of travel) or accelerating forces when PB is negative.  
3. Transverse (lateral) component PW, shown as a slanted arrow pointing diagonally downward in the y–z plane.  This represents side‐thrust or guiding forces acting across the lane surface.  
4. Horizontal inertial or centrifugal force PF·v²/g (noted simply as PF in the main view).  In the inset at right this is depicted as an arrow directed from right to left, acting at a height hs above the lane.  That offset produces a torsional moment about the lane axis.

Below the inset, a small cross‐section of the deck illustrates how PF applied at elevation hs generates an overturning couple.  The deck’s reference plane is shown at zw (the height at which constant horizontal forces act, producing additional torsion if the load has finite width B).  

Together, these arrows convey how a single point load in ELLA or SOFiLOAD must be resolved into:  
– P, the vertical wheel load (possibly scaled by an impact factor).  
– PB, the longitudinal (brake/traction) force along x.  
– PW, the lateral guidance force.  
– PF, the horizontal inertial (centrifugal) force at height hs, which is split into a pair of forces if the wheelset has width B or applied as a pure torsion if treated concentrically.  

Figure 3.42 thus serves as the graphical key for the user‐defined “TRPL” or “TREX” load records, showing how each load train input parameter (P, PB, PW, PF, YEX, etc.) is translated into line‐load or point‐load components for influence‐line evaluation and for generation of mass‐spring models in a multi‐body dynamics context.

 A freely defined loading by the user comprises an arbitrary number of loads defined relative to
 each other. The first load determines the load reference point (x=0.0). Each further loading is defined with a distance to the previous one.The distance of the point load to the last load point may be either constant or variable with a minimum value. In the latter case and additional minimum distance to the load reference point may be defined with DPOS. For the evaluation in ELLA two additional values DMIN and DMAX may be specified for special cases describing an influence region before and behind the load.
 For the evaluation of the load trains in ELLA symmetric load trains are expected. Thus, any definition of Y should be complemented with a second definition at the same position (A 0) with a negative Y-value. Thus, a second value of Y2 is no longer supported. An eccentricity may be specified with YEX with the load train. NW allows to specify directly a number of wheels with a distance B for that load element. They loads with the same load value will then add up to a total axle distributing the loading on all wheels of that axle.
 If NW = 0 the load values will be converted to a distributed load based on the width of the load train WIDT. (120kN distributed on 3m yield 40kN/m) and will be then clipped at the boundary of the the current lane width. But there are also cases (KEL of HA in BS), where the load is distributed over the lane width, which is controlled via PHI.
 A definition of BW and LW will allow to create also area loadings for every wheel.
 The loading has a vertical component P, a longitudinal component PB and two components in transverse direction. The load may be defined either as single point load, as a pair of wheels (Definition of B < WIDT) or as distributed load (Definition of BW only or B equal to WIDT) The true dimension of the wheel contact area is only used for COPY within SOFiLOAD, ELLA uses only the resultant forces for the evaluation of the influence lines.

The load may be defined either as single point load, as a pair of wheels (Definition of B < WIDT) or as distributed load (Definition of BW only or B equal to WIDT) The true dimension of the wheel contact area is only used for COPY within SOFiLOAD, ELLA uses only the resultant forces for the evaluation of the influence lines..
 Positive loadings of PB are braking loads acting in travelling direction, negative values are intended as accelerating loads in the reverse direction. Loads are applied at the height of the lane.
 The centrifugal loading acts in the height hs, the constant horizontal force in the height zw, thus creating torsional moments. If the load has a width B, this moment will be applied as a pair of forces on the lane surface, a torsional moment along the lane axis will be generated otherwise.
 With the item OPT several options are controlled:
 1 Apply impact factor

 Multiply longitudinal load value with value of design code (eg. EN),
 8 split load in transverse direction if unfavourable,
 the load is an area load, the total load value will be adopted to the lane width
 32 load is always centric, YEX is not applied
 For an analysis with multi-body-dynamics it is possible to generate masses, beams, springs and dampers via the record TREX. The mass of bogie and wheel may be specified either as a positive absolute load value or as a negative fraction of the total mass. The default values are specified with the record TRAI. For more information see record TREX.
 As an alternate method, it is possible to associate a load train to a user defined structural model of the load train. In that case CONT specifies the number of a node of the structural system, which is located at the current position of the load train. If CONT is specified with a positive number, the node will get the deformations of the structure at this point. If defined negative, the node will get only the offset of the current position for the visualization however. This has to be done for all nodes of the train model having no direct contact to the bridge.

The table shown is the complete parameter list for record “TRBL,” the user-defined line or area loads used by the TREX module.  It comprises four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and is divided into three logical groups: generic load values, track geometry, and multibody-dynamics options.  Below is a structured walkthrough.

1. General Load Parameters  
   • P  
     – Description: Vertical line-load intensity.  
     – Unit: [kN/m]  
     – Default: 0.0  
   • PB  
     – Description: Longitudinal (braking or traction) line-load.  
     – Unit: [kN/m]  
     – Default: 0.0  
   • PW  
     – Description: Transverse line-load (e.g. lateral forces).  
     – Unit: [kN/m]  
     – Default: 0.0  
   • PF  
     – Description: Centrifugal (vertical) load component.  
     – Unit: [kN/m]  
     – Default: inherits P  
   • PFAC  
     – Description: Favorable-component factor (dimensionless multiplier).  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: 0.0  
   • DIST  
     – Description: Interprets distance A as MIN (minimum relative) or ABS (absolute).  
     – Unit: literal (LIT)  
     – Default: ABS  
   • A  
     – Description: Distance from reference to last load of train.  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: 0.0  
   • L  
     – Description: Fixed or minimum length of load train (0 = unlimited; sign-sensitive).  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: 0 (unlimited)  
   • LMAX  
     – Description: Maximum extent of load.  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: —  
   • LDEL  
     – Description: Discrete increment length: L + n·LDEL.  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: 0.0  
   • Y  
     – Description: Lateral eccentricity relative to lane axis (>0 to the right).  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: 0.0  
   • HW  
     – Description: Height of wind-attack area (for transverse wind effects).  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: 0.0  
   • ZW  
     – Description: Height at which PW acts (resultant lever arm).  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: HW/2  
   • HF  
     – Description: Height of mass center (for centrifugal load PF).  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: 0.0  
   • PHI  
     – Description: Impact and special options (bitcoded flags; see remarks).  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: 1  

2. Track Geometry Parameters  
   • NW  
     – Description: Number of parallel wheel‐sets/tracks on an axle (0–2).  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: * (use global default from TRPL)  
   • B  
     – Description: Transverse spacing between tracks across the lane.  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: 0.0  
   • BW  
     – Description: Width of each track contact area. If defined, area loads are used.  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: 0.0  

   Notes:  
   – If NW = 0, all loads P, PB, PW, etc. become uniformly distributed over the lane width WIDT (clipped at lane boundaries).  
   – If NW > 0, discrete line loads are generated at ±B/2 (or as many as NW specifies).  

3. Multibody Dynamics & Animation (TREX-specific)  
   • SNO  
     – Description: Section number used for postprocessing or animation.  
     – Unit: —  
     – Default: —  
   • FRB, DAB  
     – Description: Body-spring frequency (Cb) [1/s] and its modal damping.  
     – Unit: FRB: 1/sec; DAB: —  
     – Default: * (inherit TREX default)  
   • BOGI, FRBO, DABO  
     – Description: Bogie-load, bogie-spring frequency (Cbo) [1/s], and damping.  
     – Unit: BOGI: –/kN; FRBO: 1/sec; DABO: —  
     – Default: *  
   • WHEE, FRWH, DAWH  
     – Description: Wheel-load, wheel-spring frequency (Cwh) [1/s], and modal damping of wheel support.  
     – Unit: WHEE: –/kN; FRWH: 1/sec; DAWH: —  
     – Default: *  

   Remarks:  
   – These MBD parameters are placeholders; they are currently not used in TREX’s line-load module but may govern future dynamic coupling.  
   – For full context see related records TRAI, TRPL (general train definitions), LANE (lane geometry and clamping), and TREX (load and response analysis).

sections: 3.19 TRBL – Block Load of Load Train

content:
The provided snippet is drawn from a structural‐analysis user manual (records TRAI, TRPL, LANE, TREX) under the heading “TRBL – DAWH Modal Damping of wheel support.” It explains how a “freely defined loading” is assembled by the user from any number of individual loads, all referenced to a common local coordinate system (see record TRPL for parameter definitions). Key points from the text are:

 • All user‐defined loads default to line loads.  
 • If the number of wheels NW = 0, the line loads are automatically turned into distributed loads by dividing the total load intensity by the specified train width WIDT, then clipping that intensity to the lane’s actual width. (Example: 12 kN/m over 3 m → 4 kN/m².)  
 • In some standard load‐train definitions, loads are already given as area‐loads; in other cases the switch PHI determines whether to spread the load evenly across the lane width.  
 • If NW > 0, discrete line‐loads are placed at wheel or track locations separated by the spacing B. If the wheel‐band width BW is given, an area load may be generated instead of a pure line load.  
 • If only the wheel height HW is provided, the code will compute a corresponding wind load PW based on the train’s wind‐load definition.  
 • Although the record TRBL supports multi‐body‐dynamics inputs for use in TREX, at present those inputs have no effect.

Beneath this text appears Figure 3.43, captioned “Block loading.” The drawing can be described as follows:

 1. Coordinate axes. At the far left is a small “L”-shaped assembly denoting the local origin. A horizontal arrow labeled “x” points to the right; a vertical arrow labeled “y” points downward. This establishes a right‐handed 2D frame in which +x is horizontal and +y is down.  
 2. Rigid support block. Immediately to the right of the axes is a thick right‐angle (“corner block”) symbol—two perpendicular lines meeting at the origin—which represents a fixed support or block bearing.  
 3. Beam or slab outline. Extending horizontally to the right from the support block is a single thin line, representing the bottom‐chord or underside of a beam, slab, track, or lane.  
 4. Uniformly distributed line load. Along the top edge of that beam/slab line is a series of equally spaced, solid black downward‐pointing arrows. They run the full visible length of the line and are all identical in size, indicating a constant‐intensity (block) line load applied over the entire span.  
 5. Caption. Centered beneath the drawing is “Figure 3.43: Block loading.” This labels the sketch as the canonical representation for “block loading” (i.e. a uniform distributed load, or a series of closely spaced point loads, acting on a supported beam segment).

Taken together, the text and figure illustrate how the TRBL record lets the user impose a series of wheel or track loads—either as discrete line loads or converted into a uniform area load—on a structural element, using a right‐handed coordinate system, with automatic clipping or spreading across the lane width based on NW, WIDT, PHI, and other parameters.

Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown of the three input parameters (Item, Description, Unit, Default) that control how “SAVE” records define evaluation and load‐case generation in your RAG vector store. Wherever relevant, we point out links to the surrounding syntax (POSL, LANE, TRAI, CALC, COMB) and to the examples you provided.

1. Field: LCB (Loading Case Base Number)  
   • Description  
     – LCB specifies a numerical offset that is added to every case number defined later via CALC. In essence, when you invoke SAVE, the program will take each CASE index (from CALC records, e.g. 11, 12) and add the LCB value to generate actual load‐case identifiers.  
   • Unit  
     – None (denoted by “—”). This is an integer index only.  
   • Default  
     – 0. If not explicitly set, no offset is applied and case numbers remain as defined in CALC.  
   • Contextual notes  
     – CALC defines LMIN = 11 and LMAX = 12 by default. If LCB = 200 (as in your “construction stage” example), the resulting load cases become 211 and 212. If LCB = 250 (final stage), you get 261 and 262.

2. Field: TYPE (Action for this Evaluation)  
   • Description  
     – TYPE tags each SAVE record with an action category or code (for example, “DL” for dead load, “WL” for wind load, or a user‐defined alias). This drives how load trains (from POSL, LANE, TRAI records) are interpreted, combined, or superposed.  
   • Unit  
     – Lit4. This means a 4‐character literal string.  
   • Default  
     – “*” (asterisk). If you leave this blank, the program will inherit TYPE from the first load train in the sequence or from previously saved cases if a chain of COMB rules applies.  
   • Contextual notes  
     – In many configurations, TYPE gets auto‐assigned based on the originating load trains’ TYPE fields. You only need to set it explicitly if you wish to override or to tag a combined set of cases under a new category.

3. Field: TITL (Designation of Resulting Load Cases)  
   • Description  
     – TITL provides a human‐readable label for the group of load cases emerging from this SAVE record. It can be a concise description like “Construction Stage Imposed Loads” or an alphanumeric key.  
   • Unit  
     – Lit32. A literal string up to 32 characters.  
   • Default  
     – “–” (dash). If omitted, no title is recorded. Downstream reports will still list the cases numerically but without a custom heading.  
   • Contextual notes  
     – TITL is purely informational. It does not affect the numerical or combinatorial logic of COMB. However, clear TITLs help when you extract summaries or visualize the load‐case tree in postprocessing.

How these fields work together in a SAVE record  
• You declare “SAVE LCB TYPE TITL” once at the start of each group.  
• The system reads CALC records within that SAVE block to pull out individual CASE numbers (between LMIN and LMAX).  
• It applies the optional COMB superposition rules next (if present) to create combined scenarios.  
• Finally, it writes out new, unique load‐case IDs by adding LCB to each base CASE, tags them with TYPE, and annotates them with TITL.  

Example workflows  
1. “SAVE 200 CRN ‘Crane Loads, Erection’”:  
   – CALC yields 11, 12 → plus LCB(200) → produces 211, 212 → labeled CRN → titled “Crane Loads, Erection.”  
2. “SAVE 250 * ‘Final Stage Imposed’” (TYPE inherited, no override):  
   – CALC yields 11, 12 → plus 250 → produces 261, 262 → TYPE copied from prior load trains → TITL printed as “Final Stage Imposed.”  

By indexing each load stage with a unique LCB and tagging it with TYPE and TITL, you maintain a clear, hierarchical record of every evaluation and superposition step in your structural‐analysis workflow.

content:
The input table defines two of the fundamental parameters that appear on every “saving case” or “loading case” record used in the RAG system for traffic‐induced bridge loading.  Each row corresponds to one input item; the four columns spell out its name, its semantic role, its data type or unit, and its default when no value is supplied.  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown, followed by an overview of how these parameters fit into the larger loading‐case workflow.  

1. Table Layout  
   • Item (string): the short, fixed keyword by which the parameter is referenced in input files and in downstream modules (POSL, LANE, TRAI, CALC, COMB, etc.).  
   • Description (text): a human‐readable label that explains the parameter’s role in the loading‐case definition.  
   • Unit (type): for numeric parameters, this indicates physical units; for literal inputs it often reads “LIT” (literal). A dash “—” means “no units.”  
   • Default: the value assumed when the user does not explicitly specify it.  

2. Detailed Fields  

  Item: NO  
   • Description: “Evaluation Case”  
   • Unit: — (none)  
   • Default: 1  
   • Semantics: NO is the unique identifier (an integer) of the loading‐case instance.  Each case corresponds to one assignment of load trains, lane placements, residual areas, etc.  It drives loops in the POSL (positioning) and TRAI (train definition) modules, and becomes the index for binding results in COMB (combination) and CALC (calculation) steps.  

  Item: GRP  
   • Description: “Group of Loading”  
   • Unit: LIT (literal)  
   • Default: ALL  
   • Semantics: GRP selects which standardized load‐group profile from EN 1991-2 or DIN Fachbericht will govern the train or distributed‐load pattern.  Its value must be one of the predefined literals:  
     – ALL: include every load component (vertical, horizontal, pedestrian, special vehicles, etc.).  
     – GR0: single vertical wheel loads only (no distributed or residual).  
     – GRU: vertical uniformly distributed loads + residual area.  
     – GR1 … GR5: the major vertical (GR1), horizontal (GR2, variants GR2N/GR2F/GR2L/GR2T/GR20), pedestrian (GR3), LM4/P5 area load (GR4), special LM3 vehicles (GR5).  
     – GR6, GR11 … GR17, GR21 … GR27, GR31: special max-vertical / SW/2 or multi-track combinations from Table 6.6.  

3. Contextual Rules and Workflow  
  • Lane‐clipping: any load train exceeding its assigned lane width is clipped at the lane boundary.  
  • Residual area: for GRU and GR3 the residual (pedestrian/UDL) load applies only to the gap between the defined true traffic path and the nominal lane edges.  Exception: if lane identifier = 0, then the other lanes are left entirely unloaded and no automatic extension of the residual zone occurs.  
  • GR4 special rule: whenever group=GR4, the residual load “walkway” is applied over the entire traffic area, not just between lane edges.  

4. Integration (“See also”)  
  – POSL: positions the train axles within the lane geometry.  
  – LANE: defines lane widths, offsets, and numbering (0,1,2…).  
  – TRAI: generates the axle spacings and wheel loads for the chosen GRP.  
  – CALC: performs section‐force extraction for each loading case.  
  – COMB: applies combination factors to superimpose multiple cases (NO values) and load groups.  

In practice, a user’s input file will list a series of records, one per loading case, each beginning with NO (e.g. “NO = 1”) and specifying GRP (e.g. “GRP = GR2F”).  When omitted, NO defaults to 1 and GRP to ALL.  The downstream modules iterate over all specified NO values, position the corresponding train or distributed loads per GRP, clip them at lane edges, apply residual‐area rules, and feed the result into CALC/COMB for final structural response.

However for lane 0 all other defined lanes will be spared. An automatic extension of the residual area is no longer applied..

The table in question defines two key control parameters—EXCE and EXTR—that govern how rail‐borne loads are placed and shifted across a lane during an evaluation run. Both parameters are literal (string) inputs (Unit = LIT) and have predefined defaults if the user does not override them. Below is a structured breakdown of each item, what it does, the allowed settings, and how it fits into the broader loading and superposition logic described in the surrounding specification.

1. EXCE (Automatic selection of eccentricity)  
   – Purpose: Controls whether the program searches for the most unfavorable lateral (transverse) offset of a load train within the lane. In railway bridge analysis, shifting a train left or right can change torsional and bending responses, so EXCE lets you automate that search or keep the eccentricity fixed.  
   – Allowed values:  
     • AUTO – Activate automatic eccentricity. The program will iterate through the admissible lateral range (defined by lane limits or by any SMIN/SMAX eccentricity inputs) and pick the offset that maximizes the internal forces (usually bending or torsion).  
     • FIX – Deactivate automatic eccentricity. The load train stays centered on the lane axis (or at a user-defined offset if YEX is used), and no lateral search is performed.  
   – Unit: LIT (Literal)  
   – Default: FIX  

   Contextual notes:  
   • For single­lane analyses (lane 0), FIX is typically the default so that no unintended global shift occurs. Historic behavior uses the same EXCE keyword to represent any global eccentricity set via YEX.  
   • When AUTO is used, the eccentricity search is constrained by the lane width and any SMIN/SMAX inputs. If SMIN = SMAX, the search effectively becomes a single position. If DEL is negative, the Newton‐Raphson search is deactivated.  
   • This option is especially important for load cases where torsion or eccentric loading can govern the design—e.g., certain SLW or combined wind‐plus‐train scenarios.

2. EXTR (Selection of load train position)  
   – Purpose: Determines which components of the load train are considered when seeking the most unfavorable longitudinal placement along the influence line. In a typical rail‐bridge analysis, vertical wheels, horizontal buffers, braking gear, etc., each produce their own influence on the structure; EXTR tells the solver whether to consider only the vertical loads or to include every load component in its positioning algorithm.  
   – Allowed values:  
     • VERT – Position the train based solely on vertical (vertical axle) loads. The algorithm maximizes the response to vertical actions only, then applies all other load components at that same longitudinal position.  
     • ALL – Position the train considering all load components (vertical, lateral due to wind/curvature, longitudinal due to traction or braking) simultaneously, looking for the worst‐case superposition.  
   – Unit: LIT (Literal)  
   – Default: ALL  

   Contextual notes:  
   • With ALL selected (the default), the program will place the train at up to four extremes of each influence line (vertical, horizontal, longitudinal) and then iterate to find the global worst combination.  
   • If only vertical effects are critical (for some simple beam checks), VERT can speed up the analysis by ignoring other load effects during the search. Afterwards, all other load components will still be applied at the chosen vertical maximum.  
   • When defining multiple lanes (primary, secondary, synchronized trains), EXTR interacts with POSL superposition factors and may be combined with multiple load‐train definitions (UIC, SSW, etc.) or global factors.

How these parameters fit into the overall workflow:  
– A CASE record is used first to define which load train and/or residual loading is to be applied to a given lane.  
– POSL records follow CASE and specify superposition factors for primary and secondary lanes.  
– The solver automatically searches for the worst longitudinal position within SMIN…SMAX (or across the entire lane if these are not specified), then applies EXCE and EXTR logic in the transverse and component domains, respectively.  
– Lanes without an associated load train remain unloaded. If independent movement or unsynchronized trains are required, separate lanes and possibly SYNC OFF definitions must be used.  
– Special inputs (YEX, SMIN/SMAX/DEL) can further refine eccentricity and longitudinal search behavior; EXCE and EXTR then act on the results of those intervals.

sections: 3.22 POSL – Position of the Load Trains for an evaluation

content:

 With this record the loading within a lane for an evaluation case is defined. You have to specify at TRAI the load case number of the defined load train and/or the residual loading at P. Load- ings outside of the defined lane width will not be applied. If only a residual loading is defined, the loading is applied to the right and/or the left of the lane axis without any consideration of other zeros in the transverse direction.
 To specify the superposition of the loading for primary and secondary lanes there are now the following possibilities:
 • Usage of different load trains (e.g. UIC and SSW)
 • Definition of global factors in POSL.
 • Definition of factors within the final superposition
 The record CASE must be followed by the corresponding POSL records. Lanes without load train remain unloaded.
 The program places automatically the loading at the most unfavourable position inside the above region. To achieve this, all selected points of the load train are placed at up to four extremes of the influence line. The maximum value of this initial position is used for a detailed iteration. However, the region can be input for special cases. This is the case, if:
 only one single load position should be analyzed. input of SMIN=SMAX, DEL without effect
 •
 the load train can not stand in all positions of the influence line. input of SMIN, SMAX but DEL not defined
 •
 •
 the algorithm does not find the correct extreme positions.
 input of SMIN, SMAX and DEL. If DEL is defined <0.0 the Newton search will be deacti- vated.
 In all other cases it is reasonable not to input any values for SMIN, SMAX, or DEL. Only a single intervall may be used.
 Load trains will be positioned at parallel locations in general. If independently moving trains are required, this needs separate lanes in every case and either separate geometries (eg. AXA.1 and AXB.1) or a special SYNC OFF definition. Variable load distances will then be applied as in the main lane. It should be noted that for the case of favorable contributions of the synchronized load trains, results may be on the unsafe side, especially for a classical load position analysis.
