 For a pure beam system, a transverse shift of the loading during the evaluation might be
 applicable, for FE structures such an eccentric loading will be produce reasonable results only in rare cases. Thus it is strongly recommended to define an own lane for each eccentric loading. For wide heavy load trains YEX may be used to shift the position of the load train, that only parts of the loading which are within the lane limits will be applied, but then a synchronized loading has to be assigned in the adjacent lanes. If there is only a single lane 0, YEX is still used for historical reasons as a global eccentricity for the total load train.
 ELLA tries to find the maximum forces. The influence of wind on the vehicles is considered therefore with a simplified manner: The wind acts always in the most unfavorable direction. The wind on the structure itself is not handled and detailed effects like partial loading (consideration of lee), wind on partial vehicles, coherence or unified wind directions at all parts of the structure are also not considered. However, in some case the wind may be defined with a fixed sign. Thus one may describe a few of these effects.
 In the case of a bow of the lane the masses of the load train, usually calculated from the vertical loads, are used together with the velocity and the curvature of the lane in the plan view for the calculation of the horizontal loads. Depending on the type of the load train, reductions or simplified rules may apply.
 For the eccentricity there are the following effects, which might be influenced by the EXCE value:
 • Any loading may be eccentric within a given range within the lane. Especially for railway loadings this is a very important option to select the most unfavorable eccentricity.
 • A loading may be subdivided in a right and left part based on the torsional effect. For some evaluations (e.g. SLW) a single wheel may become effective in those cases.

The table defines the structure and semantics of a single “COMB” (combination) record used to build intermediate results from up to ten basic evaluation cases in a standards-based structural analysis (for instance, railway bridge load combinations per DS 804).  Each COMB record assembles several previously defined “CASE” load scenarios by specifying which case numbers (or ranges) to include and what factor to apply to each.  If more than ten cases must be combined, multiple COMB records with the TYPE code ‘F’ can be chained.

1. Item = TYPE  
   – Description: Specifies the superposition rule and how this combination acts in the global load envelope.  
   – Possible literal codes (unit = LIT):  
     • G  → permanently acting combination (always “on” in design envelope)  
     • Q  → acting only if it unfavorably increases response (default)  
     • A0…A9 → assign this COMB to alternative group 0–9 (mutually exclusive groupings)  
     • F  → marks this record as an additional extension (used when more than ten cases are needed)  
   – Default: Q

2. Items = L1 … L10  
   – Description: Specifies the “Number/range of evaluation case” to include in the combination.  You may give a single case index (e.g. “3”) or a colon-delimited range (e.g. “2:9”).  Ranges allow internal sorting so that only non-conflicting cases are picked in multi-lane or variant superposition scenarios.  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: – (blank; if omitted, no case is referenced in that slot)

3. Items = F1 … F10  
   – Description: “Factor of an evaluation case” corresponding to the case number/range in L1…L10.  This scaling factor multiplies the effect of each selected case in the combined load result.  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: 1.0  

Key notes on usage:  
• Each Lx must be immediately followed by a corresponding Fx.  If fewer than ten cases are combined, the remaining L/F pairs can be omitted.  
• The default factor of 1.0 means full effect; lower factors (e.g. 0.6 or 0.4) allow partial superposition of less-critical cases.  
• Alternative groups (A0…A9) let you define sets of mutually exclusive combinations—only the worst (or the most unfavorable) result from within a group is carried forward.  
• For very complex load patterns (e.g., combining multiple train types on multiple tracks), you can stack COMB records: the first uses TYPE = A0 (or A1, …) with up to ten cases; a second COMB with TYPE = F includes another ten, and so on.  
• The table’s literal codes and default values ensure that, unless overridden, each new COMB is treated as an unfavorable-only combination (Q) that picks up referenced cases at full intensity.

Example snippet (as illustrated in the context text):  
  COMB A0 L1 1:3 F1 1.00 L2 1:3 F2 1.00  $ ANY TWO TRACKS WITH UIC  
  COMB A0 L1 1    F1 0.71 L2 2    F2 0.71 L3 3 F3 0.71  $ THREE TRACKS @ 71%  
  …  
In a typical workflow, after all basic “CASE” entries are evaluated, these COMB records define how to pool and reduce them to produce final envelopes of extreme responses.

See also: SAVE, CASE
 COMB
 F10
 Factor of an evaluation case
 −
 1.0
 The envelope of extreme values is calculated after the end of evaluation of all the evaluating cases. Without COMB definitions each evaluation case is mutually exclusive. However for special cases it is possible to define intermediate results with the COMB record which are then combined with variant superposition conditions.
 Each intermediate result has a superposition rule assigned and is created from up to ten basic evaluation cases with factors. If more than ten cases should be combined, additional records with COMB F may be used for that purpose.
 For the common case that a combination of multiple lanes is required with either different type of load trains or with different global factors, an internal sorting may be performed by specifying a range of case numbers "cmin:cmax". In that case only loadings are considered not having loads in any already loaded lane.
 Examples:
 COMB A0 F1 1.0 F2 0.6 F3 0.4 combines any 3 cases such that the most unfavourable will be taken with 100 %, the second with 60 % and the least unfavourable with 40 % COMB A0 L1 1 1.0 2:9 0.6 2:9 0.4 combines case 1 to 100 % with 60 % of the largest of the cases 2 to 9 and 40 % of highest remaining case.
 Example:
 A railway bridge with 3 tracks and 2 spans with 8.00 and 12.00 m length has to be ana- lyzed. According to DS 804 are to be examined:
 2 tracks with UIC 71 100% or 3 tracks with UIC 71 71% or 2 tracks with SW 100% or
 1 track with SSW and 1 track with UIC 71
 The following input is possible for the definition and the superposition of the four combinations based on nine evaluation cases:

2 tracks with UIC 71 100% or 3 tracks with UIC 71 71% or 2 tracks with SW 100% or. 1 track with SSW and 1 track with UIC 71. The following input is possible for the definition and the superposition of the four combinations based on nine evaluation cases:.

The output of an influence line evaluation can become very extensive. Therefore the use of the various ECHO options may be very helpful.

Below is a comprehensive, field-by-field description of the lane-geometry table produced by the “ECHO LINE” command.  This description is intended to guide both human readers and downstream retrieval-augmented-generation (RAG) pipelines when indexing or querying the data.

1. Table Headline Attributes  
   • DY  
     – Definition: “Influence width of the lane.”  
     – Source: Comes from the LSEL record’s width-related parameter.  
     – Usage: Specifies the lateral extent (in meters) over which superelevation, crossfall or other side-effects are interpolated.  
   • DZ  
     – Definition: “Influence height of the lane.”  
     – Source: Comes from the LSEL record’s height-related parameter.  
     – Usage: Indicates the vertical envelope (in meters) used when calculating elevation transitions or banking profiles.  
   • Load distribution  
     – Definition: How traffic or structural loads are apportioned across lanes.  
     – Source: Also drawn from the LSEL record’s third field.  
     – Usage: Guides finite-element or structural analysis modules in assigning axle loads to individual lanes.  

2. Core Data Columns  
   A single table is generated for each lane, with one row per station point.  Each row captures the local state of geometry at that station.  

   • STATION  
     – Field type: Numerical (chainage, in meters).  
     – Description: Identifies the longitudinal position along the lane from a defined origin.  This is the primary key for ordering the data, increasing monotonically.  
     – Role: Used for interpolation of geometry elements and for matching external measurement data (survey offsets, GNSS fixes).  

   • COORDINATES X,Y,Z  
     – Field type: Triplet of real numbers (meters).  
     – Description: Global or project-local Cartesian coordinates of the station.  
     – Usage:  
       • X, Y: Planimetric position (easting/northing in a specified projection).  
       • Z: Elevation (height above datum).  
     – Role: Enables 3D reconstruction of the lane centerline, collision detection, and integration with digital terrain models.  

   • SECTION LENGTH  
     – Field type: Real number (meters).  
     – Description: Distance from the current station to the next one in the sequence.  
     – Usage: Indicates segment length for piecewise-linear approximation of curves or clothoids, and for subdivision in simulation or CAD export.  

   • REMARKS  
     – Field type: String/text.  
     – Description: Encodes the local geometry type and associated parameters.  Typical entries include:  
         • “STRAIGHT” or “TANGENT” – no curvature, zero radius  
         • “RADIUS=R” – constant-radius circular arc, where R is in meters  
         • “CLOTHOID IN=Ci OUT=Co” – transition spirals with specified entry/exit lengths  
         • Superelevation flags, crossfall angles or additional notes.  
     – Role: Drives geometry-creation routines in CAD or simulation, instructing them how to transition between elements.  

3. Extended Neighbor Information (ECHO LINE FULL)  
   When you run “ECHO LINE FULL” instead of the default:  
   • Two extra lists are appended to each lane’s table header:  
       – Left-hand neighboring nodes (IDs of adjacent lanes on the left side).  
       – Right-hand neighboring nodes (IDs of adjacent lanes on the right side).  
   • Purpose: Supports network topology queries (e.g., “Which lane do I enter when I exit this one?”), routing algorithms, and conflict‐detection modules.  

4. Use in RAG Vector Stores  
   • Each row can be indexed by STATION for time-series-style queries.  
   • The COORDINATES field may be embedded into a spatial index for nearest-neighbor searches.  
   • DY, DZ, and Load distribution in the header serve as high-level metadata to filter lanes by width or load-capacity.  
   • REMARKS text fields can be vectorized for semantic similarity searches (e.g., find all clothoid transitions).  

This structured description ensures that every attribute—whether numeric, textual, or topological—is clearly documented, enabling reliable ingestion into a RAG workflow or other engineering databases.

The geometry of the lanes can be controlled with ECHO LINE. The default output results in a table for each lane with the following information in its headline:
 DY Influence width of the lane, see record LSEL DZ Influence height of the lane, see record LSEL Load distribution, see record LSEL
 The table contains the following columns:
 Data for geometry, radius, clothoidal etc.
 With ECHO LINE FULL one obtains a list of the neighbouring nodes at the left-hand side and to the right-hand side of the lane.

Influence lines can be represented and printed graphically. However, an output occurs only, if the lines have been selected with SHOW, and ECHO IL has not been set equal to NO. The graphical output is obtained only by using the record SIZE, whilst the output in the form of tables is obtained with ECHO IL FULL.
 The table of the influence lines contains in its headline the application point of the unit load and the scalar variable. The columns are as follows:
 X-VALUE X coordinate measured at the lane axis, beginning with 0.000 m PV-VALUE Influence line value for vertical loading verse wheel loadings MS-VALUE Influence line value for torsional loading PS-VALUE Influence line value for longitudinal loading (brake load) PQ-VALUE Influence line value for lateral loading
 at the lane axis resp. the mean value for two trans-
 (wind, centrifugal force) dPV/ds First derivative of the influence line values PV (corresponds to IL for -M loading) p+,p- for INT>2 r+,r- residual areas for INT>2
 Integrals of positive and negative influence values
 Integrals of influence values in the right and left
 Influence lines are plotted with a predetermined scale in the longitudinal direction and with a scale for the influence line values, which is determined by the height of the drawing bands. Maximum and minimum values are printed at the plot.
 For the graphics of the transverse influence line, the sum of the influence values of the the two wheels of the axle (Pv) and the integrals of the positive (p+) and negative (p-) influence values are also given. The values r+ and r- are the integrals of the residual areas outside the traffic lane.

The table in question is the program’s internal representation of all defined “load trains” (i.e. user- or library-defined load cases), printed whenever the ECHO TYPL setting is YES or FULL.  It brings together each load’s geometric, intensity and dynamic parameters in a compact, columnar form.  Below is a breakdown of its structure and meaning, together with the companion “dynamic factors and lane widths” table that follows:

1. Main Load Table  
   • TYPE  
     – A short alphanumeric code identifying the load definition (e.g. “TR1”, “ULS2”, etc.).  
   • Load type  
     – A plain-language description of the load configuration (“Point load,” “Distributed load with variable value,” etc.).  
   • D (sometimes shown under heading “Point load”)  
     – The design magnitude of a concentrated (point) load, in force units.  
   • E  
     – The “dynamic” version of the point load: i.e. the same concentrated force multiplied by any dynamic amplification factor(s).  
   • E-0  
     – The static (undynamic) equivalent of the point load.  If you wish to suppress all printed detail of generated loadings, you set “ECHO TYPL NO”; at FULL or YES these columns appear.  
   • G  
     – If the load type is a distributed load, “G” is the intensity of that load, typically in force per unit length.  
   • HF  
     – “Height of the Gravity‐centre for centrifugal forces.”  This is the vertical distance from the reference plane to the resultant of any lateral or rotating masses (used in curved or accelerated moving loads).  
   • LDEL  
     – When the load length is variable rather than fixed, the program prints a second line for that load containing up to three values:  
       • The minimum length over which the load can be applied (LMIN)  
       • The maximum length (LMAX)  
       • A suggested subdivision or “delta‐length” increment (LDEL) if intermediate analyses are required.  

   In fixed‐length cases, LMIN = LMAX and LDEL is not used, so only one line appears.  In variable‐length cases, two lines appear: the first shows E, G, HF etc. at the nominal length; the second shows [LMIN, LMAX, LDEL] under the LDEL heading to indicate the feasible range and step size.

2. Dynamic Factors & Lane Boundaries Table  
   Immediately following the load table, a supplementary block lists each load’s dynamic and lane‐position parameters, column-by-column:  
   • STARTING  
     – The first station (chainage) at which this load may commence.  
   • ENDING  
     – The second station (chainage) where it may terminate.  
   • PHIB  
     – Dynamic factor for unfavourable bending (bending moment amplification).  
   • PHI2  
     – Dynamic factor for favourable bending (moment reduction).  
   • PHIS  
     – Dynamic factor for unfavourable shear (shear force amplification).  
   • PHI4  
     – Dynamic factor for favourable shear (shear reduction).  
   • LPHI  
     – “Determinant length” used when calculating the influence of dynamic amplification over a finite span.  
   • YRA, YLA  
     – Lane boundary offsets at the right (YRA) and left (YLA) of the first station (STARTING).  
   • YRE, YLE  
     – Lane boundary offsets to the right (YRE) and left (YLE) of the second station (ENDING).  

Together, these two tables fully describe each load train’s application zone, intensity (static and dynamic), distribution, height of action, and permissible lateral positioning on the structure.  Users and downstream routines can rely on this standardized printout for verification, for exporting into a RAG-style vector database, or for automated post-processing (design checks, combination generation, etc.).

The load trains are described in plain text with their parameters. The output of the corre- sponding table can be suppressed with ECHO TYPL NO; with ECHO TYPL FULL the table is expanded in order to show the generated loadings. This table is also printed for user defined loadings by entering ECHO TYPL YES.
 This table contains the following columns:
 TYPE
 Load type
 Point load
 E
 E-0 Point load without dynamic factor
 Distributed load with variable value
 HF
 Height of the gravity centre for centrifugal
 forces
 For loads with variable length the output of a second line with the maximum and the minimum length and a possible subdivision length value in the column LDEL follows.
 The dynamic factors and the lane widths are output in an additional table. The parameters therein mean:
 STARTING
 first station value
 lane boundary to the right of second station
 lane boundary to the left of second station

A table of the superposition combinations always appears when such combinations have been defined. A single line is printed for each combination containing its type as well as the partici- pated evaluation cases with their factors.

The evaluation results are controlled by the two ECHO options EVAL and RES.
 When one of these two options is active, a line which contains the identification of the position is printed for each position with corresponding influence lines.
 As long as EVAL is active, the position of the load train as well as the possible convoy distances or the variable lengths are output in a succeeding table.
 If EVAL is set to FULL, the regions with different signs are printed then for each evaluation case and for each lane together with the applied dynamic factors PHI1/PHI2 for unfavourably/- favourably acting loading and the positions of extreme values.
 If RES is active, the extreme values of the internal forces or other parameters are output in an additional table. The first columns contain the number, with which the load case has to be stored, and a text for the designation the evaluation rule.

If the ECHO option STAT is used, one receives an output which shows the used CPU time and the up to now needed memory allocation at the screen or in the logfile for each part of the program. These values are important, in order to allow an estimation of the memory and the CPU time requirements for larger examples.
